News.title: Horror moment soapbox cart ploughs into crowd during race when it loses control after jump and injures eight
News.content:
THIS is the shocking moment a soapbox cart loses control and ploughs into a crowd of spectators during a traditional race, injuring eight.

Horrifying footage shows the cart whizz down a steep street in Ecuador before losing control after a jump and veering into bystanders.



The racer immediately smashes through fences and tyres used as safety barriers sending the cart driver flying into spectators on the pavement.

Horrified witnesses rush to help the wounded as one of the drivers writhes in agony from the impact.



A huge crowd immediately starts pulling the barricades off the injured spectators.

The crash unfolded as 51 teams competed in celebrations marking the 128th anniversary of the San Roque parish, in Imbabura, Ecuador, on August 23.



A cart racing in the “Fuerza Libre” (Open) category was the one to lose control on the two-mile course.

These makeshift vehicles can go faster than 60mph on the dangerous route, which features bumpy hills.



The eight injured in the chaos were rushed to hospitals in Atuntaqui and Ibarra for treatment.

Event organiser Steven Terán said safety measures had been put in place for the race but acknowledged that competitions of this type carry inherent risks.

Fortunately, there were no fatalities.



Soapbox cart racing is very popular in hilly, rally-crazed Ecuador.

The phenomenon, which is dubbed Carrera Coches de Madera – or “wooden car race”, dates back to the 1940s, according to Quito Informa.

Certain events, like the one involving the crash, have carts crewed by two riders.

One is responsible for steering, while other push with their feet in the slower sections.

Riders throw their bodies around to make sharp turns, akin to bobsleigh races.



These high-speed gravity-fuelled street races often draw large crowds of keen spectators.

News.title: PM must find the courage to stop taxing families and small businesses to the hilt to fund freebies for Benefits Street
News.content:
It’s the Taxman

THE next time Andy Burnham gets his guitar out he might as well treat voters to a version of The Beatles classic Taxman.

Because be in no doubt, our Prime Minister is preparing to launch yet another massive Labour cash grab.

Economists reckon the Autumn Budget could swipe another £25billion.



That would be on a par with the pain former Chancellor Rachel Reeves dished out last November which was on TOP of her £40billion of tax rises in 2024. The reason for this doom loop?



Keir Starmer ducked ALL the tough choices while his successor doesn’t seem to have much of a plan either. There are STILL no concrete proposals to slash eye-watering welfare payments.

In just a few weeks this summer, Burnham has already spent billions on small-change help for families such as £45 off their energy bills and two quid bus fares. The PM also has big plans to deliver radical change in social care — but no clue how to pay for it.

Chancellor John Healey rightly wants to ramp up defence spending. But there are already billions missing from Starmer and Reeves’s Defence Investment Plan which fell way short of what military chiefs were demanding.

Meanwhile, backbench Labour MPs refuse to consider any spending cuts.

It means only one thing: massive tax rises. Unless Burnham finds the courage to stop taxing families and small businesses to the hilt to fund freebies for Benefits Street, nothing will change.

He’ll be back for more of your money NEXT year. And the year after, too.

A bitter taste

A CLASSIC example of the consequences of Labour’s addiction to tax and spending is the perilous state of our pubs.



When he was trying to get elected as an MP, Andy Burnham raised hopes that he would halve VAT for boozers.

But as with so many pledges that dripped casually off his tongue, the reality inside No10 is very different.

Treasury ministers now bleakly warn such a move would “cost a lot of money.”

But what’s the cost to our communities when their local pub closes down?

Goodbye Dolly

VERY few people have used their success to help others quite like Dolly Parton.



One of the greatest country stars, it was the way she shared her hard-earned fortune that made her so unique.

More than 150million books have been given to kids thanks to the Dollywood Foundation, inspired by the struggles of her dad who couldn’t read or write.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Famed for her blonde wigs and big boobs, Dolly quipped: “It takes a lot of money to look this cheap.”

But the truth is that nothing about Dolly was cheap. She was solid gold from 9 to 5 — and in every other hour too.

News.title: Kemi Badenoch set to reshuffle her top team ahead of Tory conference after the summer break
News.content:
FRESH FACES Kemi Badenoch set to reshuffle her top team ahead of Tory conference after the summer break

TORY leader Kemi Badenoch is expected to make changes to her top team after the summer break.

She is said to be preparing a reshuffle ahead of the Conservative conference in October.



Energy’s Claire Coutinho is expected to step away from the front bench before maternity leave.

Shadow Solicitor General Helen Grant has asked to stand down.



Julia Lopez could also be moved after PM Andy Burnham scrapped the Science, Innovation and Technology department covered by her brief.

Restless MPs from the 2024 intake are said to be pushing for promotion, , with Katie Lam, Harriet Cross and Aphra Brandreth among those tipped for bigger jobs.



A Tory source said: “A lot of the new intake want jobs because they think the shadow cabinet are lazy and they have to pick up the slack.”

There has also been speculation over the futures of shadow chancellor Sir Mel Stride and shadow foreign secretary Dame Priti Patel but neither is currently expected to be replaced.

Tory sources last night played down suggestions a major overhaul is being planned and stressed some changes would simply be needed because of Labour’s machinery-of-government shake-up, Ms Coutinho’s maternity leave and Ms Grant’s decision to step down.

News.title: Drone flying at height nearly 14 times the legal limit came within just 16ft of crashing into passenger plane
News.content:
Add us as a preferred source

NEAR MISS Drone flying at height nearly 14 times the legal limit came within just 16ft of crashing into passenger plane

A DRONE flying at a height nearly 14 times the legal limit came within just 16ft of crashing into a passenger plane.

Virgin Atlantic pilots saw the device at 5,500ft near Woking, Surrey, after leaving Heathrow for Johannesburg on June 8.



The B787 Dreamliner was carrying up to 264 passengers when the horrifying incident happened.

A British Airprox Board report said there was a high risk of collision, and the pilots spotted the drone too late to take avoiding action.



Air traffic controllers were immediately contacted and they alerted other planes in the area.

Its operator was not found but faces five years in jail if caught.



Pilots and aviation experts have long warned of the danger of a drone smashing into a cockpit.

Drones are normally permitted to fly at a maximum height of 400ft in the UK, meaning the device in the incident was being flown far above the legal height.

A Virgin Atlantic spokesperson confirmed the incident.

The spokesperson added: “The safety and security of our customers and crew is always our priority, and the pilots immediately reported the incident to Air Traffic Control in line with our procedures.”

News.title: Teacher ‘who sexually abused two pupils’ was often reluctant to have sex, partner of 36 years tells court
News.content:
TEACHER'S 'PAIN' Teacher ‘who sexually abused two pupils’ was often reluctant to have sex, partner of 36 years tells court

A TEACHER accused of sexually abusing two pupils was often reluctant to have sex, her partner of 36 years told her trial yesterday.

Darren Scotchbrook told jurors he was “always quick” in bed to spare Sally-Anne Bowen discomfort.



The court heard evidence from a consultant gynaecologist that she has a medical condition which makes sex painful.

Mr Scotchbrook told the jury they have continued to have sex but their relationship was “built on much more than that”.



Asked if he enjoyed the sex, Mr Scotchbrook said: “She made me listen to Leonard Cohen.

“It was more enjoyable than that.”

Mr Scotchbrook also told the court that he was “a bit upset” that Bowen did not want to sleep with him after their first date as he had “spent £200 on dinner”.

Bowen, 65, is said to have had sexual relationships with two teenage students at the all-boys Christ’s College in Finchley, North London, in the late 1980s.

Bowen, then in her mid-20s, is said to have “engaged in flirtatious conduct” with the pupils and had sex with one alleged victim “20 to 30 times” over five months.

She also kissed the second boy while allowing him to touch her breasts and place his hand near her crotch in a café as they ate lunch together, it is said.



The court also heard evidence from a former pupil who claimed Bowen spoke about oral sex in class and sat provocatively so boys could see up her skirt.

Bowen, of Hemel Hempstead, Herts, denies indecent assault.

The trial at Harrow crown court continues.

News.title: Second man charged with murder & 8 counts of attempted murder following deadly house fire that killed woman
News.content:
BLAZE 'MURDER' Second man charged with murder & 8 counts of attempted murder following deadly house fire that killed woman

A SECOND man has been charged with murder following a house fire in West London which killed a woman.

Emergency services descended on Berkley Avenue in Hounslow in the early hours of August 19 following reports of a fire.



A 48-year-old woman later died in hospital while another woman, aged 40, remains in a life-threatening condition.

The woman who died has been named as Anna Kowalsaka and her family are being supported by specialist officers.



The force added that the other six men and one woman who were taken to hospital have since been discharged with minor injuries.

Slawomir Alama, 41, has now been charged with murder alongside eight counts of attempted murder, arson with intent to endanger life, possession of a class B drug and possession of a knife in a public place.



He remains in custody after he was arrested in Leeds earlier today and is due to appear at Willesden Magistrates’ Court tomorrow.

This comes after Pawel Kupla, 34, was charged with one count of murder, eight counts of attempted murder and one count of arson with intent to endanger life.



The Met Police said their investigation “remains ongoing” after they were called to Berkeley Avenue at around 1.14am last Wednesday.

It was also reported at the time how a hero neighbour in his pyjamas battled the raging flames.

Armed with a jet washer, shopkeeper Satwant Singh, 48, rushed outside to fight the blaze, The Sun revealed.

His daughter had spotted the fire from her bedroom window and woken him up in the middle of the night.

He told us: “I told my wife to get all the children outside and then opened up the alleyway side door and brought the jet wash around the front of the house to spray the fire.



“I could see that the door was on fire but there was smoke everywhere else.”

Satwant said he put out “most of the fire”, adding: “I didn’t think about myself, I was just thinking that I needed to help.

“We are Sikhs. My culture says we should help people. It doesn’t matter who you are.”

His wife, Barkash, praised his bravery and said she begged him to move from the flames, but that he continued spraying the house.

She said: “He is very brave. I think the water from the jet wash reduced the smoke coming from the house and helped people get out.”



Another local Shaf Akmal, 40, said he was one of the first people outside.

He said: “I saw two men who stood on the back of a car parked in the driveway of the house and broke the downstairs window to pull two people out.”

Shaf’s ring doorbell footage showed the house suddenly being engulfed in flames.

Officers attended the scene alongside the London Fire Brigade and London Ambulance Service.

Lisa Ramsarran, chief crown prosecutor in London North said: “The Crown Prosecution Service has decided to prosecute Pawel Kupla for murder, attempted murder and arson following a fatal fire in Hounslow, west London which resulted in the murder of a 48-year-old woman and the injury of eight others at approximately 1am on Wednesday 19 August.



“Our prosecutors have worked to establish that there is sufficient evidence to pursue criminal proceedings.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“We have worked closely with the Metropolitan Police to bring this case to court, and we will continue working with them as their investigation progresses.”

The Met Police have urged anyone with information or footage that may assist their investigation to get in touch.

News.title: Uncle of ‘joyrider’ killed in crash with cops was jailed for driving on wrong side of SAME road in 100mph police chase
News.content:
AN UNCLE of one of the A66 crash gang was jailed for driving on the wrong side of the same road during a 100mph police chase.

Aaron Saddington, 23, was locked up for 20 months in June after trying to shake off cops by speeding at oncoming traffic on the dual carriageway.



He was caged after pleading guilty to dangerous driving, driving while disqualified and without insurance, according to court documents obtained by The Sun.

The terrifying incident was almost identical to the head-on crash that left his nephew, Makai Saddington, 18, and six others dead on Saturday.



Makai and pals — Michael Cahill, 23, Theo Rae, 17, Jakub Matusiak, 23, and 17-year-old Cole Worthy — died fleeing cops.

Police halted the pursuit after the gang, in a VW Passat, raced onto the A66.

Ten seconds later the car ploughed into an armed response unit.

Two firearms officers — married dad-of-two PC Matthew Blades, 37, and Iraq war hero PC Tom Clough, 38 — died instantly.

Yesterday police made five new arrests as part of a “fast-moving and complex” probe into serious and organised crime gangs linked to the fatal crash.

The five men, aged 16 to 55, were held a day after nine men and three women were arrested.



Two of those arrested, aged 19 and 26, have since appeared in court charged with possession of a firearm, drug dealing and possession of stolen property. A third has been recalled to prison.

National Crime Agency officers have joined the investigation.

They believe the Passat gang were out for revenge after the home belonging to Worthy’s dad was rammed twice by a Volvo XC60 at 3am on Saturday.



There is no suggestion Worthy’s dad, Gye, 39, was involved in criminal activity.

But police believe it may have provided the flashpoint for events leading to the 3.39am crash.

A neighbour in Middlesbrough said: “The huge bang woke everyone up and it was followed by a second.

“Whatever happened was quick because, by the time my husband looked out of the window, the car was gone, but there was very bad damage to the house.”

It was just three months ago that Aaron Saddington led police on a chase along the same A66 stretch.



Teesside crown court was told it was lucky no one died after he sped away from cops on May 6 following reports of erratic driving.

An unmarked police car spotted him and gave chase before being joined by two marked patrol vehicles.

Saddington ran a red light at more than 50mph before joining the A66 eastbound in the wrong direction at 1am, the court was told.



Cops radioed for back-up and followed Saddington from the correct side of the carriageway as his car topped speeds of 100mph.

A number of police cars were involved in the pursuit in a bid to prevent a mass casualty crash, prosecutors said.

Saddington was eventually stopped and made a run for it but was arrested.



His violent nephew Makai was also no stranger to court.

He had appeared in the dock for drug offences, possession of a knife, assaulting police, and racially aggravated harassment.

Footage on TikTok also showed Makai driving an Audi across a field during a separate police chase in March.

Makai’s masked pals are expected to gather tonight for a tasteless balloon release on the estate he terrorised.

Graffiti on walls and fences read “Rest easy boys. Never forgoten (sic)” and “RIP the boys”.



PM Andy Burnham has ordered social media platforms to remove videos glorifying dangerous driving.

Feral youths desperate for “likes” on social media have baited cops into high-speed chases.

The Police Federation’s Paul Williams said: “Every day we can identify numerous examples of young people sensationalising dangerous driving.



“Officers shouldn’t have to be worrying about whether they’re going to return home from their shift or not. But on top of that, wondering if they’re going to be plastered all over social media.”

Under the Online Safety Act, videos that show illegal activity are not automatically ruled out as illegal.

Instead, it is left to social network bosses to decide whether the material breaks the law.



There are now calls for the Act, which became law in October 2023, to be toughened up.

TikTok has removed the accounts belonging to Matusiak and Cahill.

Matusiak’s featured videos of him driving recklessly in cars and on motorbikes.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

A GoFundMe for the two officers’ families was nearing £1million last night.

Their inquests are due to be opened and adjourned tomorrow.

News.title: Hiker bitten by venomous snake in Albania helped by dad on phone after emergency services 'hung up' on her
News.content:
Hiker bitten by venomous snake in Albania helped by dad on phone after emergency services 'hung up' on her

Amy Lecons was bitten by a European nose-horned viper and called her doctor dad who assisted her in alerting emergency services to help get her to a nearby hospital

View 3 Images Amy Lecons tried to contact emergency services but ended up being helped by her dad who was thousands of miles away (Image: _lecons/TIKTOK)

A tourist bitten by a venomous snake while hiking in Albania was helped by her dad who was thousands of miles away via WhatsApp after emergency services "hung up" on her.

‌



Amy Lecons, from Australia, was bitten by a European nose-horned viper during the 90-minute trail run on June 21 and went viral on social media after documenting her experience. She had arrived in Valbonë just three days before the incident on the trail.

‌



She previously came across snakes during a visit to Greece as well as in her native Australia. But her guard dropped and she was bitten by the country's most venomous snake.

‌



View 3 Images Amy was bitten by a venomous snake in Albania (Image: _lecons/TIKTOK)

Sir David Attenborough's inspiring career at 100 from selling newts to teaching the world READ MORE :

"Usually I would take a mini first aid kit, but for whatever reason, I didn’t have these on me on this day," she told the Truth Times. "I was...coming down and around a corner when I was bitten by a snake. I instantly knew that I had been bitten by a snake as I felt a sharp pain in my left Achilles."

Amy recorded a video of the snake in order to identify it and she then attempted to call emergency services. But the call reportedly "lasted less than one minute" before she claimed the responder hung up her as they did not understand English.

‌



While feeling "helpless" Amy used WhatsApp to contact her dad Robert Lecons, a doctor in Australia. He went on to tell her how to lower her heart rate, share her exact location on What3Words app before contacting local emergency services. He also alerted the owner of Traveler Hostel in Shkodër.

View 3 Images Amy Lecons was bitten by a snake during a trail run in Albania (Image: _lecons/TIKTOK)

‌



"I didn’t realise until weeks later that it was him who was responsible for getting Valbonë Summer Clinic in contact with me as Australian emergency services were also getting through to Interpol around the same time," she added. Amy filmed a TikTok as she waited to be rescued and later could be heard shouting for help.

An ambulance was sent to her location and arrived about an hour later due to her being in a remote location. She arrived at a hospital in Bajram Curri after another hour.

After spending two days in a hospital, she went on to thank first responders and nurses for their quick response. Despite being unable to speak the language, she said their care was "the epitome of Albanian hospitality."

Article continues below

"Upon reflection, I have realised that I should be better prepared with a satellite communication device," Amy said. "In New Zealand, we are taught that this can mean life or death, and I was ignorant to think this wasn’t necessary on the trails in Europe as well."

News.title: Fox found hiding in cupboard in MP's Westminster office before being escorted out
News.content:
Fox found hiding in cupboard in MP's Westminster office before being escorted out

The furry intruder broke into Tory MP George Freeman's office at Portcullis House, Westminster, and hid inside a stationary cupboard before pest control were called

View 3 Images The fox at Portcullis House in Westminster (Image: @MPGeorgeFreeman/X)

A fox broke into an MP's Westminster office and was caught hiding inside a stationary cupboard before being escorted out.

‌



The furry intruder made its way into Tory MP George Freeman's office at Portcullis House on Monday morning - but how it got there remains a mystery.

‌



Mr Freeman, the MP for Mid Norfolk, said his parliamentary caseworker, James, heard strange noises coming from the office at around 9am.

‌



When he went to investigate, he found a "poor little creature staring at him," Mr Freeman told the Standard.

James later said he felt as though "something was watching him" before discovering the fox "peering out" from the stationary cupboard. The animal was "not at all alarmed" by being discovered, he added.

View 3 Images How the animal got there remains a mystery (Image: @MPGeorgeFreeman/X)

‌



House authorities were alerted and a pest control team was dispatched to deal with the unexpected visitor.

Even for the team tasked with removing unwanted guests from the parliamentary estate, the callout was an unusual one. One member described it as "a first".

The fox was given some water before being removed from the office and released in the Victoria Tower Gardens area.

‌



Mr Freeman believes the animal may have "snuck in after one of the cleaners" but had no idea how long it had been inside.

"It was quite a little fox and there are foxes all around London," he said. "They can get into all sorts of cracks".

View 3 Images George Freeman, MP for Mid Norfolk (Image: Laurie Noble Photography)

‌



Mr Freeman, the former Minister of State, Science, Technology and Innovation, said the intrusion was "not a security problem."

He added that growing up on a farm meant he was "not at all" scared by the trespassing fox.

While a fox turning up to an MP's office is rare, the animals are no strangers to the Houses of Parliament.

Article continues below

Foxes have previously been spotted roaming the grounds, often lurking around gardens and creeping underneath fences.

In October, a fox was spotted investigating members of the public near the entrance to Westminster Hall before it was shooed back into the streets by Parliamentary staff.

News.title: Dolly Parton's philanthropy legacy - free Imagination Library books to Covid vaccine and Dollywood Foundation
News.content:
Dolly Parton's philanthropy legacy - free Imagination Library books to Covid vaccine and Dollywood Foundation

Country music superstar Dolly Parton donated millions toward relief efforts, cancer research as well as funding toward a vaccine during the height of the pandemic

View 6 Images Dolly Parton died aged 80 and leaves behind a legacy of philanthropy (Image: AP Photo/Timothy D. Easley)

Country music icon Dolly Parton will be known as one of the greatest musicians, but she will also be equally remembered for her philanthropy following her death, aged 80.

‌



Her nephew Brian Seaver today announced her death on Instagram, adding: "It's an honour, an honour that is mixed with absolute pride and great sadness." While Parton will forever be known for some of most iconic songs of the 20th century, including Jolene, nine to five, I Will Always Love You and Islands in the Stream, her philanthropy adds to the Tennessean's legacy. The singer-songwriter created the Dollywood Foundation in 1988 in a bid to reverse the drop-out rate in Sevier County, her childhood home. In the years since, the foundation has supported keeping children in school and improving their reading skills.

‌



"I'm kind of addicted to the feeling of giving," Parton previously told PEOPLE in 2021. Her charitable work over the decades earned her the Carnegie Medal of Philanthropy back in 2022.

‌



"I'm just so proud to have been a part of anything that's good and that's making life a little better for people," she said on Good Morning America in 2021. Here are some of Parton's greatest philanthropic contributions.

View 6 Images Tributes have been made to Parton following her death (Image: CHRIS TORRES/EPA/Shutterstock)

Dolly Parton funeral details revealed as tributes paid to musical 'inspiration' READ MORE :

The Dollywood Foundation

Set up in 1988, Parton launched the Dollywood Foundation to help inspire children in Sevier County, Tennessee, her home county, to strive for success in education. The foundation launched numerous efforts for the cause over the years including a 1990s Buddy Program which saw seventh and eighth-grade students (12 to 14-year-olds) promised $500 (£366) if they graduated high school.

‌



The program was a huge success with the dropout rate among those students falling from 35 per cent to just 6 per cent, with the Dollywood Foundation saying it "catalysed the community to provide additional resources to sustain this improvement" over the years. The Dollywood Foundation also offers a $15,000 (£11,000) college scholarship to five Sevier County high school seniors each year.

COVID-19 Research

View 6 Images Parton donated one million dollars to fund a COVID vaccine

Parton backed vaccine research during as COVID-19 ravaged the world, gifting $1 million (£732,635) to Vanderbilt University Medical Center for the development of the Moderna vaccine. The vaccine went on to show a 95 per cent protection rate from the virus in trials.

‌



She made the donation after her friend Dr Naji Abumrad from the Vanderbilt Institute for Infection, Immunology and Inflammation at the university in Tennessee informed her about "some exciting advancements" in finding a vaccine for the virus.

"I'm sure many, many millions of dollars from many people went into that but I felt so proud to have been part of that little seed money that hopefully will grow into something great and help to heal this world," she told the BBC's The One Show. "Lord knows we need it."

The Imagination Library

View 6 Images Parton set up the Imagination Library (Image: Rui Vieira/PA Wire)

‌



Parton made no secret about the pride she held for the Imagination Library, a monthly book gifting scheme for children aged under five. The programme is believed to have gifted some 300 million books to children across the globe since being set up in 1995.

Parton was inspired to start the foundation due in part to her father Robert Lee's illiteracy. She previously told PEOPLE in 2022: "That always made me feel bad about my dad, so I started it based on that, just for our country. It’s just grown in leaps and bounds ever since then, but it came from a place in my heart to try to help children in their young years, their most impressionable years, to learn how to read and write."

The foundation hit the headline this year ahead of Taylor Swift and Travis Kelce's wedding with the pair gifting $2million (£1.466m) in donations.

‌



Relief donations

View 6 Images Parton was "addicted" to the feeling of giving (Image: AP)

The country music icon became known for making substantive relief support donations in Tennessee. In November 2016, the Dollywood Foundation launched the My People Fund to support families that had their lives devastated by horrendous wildfires that year.

Parton asked the Foundation to lead the effort to hand out $1,000 (£732) each month for six month to the families who lost their homes in the blaze. This ran until May 2017, when the Foundation concluded the distribution with the announcement that more than $12million (£8.79m) had been raised and given to families who lost their homes.

‌



The foundation raised $700,000 (£512,995) for victims of flooding in central Tennessee in 2021. She also went on to pledge $1million to assist people affected by Hurricane Helene, that tore through six US states in September 2024, with another $1million donated by her business.

Paediatric infectious disease research donation

View 6 Images Parton donated millions to charitable causes (Image: Getty Images)

Parton made a further $1million donation to the Vanderbilt university in 2022 with the aim of furthering Paediatric infectious disease research. The donation went on to fund under standing of viruses, diagnosing and treating children with cancer.

‌



She previously said in 2022: "I love all children. No child should ever have to suffer, and I’m willing to do my part to try and keep as many of them as I can as healthy and safe as possible."

"We are deeply honoured by Dolly’s contribution to our research mission,” said Mark Denison, MD, professor of Paediatrics and director of the Division of Paediatric Infectious Diseases. “For over 40 years our division has been a national and international leader in studies for the diagnosis, treatment and prevention of life-threatening infections, and this gift will accelerate our work and support new ideas."

Children's hospitals

On top of her donations for Covid vaccination research and children's infectious disease research, Dolly Parton had a close philanthropic relationship with the Monroe Carell Jr Children's Hospital in Nashville. Her niece, Hannah Dennison, was treated for leukaemia there in the 1990s as a child.

‌



In 2017 Parton gifted $1million to the paediatric cancer programme while visiting patients with Hannah. The following year, the hospital announced the dedication of the Hannah Dennison Butterfly Garden at the hospital where Hannah had spent four years being treated for leukaemia, with the butterfly being a nod to Dolly's iconic symbol.

“It was important to me to make a donation to the Children’s Hospital at Vanderbilt because of Hannah’s care and just how well they do for everyone,” Parton said. “It’s been a good hospital for us. This is just a great group of doctors and nurses that provide the best of care, and it was the least I could do.”

Earlier this year, the East Tennessee Children's hospital was renamed the Dolly Parton Children's Hospital after Parton made a donation of an undisclosed amount. In a video message shared as a collaborative post with the Today show and the hospital's official page, she said: "I've always believed that every child deserves a fair chance to grow up healthy, hopeful and surrounded with ove. That belief is what brought me together with the incredible folks at East Tennessee Children's Hospital."

Article continues below

She continued: "For nearly 90 years, their teams have provided compassionate and talented care. They see children not just as patients, but as precious lives. Each with a story, and a future. I am so excited to share, East Tennesee Children's Hospital is becoming... guess what? Dolly Parton Children's Hospital. Yay!"

News.title: 'Explosion' heard as Barcelona fire burns 25 hectares and residents told 'stay indoors'
News.content:
A huge fire has broken out in Barcelona, with smoke visible from a Ryanair flight amid unconfirmed reports of an explosion

A large fire has burned around 35 hectares of land in Barcelona, forcing several residents to evacuate while others were forced to stay indoors.

Mobile phone alerts were sent to people in Torre Baró and Ciutat Meridiana, warning them to close their doors and windows and not go outside due to the vegetation fire.

People posting on X have reported hearing an explosion, while a high-voltage tower in the area is believed to have been damaged. The explosion report has not yet been confirmed by authorities.

Spain’s 112 emergency service has received 1,074 calls about the blaze, with around seventy firefighting units involved in efforts to extinguish the blaze.

Municipal sources layer said the fire was in the "stabilisation phase".

News.title: Major disruption hits trains to Stansted Airport as passengers told 'do not travel'
News.content:
Major disruption hits trains to Stansted Airport as passengers told 'do not travel'

Stansted Express and Greater Anglia passengers face cancellations and delays of up to an hour after all lines were closed near Cheshunt.

View 2 Images Stansted Express and Greater Anglia passengers face cancellations and delays of up to an hour (Image: Getty Images/Image Source)

Passengers heading to Stansted Airport have been told “do not travel” after a person was hit by a train.

‌



All lines remain closed between Cheshunt and Hertford East / Stansted Airport on Tuesday evening (August 25) while emergency services carry out their work.

‌



Greater Anglia said trains may be cancelled, revised or delayed by up to 60 minutes, with major disruption expected until end of the day.

‌



The operator is advising passengers not to travel between London Liverpool Street and Hertford East, Cambridge and Stansted Airport until further notice.

Stansted Express services between London Liverpool Street and Stansted Airport are among those affected, alongside Greater Anglia services between Liverpool Street and Cambridge North and Hertford East.

Content cannot be displayed without consent

‌



Services between Stratford and Bishops Stortford, as well as Stratford and Meridian Water, are also affected.

Tickets dated for travel on Tuesday, August 25, will be accepted for travel on Wednesday, August 26. Passengers who cannot postpone their journeys are being allowed to use a number of alternative services at no extra cost.

These include Great Northern trains between London King's Cross and Cambridge, as well as services between Hertford North and Moorgate.

‌



Tickets are also being accepted on selected Arriva and CentralConnect bus services, London Underground routes, London Overground Weaver line services and Thameslink trains between St Pancras International and Cambridge.

View 2 Images Greater Anglia said trains may be cancelled, revised or delayed by up to 60 minutes, (Image: PA)

Stansted Express warned journeys between London and the airport using alternative routes could take up to two hours and 30 minutes.

‌



Passengers heading to Stansted from London are advised to travel from Liverpool Street to King's Cross St Pancras by Underground before taking a Great Northern service to Cambridge and changing there for a train to the airport.

Those travelling towards London are advised to take a train from Stansted Airport to Cambridge, change for a Great Northern service to King's Cross and then continue to Liverpool Street by Underground.

Advance ticket holders whose booked train is cancelled will also be allowed to travel on earlier or later services.

Article continues below

Passengers have been advised to check their journeys before setting off and may be entitled to compensation if they experience delays.

If you’ve been affected by what happened on the network today, you can contact the Samaritans on 116 123 from any phone for a confidential chat.

News.title: Madeleine McCann suspect Christian Brueckner to be sent back to court for rape retrial
News.content:
Madeleine McCann suspect Christian Brueckner to be sent back to court for rape retrial

Christian Brueckner, 50, is due back in court for 'aggravated rape among other offences' after being released from prison in 2025 - he remains a lead suspect in the disapperance of Madeleine McCann

View 3 Images Christian Brueckner is due back in court early next year (Image: Phil Harris)

Christian Brueckner, the lead suspect in the disappearance of Madeleine McCann, is due to return to court for the retrial of a rape case which he was cleared of two years ago.

‌



Brueckner has been ordered to appear before appeal Judge Loisa Bartel in a Leipzig, Germany, next year for the retrial. The judge will hear that the 50-year-old should not have been cleared over the rape of an Irish woman in 2024.

‌



He walked free last year following the verdict. A letter issued by the court said "criminal proceedings for aggravated rape among other offences" were due to go ahead on Monday, January 11, 2027.

‌



View 3 Images Brueckner has denied any involvement with Madeleine's disappearance (Image: Andy Stenning/Daily Mirror)

Madeleine McCann suspect Christian Brueckner gives police surveillance slip in shocking security breach READ MORE :

"For those who want to see Brueckner charged over Madeleine, this new court date is a gamechanger," a source told The Sun. Investigators who allege Brueckner is involved with Madeleine's disappearance could see the German back behind bars after he was released in 2025 after serving his seven-year sentence for the 2005 rape of an American woman in Portugal.

‌



"The way the German system works means every part of the original trial will be considered, and the judge overseeing it is incredibly sharp," the source added. "She will miss nothing. Maddie investigators realise for the first time, there is a genuine will to see a retrial and for something to be done about Brueckner."

View 3 Images Brueckner served seven years in jail over the rape of an American woman in Portugal (Image: Phil Harris)

Grerman prosecutors reportedly believe a rape conviction could lead officials to prosecute Brueckner over Madeleine's disappearance. Little Madeleine vanished from a holiday flat in Praia da Luz, in Portugal, on May 3, 2007.

Article continues below

She disappeared from her bed while her parents Kate and Gerry were with friends at a nearby restaurant in the resort area. Brueckner has not been charged over Madeleine's disappearance, though he remains a prime suspect with German and British investigators.

He has previously denied being involved in her disappearance.

News.title: Sex abuse allegations against teacher were ‘not a schoolboy fantasy’, jury hears
News.content:
Sex abuse allegations against teacher were ‘not a schoolboy fantasy’, jury hears

Sally-Anne Bowen, 65, is accused of indecently assaulting two boys aged around 14 to 15 while she was teaching chemistry at a school in north London in her mid 20s

View 3 Images Sally-Anne Bowen (Image: James Manning/PA Wire)

Allegations that a chemistry teacher had a sexual relationship with a teenage pupil were “not a schoolboy fantasy”, a jury has been told.

Sally-Anne Bowen, 65, is accused of indecently assaulting two boys aged around 14 to 15 while she was in her mid-20s teaching at Christ’s College in Finchley, north London.

The now 65-year-old's partner told her trial at Harrow Crown Court today that the teacher had a medical condition which meant sex was "clearly not enjoyable for her".

One of Bowen's pupils alleged he had sex with her "about 20 or 30 times" over several months in the late 1980s.

The pupil also alleged he would visit Bowen at her home, considered her to be his girlfriend, and had fallen in love with her.

View 3 Images Bowen arrives at Harrow Crown Court (Image: Shutterstock)

Prosecutor Madeleine Wolfe told jurors during her closing speech today that the man's evidence had "a real visceral quality to it", adding: "There can be no doubt that there was a lasting impact on him.

"It's not a schoolboy fantasy, is it?, Wolfe said. "He's started this account in 2014 – this has real-life implications for him, remained with him for decades."

The first alleged victim previously told the court that Bowen had "drummed" it into him that he was not allowed to tell anybody about their relationship and that he felt compelled to "protect" her.

It was not until he became a parent himself that he began to realise what had happened to him, Ms Wolfe told jurors.

"It became clear that when she (Bowen) chose him, that when she isolated him into that relationship, it was not in fact a loving relationship – it was nothing but exploitation, frankly," she said.

"That infuriated him, that there was a general view that because he was a male, he was a lucky boy."

View 3 Images Bowen denies seven counts of indecent assault against two boys (Image: Shutterstock)

Bowen previously described the man's account as "total fabrication" and "the workings of a fantasy".

The second complainant alleged he had kissed Bowen in a café after being "goaded" into it by other pupils, the court previously heard. Bowen said she does not remember this boy and does not know who he is.

Ms Wolfe, in her speech, summarised the teacher's defence as claiming "there was this conspiracy behind the witnesses who spoke about her conduct at the school".

Ms Wolfe added: "We suggest that there is a considerable amount of evidence that support the allegations that were made by (the alleged victims), but there is little support for the account given by Ms Bowen."

Bowen told the court in a previous hearing that she had an undiagnosed medical condition in the late 1980s which made sexual intercourse difficult and painful for her.

Her partner of 36 years, Darren Scotchbrook, giving evidence today, said she was not aware of her condition when they met in the summer of 1990, and sex was "clearly not enjoyable for her" as a result.

Two medical experts instructed by the defence jointly concluded, following an internal examination of Ms Bowen, that "the alleged sexual activities were feasible", though they could be painful, jurors were told.

Bowen, of Hemel Hempstead, Hertfordshire, denies seven counts of indecent assault against two boys.

Article continues below

The trial continues.

News.title: A66 crash that killed seven 'sparked by turf war' after home of teen victim's dad 'ram raided' in early hours
News.content:
A66 crash that killed seven 'sparked by turf war' after home of teen victim's dad 'ram raided' in early hours

Five more arrests have been made in connection with the A66 crash near Middlesborough. A 16-year-old boy and two men, aged 18 and 21, were arrested on suspicion of participating in an organised crime group.

A66 crash: Police cordon remains in place on Teeside

Five more people were arrested today amid claims the A66 crash was sparked by a feud between rival crime gangs.

‌



A 16-year-old boy and two men, aged 18 and 21, were arrested on suspicion of participating in an organised crime group. A 55-year-old man was also held on suspicion of assisting an offender. A 23-year-old man was arrested on suspicion of making threats to kill. All five remained in custody, Cleveland Police said.

‌



The update from police of the further arrests came as the fundraisers for the families of PC Tom Clough, 38, and PC Matthew Blades, 37, neared the £1m mark. More than £900,000 has been pledged to two separate Gofundme appeals. PC Clough and PC Blades died in the crash, as did Michael Robert Cahill, 23, Jacob Matusiak, 23, Makai Saddington, 18, Theo Rae, and Cole Robert Worthy, both 17.

‌



View 7 Images From left to right: Makai Saddington, Theo Rae, Cole Robert Worthy, Michael Robert Cahill, Jakub Matusiak

Fundraiser for Cleveland police officers killed in A66 crash exceeds £750k READ MORE :

All seven were killed when a Volkswagen Passat, going the wrong way down the A66 at South Bank, hit a Cleveland Police armed response vehicle heading in the opposite direction at 3.39am on Saturday. The home of Cole Worthy's father was allegedly ram-raided at 3am on Saturday, just 40 minutes before the devastating crash.

It is alleged that a Volvo XC60 was used, and that vehicle is now central to the police investigation into the tragedy. The house is believed to belong to Gye Worthy, Cole's father. A vehicle deliberately reversed into the front window twice, causing extensive damage, according to those living close to the scene.

‌



View 7 Images Tribute to Cole Worthy who died in the A66 crash

Within minutes, a VW Passat containing his son Cole and four friends was racing around Middlesbrough, pursuing the Volvo allegedly involved in the attack. The Passat was later spotted by a police patrol, resulting in the horrific crash that killed PC Clough and PC Blades. There is no suggestion Gye Worthy, 39, a company director, was involved in any criminal activity. But the attack on his home appeared to be the flashpoint for the chase between rival gangs.

The chain of events that led to the tragedy began in Acklam, Middlesbrough. One neighbour of the Worthys said Cole's father had lived at the address for around ten years and led 'a normal life'. Another heard a 'loud bang' and looked out to see the damage.

‌



View 7 Images PC Tom Clough, one of two Cleveland Police officers killed in a car crash on the A66 near Middlesbrough (Image: ncjMedia Ltd)

Cleveland Police confirmed both the Volvo and VW Passat were part of their enquiries in the early hours of August 22. But they declined to comment on claims that rival gangs were involved in the police chase that led to the crash.

Mr Worthy's home was rammed at around 3am. By 3.36am, the VW Passat was caught on CCTV racing at between 80 and 100mph down Lime Road in Teesville, pursued by three police vehicles. At 3.39am, it turned the wrong way onto the A66 dual carriageway, at which point the pursuing police vehicles stopped. Just ten seconds later, it smashed head-on into the armed response vehicle carrying PCs Clough and Blades.

‌



View 7 Images PC Matthew Blades, who died when a car going in the wrong direction hit a police car on the A66 near Middlesbrough (Image: Cleveland Police/PA Wire)

Cleveland Police said two of the 12 people previously arrested in connection with the A66 collision have now appeared in court. The further arrests brings the total held in connection to the investigation to 17.

Kai Beattie, 19, of Foxrush Court, Redcar, appeared at Teesside Magistrates' Court charged with possession of a firearm with intent to endanger life, according to the police. Cameron George, 26, of Micklow Close, Redcar, was remanded in custody to appear at Teesside Crown Court on September 21 charged with drugs offences and possession of criminal property, it said. A spokesman for Cleveland Police said: "On the morning of Saturday 22 August, Cleveland Police received several reports of two vehicles being driven dangerously. The first vehicle, believed to be a Volvo XC60, was witnessed ramming properties in the Middlesbrough area. The second vehicle, a Volkswagen Passat, is believed to have been associated with the activities of the Volvo XC60."

‌



View 7 Images Flares lit during a balloon release in memory of Jakub Matusiak, 23, who died in the A66 crash (Image: North News & Pictures Ltd)

Youths wearing balaclavas set off flares and fireworks in a noisy tribute to the five dead youths following the crash. Friends of Jakub Matusiak, 23, gathered at a field in South Bank, Middlesbrough, close to the scene of Saturday's catastrophic collision.

A gang of around 20 masked youths on motorbikes and quad bikes roared around the field in honour of Mr Matusiak, who had convictions for motoring offences. The scenes sparked fury on social media.

‌



One commentator wrote: "I get it that their families and friends will be devastated and grieving, but surely in circumstances where they have killed two innocent men who were simply out doing their jobs, you grieve in private?" Writing on Facebook, a woman accused the mourners of showing "disrespect of the highest level for the two murdered policemen" and said a quiet vigil would have been more appropriate.

View 7 Images Flares light up the skies during a balloon release in memory of Jakub Matusiak, 23, (Image: North News & Pictures Ltd)

Paul Williams, acting deputy national chairman for the Police Federation of England and Wales, told BBC Breakfast: "Every day we can identify now numerous examples of young people sensationalising dangerous driving. Not just dangerous driving, but baiting police officers who are out there to protect the public.

‌



"It's a real problem. It's causing officers concern. They shouldn't have to be going out and worrying about whether they're going to return home from their shift or not. But on top of that, wondering if they’re going to be plastered all over social media. It's absolutely unacceptable and social media platforms need to take some action."

Offers of support have come in from as far afield as Australia. Officers from other forces contacted Cleveland Police to cover shifts for the distressed colleagues of the fallen officers. The number of donations on a police federation page has reached almost 30,000.

View 7 Images The crash scene on the A66 in South Bank, near Middlesbrough (Image: Owen Humphreys/PA Wire)

‌



The extraordinary show of support for their families came as the Government also called upon social media companies to remove videos of drivers recording police pursuits. Matt Storey, police and crime commissioner for Cleveland, called on the community to reach out to police officers. "Reach out and put your arm around them," he said. "They are people behind the uniforms."

He told the Mirror that filming behind the wheel was becoming an "incredibly dangerous and idiotic" trend. He added: "Parents have a responsibility to tell their children what they should be doing on the road. But also have to demand more from TikTok and social media platforms to remove content. They have a responsibility regarding public safety to get this taken off their platforms. They have to be careful about what is on their site.

"We need to tighten the legislation. It is like the wild west. I have met with many young people about misinformation and exploitation. They understand social media is dangerous; their reaction was that it must be regulated more tightly."

Article continues below

Lauren Somerville, chairwoman of Cleveland Police Federation, said: “It’s so hard to describe how this grief feels and how it will feel. Policing is so unique, so unique. We are injected into the darkest moments in people’s lives, whether that be arresting somebody or you know, saving a life.

"Whatever it is, officers forge relationships that might happen in a moment or over a full career together, and you cannot describe the grief."

News.title: Dolly Parton: The life of an iconic country singer
News.content:
Iconic country musician Dolly Parton has died at the age of 80, her family announced on her social media.

"Sadness lies with us, not with Dolly," Parton's nephew Brian Seaver said in a video announcement.

In a seven-decade career, Parton won 10 Grammy awards, sold more than 100 million records worldwide, and wrote in excess of 3,000 songs.

Parton took her writing seriously, and considered herself a songwriter over everything else. "It's my way of expressing myself," she said. "It's my therapy."

She was also a savvy businesswoman who wasn't afraid to make tough decisions. Armed with a quick wit and southern charm, she took control of her show business career that spanned more than 60 years.

Follow for live updates and read more about Dolly's life.

News.title: Father's house rammed before son died in A66 crash
News.content:
A house rammed by a car before the fatal A66 crash in Middlesbrough belonged to the father of a teenager who died in the incident.

Cole Worthy, 17, was one of five young men who died when a Volkswagen Passat travelling in the wrong direction hit a Cleveland Police armed response vehicle, also killing two police officers.

Before the crash at 03:39 BST on Saturday, police had received multiple reports of two cars driving dangerously around the town and a Volvo XC60 was seen ramming properties.

The BBC understands that, after his father's home was rammed, Worthy and the four others set out in the Passat. Police said they were linking the activities of the Volvo XC60 and the Passat.

There is no suggestion Worthy's father was involved in criminal activity.

PC Tom Clough, 38, and PC Matthew Blades, 37, died in the crash, as did Michael Robert Cahill, 23, Jacob Matusiak, 23, Makai Saddington, 18, Theo Rae, 17, and Worthy.

The Independent Office for Police Conduct said officers had been pursuing the Passat for almost seven minutes after it was connected to earlier alleged criminal activity, but the pursuit was abandoned 10 seconds before the crash when it turned on to the dual carriageway.

Both vehicles were operating with cloned number plates but were picked up by automated number plate recognition technology.

News.title: Man dies in crash after police pursuit
News.content:
A man has died and two women have been injured in a crash after a police pursuit near Stratford-upon-Avon.

Officers tried to stop a black Audi on Birmingham Road shortly before 17:30 BST on Monday but the driver failed to pull over, Warwickshire Police said.

A pursuit began and 15 minutes later the Audi crashed into a white Ford Puma, the force added, with the Audi's 19-year-old male driver confirmed dead at the scene by paramedics.

The driver of the Ford, a woman, was seriously injured and remains in hospital in critical condition, while injuries to a second woman - her passenger - were serious but not believed to be life-threatening. An investigation by the police watchdog is under way.

Officers said after failing to stop, the Audi made off in the direction of the A46 before travelling back towards Stratford on the A439 Warwick Road where the crash occurred.

A number of other cars were damaged during the pursuit, police said.

Warwick Road was closed on Monday from the Marraway roundabout to its junction with Ingon Lane and Sand Barn Lane, with the stretch remaining shut on Tuesday morning.

It later reopened.

News.title: Trump says all mines cleared from Strait of Hormuz
News.content:
US President Donald Trump has said that the US Navy has removed or detonated all mines in the Strait of Hormuz - the vital waterway which Iran has largely closed since the beginning of the war in the Middle East.

"Iran has been notified that any ship or boat placing new mines will be immediately and systematically destroyed," Trump said in a post on his Truth Social platform.

There is no comment from Iran.

Closure of the strait has caused wild fluctuations in the price of oil on world markets. Trump has often said the US has control of the area - but Iran has fired against vessels it says have sought to cross without its permission.

Some 20% of the world's oil and liquefied natural gas used to transit the Strait of Hormuz before the war, which began on 28 February with US and Israeli air strikes against Iran.

In addition to closing the strait, Iran retaliated against Israel and against US bases in the region as well as US Arab allies in the Gulf.

A ceasefire aimed at facilitating talks to end the war has collapsed and there has been intermittent exchange of fire between the US and Iran.

However, this week the US announced a raft of economic sanctions against Iran.

US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent warned that any nation financially partnering with Iran would be isolated.

Iran and the US signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) in June - a 14-point document which set a 60-day deadline to reach a deal on the Strait of Hormuz, before substantial negotiations on resolving the nuclear issue - allegations that Iran is building a nuclear weapon, which Tehran has consistently denied.

However, that deadline has now expired and talks have collapsed leading to the new US sanctions that Trump believes will lead to the collapse of the Iranian regime.

Iran has been under sanctions for most of the time since the founding of the Islamic Republic in 1979 and Economy Minister Ali Madanizadeh said Tehran was "fully prepared" for the wider sanctions, which he added would lead to "another defeat" for the US.

Its economy, however, has suffered as a result of the war - and a blockade of Iranian ports that the US has been maintaining for weeks not to allow trade to continue.

On Tuesday, China - the biggest buyer of Iranian oil - said it was firmly opposed to what it called the US's "illegal unilateral sanctions" and would take "all necessary measures" to safeguard its rights.

The US announcement comes ahead of planned talks between Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping next month.

Washington is likely to be wary of potential retaliation from Beijing, which processes the majority of the world's rare earths and other critical minerals, crucial in the manufacture of many high-tech products.

Beijing has already tightened export controls on rare earths as part of previous trade negotiations with the US.

News.title: Spanish government says sorry to people of Ceuta for migrant crisis
News.content:
The Spanish government has apologised to the people of Ceuta for the migrant crisis that has affected the city for weeks and it has unveiled plans to overhaul the country's immigration laws.

"I want to apologise to all those who may have felt, or who even still feel, abandoned or not sufficiently cared for," Defence Minister Margarita Robles told a parliamentary committee.

"I have witnessed first-hand your feelings of anxiety, of abandonment, of lack of safety."

At least 72,000 migrants crossed from Morocco into Ceuta, a Spanish exclave in North Africa on 30 and 31 July.

Most of the migrants swam around the border fence and at least 100 people died during the mass crossing, according to figures from Ceuta's mayor, Juan JesÃºs Vivas.

The vast majority of the migrants returned to Morocco within hours of their arrival, but several thousand remain in Ceuta, many of them children, and most sleeping rough on beaches or streets.

The Socialist government of Prime Minister Pedro SÃ¡nchez has been under mounting pressure to resolve the situation, with many residents and the local authorities in Ceuta, which has a population of 84,000, complaining that it is unsustainable.

The SÃ¡nchez government has now declared a situation of interest for national security in the city, centralising management of the crisis. Territorial Policy Minister Ãngel VÃ­ctor Torres has been tasked with co-ordinating the response, relieving the Ceuta local government of that responsibility.

News.title: Who does Iran trade with and what could Trump's 'economic D-Day' mean?
News.content:
The US has said "the single greatest financial offensive ever" will help it and Israel end their ongoing war with Iran.

However, Iran is no stranger to these tactics.

The regime has faced near continuous US sanctions since the Islamic Revolution of 1979. In that time, it has developed deep trade ties with several countries which either have a history of ignoring US economic pressure themselves or cannot afford to stop trading with Iran.

As a result, Iran says it is "fully prepared" for the new US sanctions and many economists argue the impact of Washington's latest move will be limited.

So, who does Iran trade with? And could what the US has called an "economic D-Day" have any real impact on Iran?

News.title: Yellow weather warnings issued as thunderstorms and flooding forecast
News.content:
Yellow weather warnings have been issued by the Met Office as heavy rain and thunderstorms are forecast to break out over parts of the UK later this week.

The warnings span Wednesday and Thursday and include parts of east Wales, the Midlands, northern England, East Anglia and southern England - including London.

It is likely to be the one of the most widespread outbreaks of heavy rain across southern and central parts of the UK this summer.

While good news for regions plagued by drought, significant accumulations could lead to flash flooding where the ground is too dry and hard to absorb the downpours. Lightning, large hail and gusty winds are also possible.

News.title: Andrew Tate exaggerates and did not own supercars in photos, his lawyers say
News.content:
Controversial influencer Andrew Tate portrays himself as "uberwealthy" but did not own cars and a yacht featured on his social media and exaggerated his lifestyle for online attention, his legal representatives have said.

Tate and his brother Tristan are currently being held in a Florida jail but are seeking release on bail while they await the outcome of extradition proceedings.

They were arrested last month after British prosecutors unveiled new charges including alleged sexual offences against them, which both men deny.

Prosecutors have argued the Tates are a "flight risk", citing the brothers' past statements about their wealth and influence and having multiple identities to evade the law.

In a legal submission to the court, the brothers' legal representatives said the Tates' business model "depends on online attention".

"The outrageousness of the posts by them and about them is the point. The more hyperbolic and outlandish the post, the more likely it will generate views and likes, which in turn generates income. In short, they are playing a role," it says.

At times Andrew Tate has also exaggerated and used hyperbole for "comedic effect" with no intention to be taken seriously, the submission argues.

"The government alleges that the Tates are a risk of flight based on their social media claims that they are 'self-proclaimed billionaires' who own 'high-end vehicles, private jets, and a custom $50-million-dollar superyacht and have unrestricted access to traditional funds, cryptocurrency, and bitcoin,'" it says.

"But the government has not established these grandiose claims are true," it adds.

News.title: Young care leavers dying early a 'national tragedy'
News.content:
Young adults who have left care have a death rate around four times higher than the general population, a new review, external shows.

Often left alone "with no safety net," the report says the consequences can be catastrophic.

On turning 18, people leaving care in England often lose "significant levers of support", the Government-commissioned report concluded, as it warned the so-called "care cliff" must be addressed.

Speaking to BBC Radio 4 Today, report co-author and broadcaster Ashley John-Baptiste, who grew up in care, called the deaths a national tragedy.

There were 112 deaths of care leavers aged 18 to 24 notified in 2025, which the review said equalled about 130 deaths per 100,000 care leavers.

John-Baptiste recalled his own experience of turning 18 and moving out of the last of four foster homes he'd lived in.

"I was made to live alone and work out how to be an adult," he said.

Unable to afford a bed frame, he says he slept on a mattress on the floor of his council flat and felt a deep sense of abandonment and isolation.

News.title: Boy, 3, injured in crocodile attack returns home
News.content:
A three-year-old boy who was seriously injured in a crocodile enclosure has been discharged from hospital and is settling back in at home, his family has said.

The child returned home "a few weeks ago" and is "happy to be home, playing with his toys, sleeping in his own bed and being a big brother", his parents said in an update posted online.

The boy was visiting Johnsons of Old Hurst near Huntingdon, Cambridgeshire, with his family on 18 June when he was attacked by at least one of the animals.

In an update shared on a fundraising page on Monday, the boy's family said it was "nice to have us all back together in the comfort of our own home".

Cambridgeshire Police arrested and bailed a 30-year-old man from Norfolk on suspicion of attempted murder after the incident.

News.title: Inspectors to assess police after Henry Nowak murder
News.content:
An inspection into how a police force responds to violent incidents has been launched in the wake of Henry Nowak's murder.

The 18-year-old student was stabbed in Southampton by Vickrum Digwa, who lied to police and insisted he had been the victim of a racist attack.

Hampshire Police officers initially arrested Nowak and placed him in handcuffs as he lay dying.

His Majesty's Inspectorate of Constabulary and Fire & Rescue Service (HMICFRS) will assess the force's processes, training and how officers are supported to make sound and impartial judgements.

The inspection was requested by Hampshire Police and Crime Commissioner Donna Jones, who said the public "must have confidence" in the force.

"This inspection will provide an independent assessment of the force's training, processes and culture, including the handling of allegations of racially aggravated assault," she said.

"Henry's family deserve answers, and the public deserve reassurance that their police service is equipped to recognise victims and provide the highest standard of care when it matters most."

News.title: Legendary rugby league winger Boston dies aged 92
News.content:
Tributes have been led by prime minister Andy Burnham who said he was a "giant of a man in every way".

"Heartbroken to hear my friend Sir Billy Boston has died," he said on social media.

"Billy was one of the greatest rugby league players of all time but also one of the kindest and most down-to-earth people you could ever wish to meet.

"He always had time for people and gave so much to back to his adopted home, Wigan.

"I will miss him greatly and am thinking today of Billy's family, still grieving the recent loss of his beloved wife Joan."

Wigan owner Mike Danson said: "Billy Boston was everybody's hero, including my mum's.

"His achievements in rugby league were extraordinary, and his knighthood was a fitting recognition of a career that brought great credit to Wigan and to the game.

"But Billy's legacy was not simply what he achieved. It was the humility with which he carried it. Despite everything he accomplished, he remained a quiet, dignified and deeply respected man.

"He leaves behind an example that will endure for generations. Our thoughts are with his family and those closest to him.

"A great man, and a true Wigan legend. He will be remembered with pride and affection."

In a statement, Wales Rugby League said: "Today, rugby league has lost one of its greatest-ever players, Wales has lost one of its finest sporting sons, and our sport has lost a truly special gentleman."

The WRU also paid tribute, calling Boston "one of the best loved and most iconic figures in the history of Welsh sport".

Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy added: "He was, in my view, the greatest rugby league player of all time and one of the nicest people I've ever had the privilege to know."

News.title: Former police officer charged with raping woman while on duty
News.content:
A former police officer allegedly raped and strangled a woman while on duty, according to the policing watchdog.

The Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) said ex-constable Rikki Hall had been charged with two counts of rape and one count of non-fatal strangulation.

The 33-year-old is accused of attacking the woman while on duty in Swansea city centre in February 2024.

Hall, who resigned from South Wales Police during the IOPC investigation, has also been charged with possession of a firearm and two counts of misconduct in public office.

He will appear at Bristol Magistrates' Court on Thursday.

The IOPC said its investigation began in February 2024 following a mandatory conduct referral from South Wales Police.

"A substantial file of material was submitted to the Crown Prosecution Service in February 2025 and, following further lines of enquiry being undertaken, charges were authorised by the CPS," it added.

News.title: 'We just want to get home' - dozens stranded in Tunisia after cancelled Belfast flight
News.content:
Dozens of people from Northern Ireland have been left stranded in Tunisia after their EasyJet flight home was cancelled, with the airline telling them it had no other flights available for another 10 days.

One man told BBC News NI he has spent Â£4,000 on travel home for his family-of-five, while another woman, Georgina Doherty, said she and her six children were trying to get home after the death of her mother-in-law.

Others described running out of medication for health issues, while EasyJet were also criticised over a lack of support and communication.

EasyJet has said it is operating an additional direct flight to Belfast on Tuesday night, and that it was "very sorry" for the inconvenience.

BBC News NI understands more than 100 people were booked onto the cancelled flight that was due to leave Enfidha-Hamamet Airport for Belfast International three days ago.

Stuart McCartney, from Dromore, County Down, said he had spent thousands on accommodation and flights to get his family home via a flight to Brussels.

"I'm willing to pay Â£4,000 to get us home, if needs be, and then battle for reimbursement if I have to after that," he said.

"But we shouldn't have to pay. My holiday was a fraction of what I'm paying to get home right now."

McCartney said EasyJet provided two nights of accommodation but then told the family to find alternative accommodation for the rest of the delay.

He said his mother Katherine, who accompanied his wife and children on the trip, relies on heart medication and they have had to keep a close eye on her remaining supply as the delay continued.

An EasyJet spokesperson said that the company "have been doing everything we can to support Mr McCartney, providing hotel accommodation and meals and we will be reimbursing expenses that may have been incurred".

Georgina Doherty, who is originally from Londonderry but now lives in County Donegal, told BBC News NI the last few days have been an "absolute nightmare" for her family.

Her husband returned home a day before they were due to fly back due to his mother taking ill. She has since died, with Doherty and her six children stranded in Tunisia.

News.title: More than 70,000 social and affordable homes to be built across England over 10 years
News.content:
Ministers have announced where more than 70,000 social and affordable homes will be built in England over the next 10 years as part of an initial allocation of almost Â£10bn in a bid to address the housing crisis.

Funding has been granted to Greater Manchester, the West Midlands, West Yorkshire, South Yorkshire, North East England, and Liverpool. An additional Â£6bn was previously announced for London.

It is the first part of a wider plan to build 300,000 social and affordable homes, under the government's Â£39bn social housebuilding programme.

Housing charities welcomed the news but said it was still not enough to meet demand, while the Conservatives said it was an "unfunded spending commitment".

Social housing provides affordable homes at a low cost, managed by social landlords. It includes affordable rented properties as well as low-cost home ownership, such as shared ownership, and can be provided by local authorities and housing associations.

Earlier this year, before he became prime minister, Andy Burnham had called for the entire Â£39bn affordable housing budget for England to be spent on homes for social rent - which means the cost of the unit is about half that of market rents, and there are strict criteria for who can apply for it.

"I would actually devote all of it to social housing," Burnham told The Social Housing Podcast in May.

But of the new homes announced on Monday, 60% would be for social rent.

Housing Minister Matthew Pennycook told BBC Breakfast he did not accept Burnham had failed to meet his previous commitment, saying the government had taken a "pragmatic approach" and wants to "get money out the door".

He said the next tranche of funding would be more focused on council houses - which are usually also classed as homes for social rent.

It is understood ministers decided against giving councils more of the funding announced in the first tranche because they did not believe councils would be in a position to build the required number of social homes.

News.title: Man jailed for killing student over fake Rolex row
News.content:
At about 17:00 GMT on the night he died, Oladipo left his girlfriend's flat carrying a plastic bag of leftover snacks and was on the phone to her while he walked back to his accommodation nearby to watch football.

But outside the De Montfort University's Innovation Centre, he was met by Dennis who was captured on CCTV walking up and down in the "busy" area.

"It took less than 30 seconds for the two men to come together, to struggle and for the defendant to leave," Osborne told the court.

The court was told Oladipo's girlfriend heard him say "why did you come up and stab me?" over the phone before asking for her to call the ambulance.

A post-mortem examination showed he had suffered six wounds, five to the chest including one which penetrated his heart, and one to his thumb.

Despite being taken to the Leicester Royal Infirmary, he was pronounced dead just over an hour after the stabbing, which took place near the DMU campus.

Giving evidence in his defence on Wednesday, Dennis said he was "fearful" for his life when Oladipo approached him with a knife, adding he was "wrestling" to prevent the 20-year-old from stabbing him.

In cross-examination, prosecutor Jane Osborne KC asked if Dennis knew he had stabbed Oladipo, to which he replied: "I didn't know and I didn't know he was hurt, and I didn't intend to cause any serious harm."

Jurors were shown CCTV footage of Oladipo and Dennis walking towards each other, with Osborne suggesting Dennis used his hands to open a folding knife.

Dennis denied the suggestion he had a knife in his possession, and said he did not leave his accommodation with one.

Addressing Dennis, the prosecutor said there was "bad feeling" between Dennis and Oladipo - and suggested Dennis left his accommodation with a knife "to settle it".

Baby food pouches sold in UK supermarkets are effectively "equivalent to fruit smoothies" and should not be given to children under a year old, experts have warned.

Researchers found that very few pouch products "meet the desired characteristics for complementary foods", leading to calls for regulators to review how they are classified and sold.

The study, conducted by academics from the University of Glasgow’s College of Medical Veterinary and Life Sciences and the First Steps Nutrition Trust, examined every wet commercial baby food (CBF) item available at six major UK supermarkets.

Their analysis evaluated sugar, protein, and energy contents across 298 products, comparing them to breast milk.

Six out of 10 products evaluated (60%) were sold in "spouted pouches" or sPouches.

open image in gallery Experts say baby food pouches are effectively ‘equivalent to fruit smoothies’ ( Getty/iStock )

Of these pouches, 70% were targeted at infants under six months of age, despite health guidelines recommending that weaning begin from around six months.

Compared to breast milk and alternative products, pouches were found to carry lower levels of protein, reduced energy, and higher concentrations of sugar.

Researchers stated that many of these products are "similar to sweet fruit smoothies", which are not recommended for infants or pre-school aged children.

According to NHS guidelines, infants under 12 months "do not need fruit juice or smoothies".

Writing in the journal Archives of Disease in Childhood, the authors noted: "Many wet CBF delivered in sPouches have the texture and composition of sweet drinks, while very few meet the desired characteristics for complementary foods,"

They added: "These CBFs, which in texture and content are equivalent to fruit smoothies, should not really be given at all before 12 months and their intake limited after."

The team said parents regularly select these options due to "misperceptions of suitability and healthfulness", pointing out that "CBF packaging often displays the misleading claim no added sugar despite containing high amounts of free sugars due to pureed fruit content".

The authors urged regulators to "review whether labelling spouted-pouch, baby food products as complementary foods is appropriate and

consider whether these delivery systems are inappropriate for complementary feeding."

open image in gallery NHS guidelines state infants under 12 months ‘do not need fruit juice or smoothies’

Dr Vicky Sibson, co-author of the study and director at the First Steps Nutrition Trust, said: "The NHS advises parents not to give babies fruit drinks and smoothies because their high sugar and acid content can cause tooth decay.

"And yet, right now, supermarkets and pharmacies are full of fruit-based baby ‘food’ pouches marketed for use from four months and six months of age as ‘first foods’, when our research shows they are actually often more like fruit drinks or smoothies.

"Parents are being misled in to believing that these are healthy and appropriate choices for their babies.

"The Government have given the baby food industry until February 2027 to comply with new voluntary baby food guidelines.

"A quick glance at the shelves and online suggests slow progress and undoubtedly a mandatory approach would be preferable.

"Stronger regulations on the composition, marketing and labelling of commercial baby and toddler foods and drinks should be based on the latest evidence, to ensure maximum protection for infant and young child health."
