Liberia’s Ministry of Justice has not yet released full identifying details or the specific charges against the Serbian and Spanish nationals, and FrontPageAfrica is continuing to press both the Ministry and the Joint National Security Investigative Team for those records. What is already clear, even without their names in print, is that the case against Ivancic, Vrovac and Zadereiko was never really a story about three men. It sits inside a wider, quieter pattern of European nationals moving through Liberia’s ports, airports and government circles over several years — arriving under different passports, answering to different names, and, investigators say, working toward the same end.

An Operational Divide, and a Network Built for the Long Game

Nothing about the way this network was structured looks accidental. Investigators describe a syndicate that spread its key organizers deliberately across three separate geographies, precisely so the loss of any single man would not bring the whole operation down. Ivancic stayed in the relative safety of Dubai, managing finance and negotiating bulk shipments over encrypted channels he believed no one could read. Vrovac put himself in Ghana, close enough to the action to oversee shipping networks, container logistics and payoffs, far enough from Liberia to avoid becoming its most obvious face. Zadereiko moved through Liberia and the wider region under a borrowed name, structuring the money-laundering and distribution side of the business from the inside. A financier abroad. An operator in the region. A technician embedded in the target country. It is a division of labor that let the network survive years of quiet operation — until a single stash house in Paynesville brought the entire architecture, at last, into public view.

The Dubai Link and the “Gift” Call

Every network needs a door in, and investigators say this one’s door opened in 2022, in a hotel meeting room in Dubai. Sheikh Bassirou Kante, the middleman, introduced then-Vice President Howard-Taylor to Zadereiko, Ivancic and Vrovac, presenting the three as legitimate, high-profile investors eager to inject roughly US$250 million into the Liberian economy. Howard-Taylor traveled to Dubai later that year and met the group face to face, according to investigators, personally welcoming their stated interest and assuring them Liberia was open for business.

Kante’s own legal troubles in the United States — a fraud and money-laundering case that turned an accused man into a cooperating witness — are what investigators say ultimately transformed that 2022 introduction into the evidentiary backbone of the case against Howard-Taylor. She has heavily disputed prosecutors’ reading of that meeting. While she acknowledges meeting numerous groups of foreign nationals during official travel to secure development funding for Liberia, she maintains she never personally knew Zadereiko or his partners and interacted with them only under the belief they were legitimate developers. Investigators see it differently. To them, the Dubai summit and the “gift” call that followed it are the clearest evidence available of how top-tier political access was quietly leveraged to secure a pipeline for a cocaine network now valued in the hundreds of millions of dollars.

Twelve Indicted, and a Manhunt Still Underway

The case in Liberia has already produced an indictment of 12 individuals and ongoing court proceedings, spanning the network’s local facilitators, its cooperating informants, and the foreign nationals charged in absentia. But the men who investigators say built and ran this operation — Ivancic in Dubai, Vrovac in Ghana, Zadereiko believed to be moving through the wider region — remain outside Liberian custody. Justice Minister Tweh has said Liberia is pursuing formal international arrest warrants through Interpol and other channels, hoping to bring the trio, along with the Serbian and Spanish nationals charged earlier, back to Monrovia to finally face the courts of the country they spent years quietly making their own.

Whether that effort succeeds will likely decide how this case is remembered years from now: as the moment Liberia’s institutions proved capable of dismantling a transnational trafficking network stretching from Croatian courtrooms to Dubai wire transfers to a stash house in Paynesville — or as a case that named its most senior organizers loudly and publicly, only to watch every one of them remain, for now, exactly where the law cannot yet reach them.

World.title: The Flag Asks for Courage and Purity; This Year, Liberia Owes it Both
World.content:
One hundred and seventy-nine years ago, seven women stitched a promise into cloth. This Flag Day, as a former Vice President stands charged and a police chief’s own claims go unanswered, Liberia should ask honestly whether it has kept it.

PICTURE IT: SEVEN WOMEN, all of them born in America, none of them born free, bent over a length of cloth in 1847, needles moving by hand because there was no other way to make a flag mean something back then. Governor Joseph Jenkins Roberts had asked them to do what no committee of statesmen had been asked to do — to design and stitch, thread by thread, the symbol of a country that did not yet officially exist.

SUSANNAH ELIZABETH LEWIS led them. What they were replacing was itself only twenty years old: the colony’s 1827 flag, nearly a copy of the American Stars and Stripes except for a white Christian cross sitting where stars should have been, a quiet nod to the religious societies that had shipped many of Liberia’s settlers across the Atlantic in the first place. A cross had been enough for a colony still waiting on someone else’s permission to exist. It was not enough for a nation. So the women took it out, and in its place, they sewed a single five-pointed star. On August 24, 1847, one month after the Declaration of Independence was signed, that flag went up for the first time over Africa’s first independent republic. It was a small change in a corner of blue cloth. It meant everything.



NOTHING ABOUT THAT FLAG was left to chance, and nothing on it was there simply to look good. Eleven stripes, six red and five white, for the eleven men who put their names to Liberia’s Declaration of Independence — men who signed knowing the document offered no guarantee, no safety net, nothing but the risk itself. Red for courage, valor, bravery: the nerve it takes to build a country out of conviction and little else. White for moral excellence, purity, peace: the character the founders hoped would still be standing long after the courage that built the place had been spent.

THE BLUE SQUARE for the African continent, and for liberty bound to fidelity — not freedom on its own, but freedom married to faithfulness, to the idea that liberty means nothing if nobody keeps faith with the people standing next to them. And the lone star, for freedom itself, and for the singular, still-remarkable fact of what Liberia was in 1847: the only independent republic on African soil, kneeling to no colonial power. Courage. Purity. Fidelity. Freedom. Read it plainly and it stops looking like a flag and starts looking like a promise — one eleven signers and seven seamstresses handed down to every Liberian who would ever stand under it again.



THIS YEAR, THAT PROMISE COMES due at an uncomfortable time to be read honestly. Liberia reaches its 179th Flag Day in the middle of the largest drug scandal in its history. A network of European traffickers spent years quietly making themselves at home inside Liberian government circles before a stash house in Paynesville finally showed the country the scale of what had been built under its own roof. A former Vice President and First Lady now stand formally charged in connection with it. An Inspector General’s own claim — that trafficking in Liberia was “sanctioned at very, very senior level” — has sat in the open for months without a single name attached to it. Two currently serving police officers, alleged to have escorted the very shipment at the center of this case, remain unnamed and unarrested, while a former official was taken into custody within days. Hold all of that up against red, white and blue, and the colors do not sit together the way they used to.



SO, ASK IT PLAINLY, the way Flag Day deserves to be asked. Where is the courage in a case where the country’s own chief investigator will not name the “senior level” he described with his own mouth? What do moral excellence and purity mean in a republic that spent an entire summer discovering how comfortably foreign traffickers had settled into its own institutions, its own neighborhoods, its own friendships? And what does fidelity require, if not that the law move against a serving officer with the same speed it moved against a former Vice President — fidelity not to whoever holds power this year, but to the ordinary Liberians that blue square was always meant to stand for? The eleven men who signed their names in 1847 risked their safety and their futures on a document that promised them nothing back. It is a fair question, on the very anniversary of the flag their courage produced, whether the officials entrusted with its legacy today are willing to risk even a name.

NONE OF THIS IS WRITTEN AGAINST THE FLAG, or against what Monday represents. It is written for it. A flag that means courage, purity and fidelity is not honored by a parade alone — it is honored by a country willing to measure itself against those three words every single year it raises the cloth. This Flag Day, Liberia should do more than lift the Lone Star and admire it from a distance. It should ask, without flinching, whether the republic underneath that flag still resembles what seven women stitched into being 179 years ago — or whether “no sacred cows” has quietly become this generation’s replacement for what “sacred honor” once meant to eleven men who signed their names to a nation instead of hiding behind one. The flag will go up Monday no matter how that question is answered. What Liberians do with the answer, long after the parade has ended and the flags have come back down, is the part of this holiday that will actually matter.

World.title: Liberia: Backed By The President, IG Coleman Defends His Record — But Not All The Questions
World.content:
MONROVIA — Gregory Coleman did not sound like a man bracing to lose his job. He sounded like a man explaining, patiently and at length, why the job was always going to cost him something — and why he had made his peace with that a long time before Liberians started calling for his head. In extended remarks this week, the Inspector General of Police laid out, more fully than he ever has before, how he sees the fight he is leading, what he owes the president who defended him, and what he is and is not willing to say to the man publicly asking him to step aside.

By Rodney D. Sieh | [email protected]



“It Transcends Beyond Our Border”

Coleman began where he usually begins: with gratitude, and with scale. “I want to thank the president for being extremely generous to our team for the fight against this narcotic operation, not just in Liberia, but in the sub-region,” he said. “Our mandate has been clear, not just arrest and seizure, but dismantling the roots of these operations, and it being transnational, it doesn’t just affect Liberia, it transcends beyond our border. The spillover risk factor, if not dealt with here in Liberia, could be great.” It is a framing that matters for how he wants Liberians — and the region’s other governments — to understand what his team is doing: not a domestic drug bust that happened to grow large, but a transnational network whose consequences were never going to stay inside Liberia’s borders, whether or not the country was prepared to confront it.

“A Collective Effort”

He was equally deliberate about whose credit this is. “I think working together as a team, the joint security investigative team, my name may have been mentioned, but it has been collective effort, and we are very, very proud of the work that each and every member of that team has done,” he said — a line that reads, in the context of a week spent almost entirely discussing his own individual fate, like a man trying to redirect attention away from himself and back onto the institution he leads.

To Martin: “Keep Up the Advocacy”

It was in this fuller, calmer register that Coleman finally addressed Hassan Fadiga directly. “I don’t have anything to say to Martin. Martin is a brother who has been a great advocate,” he said. “He has made some accusations, maybe he has something, let him come forward with it.” Then, notably, he did not stop there the way his earlier, terser response had. “So, to Martin, keep up the advocacy, keep up the good work you have been doing well. If there’s anything credible, please bring it forward.”

It is, point for point, the same substantive position Coleman took in his first response to the recusal calls — he is not compromised, and he will step aside on his own if he ever believes he is. What is different here is the tone. Where his first answer read as defensive, this fuller version reads as something closer to magnanimous: an invitation to Fadiga to keep pushing, dressed in the language of brotherhood rather than dismissal. Whether that changes how Fadiga’s specific, narrower argument — that the appearance of a conflict matters regardless of what Coleman privately believes about himself — lands with the public is a separate question. Coleman is not so much answering that argument here as declining, warmly, to be moved by it.

“I Didn’t Expect to Be Loved”

Coleman’s fullest answer to his critics, in the end, was not really about Fadiga, or about any single accusation. It was about the nature of the job itself, in a country as small and as tightly woven as Liberia. “My commitment to this fight remains firm,” he said. “Like I said earlier, when I took on this role, I didn’t expect to be loved. This is a very difficult task. Liberia is a very small place. We’re dealing with people who we know, I mean, at different levels, people we’ve admired, people we’ve seen over the years. So it is a challenging thing, but we are committed to what we 

That admission — that the people his team investigates are, in many cases, people he has personally known and admired — is as close as Coleman has come to acknowledging just how personally corrosive this kind of work is in a country where everyone of consequence tends to know everyone else. It is also, implicitly, an answer to why an investigation this sensitive was always going to generate exactly the kind of institutional entanglement now fueling calls for his recusal: in a country this small, the line between investigator and investigated was never going to be perfectly clean, no matter who held the job.

“He Inherited Corruption as the System”

The most striking thing Coleman said all week was not about Fadiga, or the president, or even his own resolve. It was about the country he was hired to police. “One thing, when we took on this role, we did a deep dive as to how could we help,” he said. “And the president didn’t just inherit a broken or corrupt system. He inherited corruption as the system. So in order to fight it, our contribution has been to deal with that which it is ferried upon, and it’s the culture of impunity, where people believe that they can use their power, political connection, and social status, and just get away with things.”

He described the strategy in almost architectural terms — start small, and let the foundation work upward. “That’s why we started with the lowest things, traffic infraction, restoring orders on the road. It started with complaints from the travel unions, because they started to get more tickets, going up to people answering for all of the crimes that are committed. This is a new day in Liberia. The culture of impunity has been fought.” It is a theory of institutional change that runs directly through this newspaper’s own reporting on this scandal: that a country which cannot enforce a traffic stop consistently was never going to enforce accountability at the top consistently either, and that closing that gap has to start somewhere unglamorous before it can reach somewhere powerful.

The President Backs Him, By Name

Coleman’s own account of his mission did not arrive in a vacuum. Days earlier, President Boakai had already settled, publicly, where he stood — addressing Coleman not through a spokesperson, but by first name. “Greg, my government remains fully supportive of your actions and leadership as you continue to spearhead the fight against illicit drugs in Liberia,” the president wrote. “You have the full backing of my government. We stand firmly behind your actions in the ongoing fight to rid Liberia of illicit drugs and protect our people.” Coleman thanked him publicly on Facebook within hours: “Thank you, Mr. President, for your continued confidence, support, and recognition of the work of the Joint Security. We remain committed to serving Liberia with professionalism, and integrity.”

Executive Protective Service Director Sam Gaye followed with a defense of his own, less measured than either man’s exchange. “When you live in a culture of impunity, the investigation and arrest of a high-profile person are unimaginable,” Gaye wrote.

“Unfortunately, and sadly, law enforcement officials become public enemy number one.” He credited Coleman with spearheading the Capitol Hill arson investigation, which produced charges against high-profile lawmakers in a case still pending, and with leading the transnational narcotics case that has now produced charges against a former Vice President — “the first time in our nation’s history,” as Gaye put it, that government actors at that level have faced this kind of prosecution. “The IG has become public enemy number one for doing his job,” Gaye wrote, closing with a line pitched at history itself: “History will judge all of us. Mr. IG, Godspeed!”

What None of It Answers

Here is the tension none of these statements — not Coleman’s own extended remarks, not the president’s message, not Gaye’s defense — actually resolves. Coleman describes a culture of impunity being dismantled from the bottom up, traffic stop by traffic stop, until it reaches the top. But two specific, unresolved threads sit inside his own institution, unmoved by any of this week’s rhetoric. Months ago, Coleman told this newspaper that trafficking in Liberia was “sanctioned at very, very senior level.” He has never named who. And FrontPageAfrica has reported that two currently serving Liberia National Police officers — answering, ultimately, to Coleman himself — are alleged to have escorted the drug shipment at the center of the Howard-Taylor case to the stash house in Paynesville. Neither has been named. Neither has faced anything resembling the swift, public reckoning applied to Howard-Taylor. If the culture of impunity really is being fought “going up to people answering for all of the crimes that are committed,” as Coleman put it, Liberians are owed an honest account of how far up inside his own force that climb has actually reached.

Fadiga’s Appeal, in Full

It is worth reading Fadiga’s original plea again, now that Coleman has answered it twice. “IG Coleman, my Bassa brother, this is not a personal attack,” the former LDEA deputy director wrote. “It is an appeal for transparency, accountability, and public confidence.” He said he sent the same message directly to President Boakai, and that the backlash since had been immediate. “They have been blowing up my phone with insults, anger, and frustration,” he told FrontPageAfrica.

Fadiga never accused Coleman of wrongdoing, then or since. His argument was always narrower than that: that perception itself, in an investigation this consequential, is a variable worth protecting deliberately rather than trusting to one man’s own confidence in his own ethics. “Sometimes,” Fadiga wrote, “true leadership means stepping aside to protect the greater good.” Coleman’s answer, however warmly delivered the second time around, is still fundamentally a request that Liberians trust his own judgment about his own conflicts — precisely the trust Fadiga’s appeal was built to question.

What Happens Next

For now, Coleman keeps his post, backed publicly by the president, defended publicly by the head of the Executive Protective Service, and speaking, at length and for the first time, in his own voice about why he believes the fight is worth what it is costing him personally. What remains unsettled is not his job security — that question, for the moment, appears closed. What remains unsettled is whether the culture of impunity he describes fighting, traffic stop by traffic stop, will ever climb high enough to reach the two unnamed officers inside his own force, or the unnamed name behind his own “senior level” claim. Coleman has told Liberians, in his own words, that he didn’t take this job expecting to be loved. He has not yet told them who, exactly, benefited from the system he says the president inherited — and until he does, that is the answer this newspaper, and Liberians who found his words this week persuasive, should keep asking for.

World.title: Weah Warns African Leaders at 66th Annual General Conference of the Nigerian Bar Association
World.content:
PORT HARCOURT, Nigeria — Former Liberian President George Manneh Weah has delivered a forceful warning against the erosion of democratic institutions in Africa, cautioning that leaders who come to power through elections can still become authoritarian if they undermine the judiciary, weaken legislatures and suppress institutional checks on executive power.

By Gerald C. Koinyeneh, [email protected]

Weah made the remarks Sunday, August 23, while delivering the keynote address at the 66th Annual General Conference of the Nigerian Bar Association (NBA) in Port Harcourt, Rivers State, under the theme “Beyond Limits.”

Addressing lawyers, judges, government officials and other dignitaries, the former Liberian leader argued that democracy does not begin and end with elections, stressing that strong institutions are essential to preserving democratic governance.

“Democracy does not survive on the strength of elections alone,” Weah said. “Elections are the doorway into democracy, not the house itself.”

He said independent courts, a principled legal profession and effective legislative oversight are among the institutions that sustain democratic systems after elections have ended.

‘A Tyrant With a Certificate of Return Is Still a Tyrant’

Weah delivered one of the strongest portions of his address when he warned that the threat to democracy does not come only from military coups or defeated candidates refusing to concede elections.

He said democratically elected leaders can gradually undermine the same institutions that brought them to power.

“The danger is not only that soldiers might seize power in the night, or that a defeated candidate might refuse to leave office,” he said.

“It is also that a leader who arrives in office through a free and fair election can, over time and often gradually, begin to govern like the very dictators the ballot was meant to guard against.”

According to Weah, such leaders may attempt to influence the judiciary, pressure legislatures and turn institutions designed to provide checks and balances into instruments of executive power.

“A tyrant with a certificate of return is still a tyrant,” he declared.

He warned that democracy must be tested continuously after elections by examining how political power treats courts, legislatures, journalists and ordinary citizens.

Weah Calls for Strong Institutions

Weah referenced a statement by outgoing NBA President Mazi Afam Osigwe that “democracy cannot survive on strong men. It survives on strong institutions.”

He said the principle should be displayed prominently in African parliaments and courtrooms.

“The rule of law is not an abstract phrase for law school lecture halls,” Weah said. “It is the practical guarantee that a citizen’s rights do not depend on who is in office or what favor they can secure.”

He argued that the rule of law must provide equal protection to ordinary citizens, including journalists, traders and students, regardless of their social or political status.

“When that guarantee weakens, everything else in a nation weakens with it: investment, security, public trust, and peace itself,” he said.

Warning Against Judicial Interference

The former Liberian president also cautioned against executive interference in the judiciary, citing what he described as examples across the region involving manipulation of judicial budgets, questionable appointments, pressure on judges and the creation of special courts for political purposes.

He also referenced the wave of military takeovers that has affected several African countries since 2020.

While condemning coups, Weah argued that governments operating under democratic labels must also guard against institutional erosion.

He called on the Nigerian Bar Association to remain vigilant in defending judicial independence and citizens’ rights.

“This is why I say to you: the Nigerian Bar Association is not merely a professional association negotiating welfare for its members,” he said.

“You are a standing sentinel of this Republic’s democracy.”

According to Weah, when the legal profession remains silent, courts become more vulnerable to political capture, while a united and principled Bar can deter executive interference.

Weah Revisits 2023 Concession

The former president also used the address to revisit his decision to concede Liberia’s 2023 presidential runoff election to current President Joseph Nyuma Boakai.

Weah said he congratulated Boakai while the vote count was still underway after preliminary results indicated that his opponent was leading.

He said some people around him had advised waiting until the final results were formally certified before conceding.

“I chose to concede while the counting was still underway, because I have always believed, and still believe, that the will of the people must stand above the ambition of any one man in a democratic setting,” Weah said.

He argued that electoral disputes and the failure to respect democratic principles can have serious consequences for national peace and security.

Weah said the NBA’s recognition of his 2023 concession was particularly meaningful because it demonstrated the importance of placing national peace and the people’s will above personal political ambition.

“If a small nation like mine can insist on that standard for itself, then surely this continent…can insist on standards beyond the limits others have too often assumed for us,” he said.

From Monrovia’s Ghetto to the Presidency

Weah also drew heavily on his personal journey, linking his rise from the Gibraltar community in Monrovia to the broader theme of overcoming limitations.

The former football star recalled growing up largely under the care of his grandmother in circumstances where few people expected him to reach the highest levels of international football or become president of Liberia.

“I did not accept them—not out of arrogance, but because the limits placed on us by man are not the same as the limits placed on us by God,” he said.

Weah became the first and remains the only African male footballer to win the Ballon d’Or, following a celebrated international football career before entering politics.

He later became a senator and was elected president of Liberia in 2017, serving from 2018 to 2024.

Beyond ‘Brain Drain’

Turning to Africa’s development, Weah said the continent’s greatest limitations are not a lack of talent or intelligence, but inadequate infrastructure and insufficient political and institutional organization to harness African expertise.

He called for a shift in thinking about the African diaspora—from viewing migration primarily as “brain drain” to developing systems that encourage “brain circulation.”

Weah argued that African professionals living and working abroad can contribute significantly to national development if governments establish mechanisms that enable them to share their expertise without requiring them to abandon opportunities overseas permanently.

He cited African diaspora remittances as evidence of the enormous economic contribution already being made from abroad.

“Imagine that same energy formally invited into legal reform and judicial modernization, as a deliberate national strategy,” he said.

Five Values for Breaking Limits

Weah said Africa’s effort to overcome its challenges must be anchored in five values: discipline, hard work, respect, perseverance and spiritual strength.

He drew parallels between football and the legal profession, saying talent without discipline is insufficient for success.

In the legal profession, he said, intellectual brilliance must be matched by discipline, ethics and commitment to justice.

He similarly described hard work as essential to overcoming corruption, weak infrastructure and institutional inertia.

Respect, he said, must extend to the dignity of every human being, national constitutions and independent institutions.

Perseverance, he added, is necessary because individuals and nations will inevitably face setbacks.

“Perseverance is the internal voice that says, ‘I will rise again,’” Weah said.

He also stressed the importance of spiritual strength, arguing that leadership should be viewed as temporary stewardship rather than permanent ownership of power.

‘Africa Must Stand Up for Democracy’

In closing, Weah called on African lawyers and institutions to defend justice, equality, accountability and free elections.

He urged the Nigerian Bar and legal professionals across the continent to remain independent and protect the rights of people regardless of wealth, political influence or social status.

“The law must never be an instrument of chaos. It must never become a weapon of war,” he said.

“It must remain what it was always meant to be: an instrument of remedy, of peace, of unity, and of accountability.”

Weah concluded by calling on Africa to stand for the rule of law, fairness, impartiality, gender equality, human dignity, peace, democracy and free and fair elections.

“Africa must continue in peaceful coexistence, and we must all stand up for the rule of law,” he said.

The address comes as Weah remains active on the African and international stage following his presidency. He has also signaled his intention to seek the Liberian presidency again in 2029, setting the stage for his continued political relevance ahead of Liberia’s next presidential election.

World.title: Liberian Model Francis Dine Set to Chase Africa’s Next Supermodel Crown
World.content:
MONROVIA — From the classrooms of BlueCrest University to the international fashion spotlight in Nairobi, Liberia’s Francis A. Dine is preparing to take her runway ambitions to the continental stage after being selected to represent Liberia at Africa’s Next Supermodel this November in Kenya.

Dine, a student of BlueCrest University, was discovered and recommended for the competition by Liberian-American international fashion show producer and talent scout Junda Morris, who has built a reputation for identifying and mentoring emerging African talent.

Morris said Dine’s striking presence, discipline and runway potential made her stand out as a promising representative of Liberia.

“As a Liberian fashion producer and talent scout, I am proud to see Francis step onto this international stage,” Morris said. “She represents the beauty, confidence, resilience, and limitless potential of young Liberian women. Nairobi is about to experience Liberia’s next superstar.”

From Liberia to the Continental Runway

Dine’s selection provides another opportunity to showcase Liberia’s emerging fashion and creative talent beyond the country’s borders.

Her participation in Africa’s Next Supermodel, described by organizers as one of the continent’s leading model-search platforms, is expected to bring Liberia into greater focus within Africa’s competitive fashion industry.

For Dine, the Nairobi appearance will be more than a personal modeling opportunity. It will also place her in a position to represent Liberia’s style, creativity and growing generation of young talents seeking opportunities on the international stage.

A New Face for Liberian Fashion

Morris’s involvement highlights the increasingly important role of talent scouts and fashion producers in identifying African models and connecting them with opportunities outside their home countries.

According to the statement announcing Dine’s selection, Morris recognized her potential and recommended her for the continental platform after seeing qualities he believed could translate to an international runway.

Her selection comes as Liberia’s creative sector continues to seek greater international exposure, particularly in fashion, music, film and other youth-driven industries.

‘Representing Liberia With Purpose’

As she prepares for her trip to Kenya, Dine is expected to carry with her the support of Liberians at home and in the diaspora.

Her journey from university student to continental modeling contestant is being presented as a story of ambition, confidence and opportunity—and a reminder that Liberia’s fashion talent can compete beyond its borders when given the right platform.

With Nairobi as her next runway destination, Dine now has an opportunity to turn recognition at home into a much bigger continental breakthrough.

Francis A. Dine — representing Liberia with elegance, confidence and purpose.

World.title: Liberia: Boakai: Flag Day Must Move Us To Action
World.content:
Monrovia – President Joseph Nyuma Boakai has urged Liberians to turn national pride into daily responsibility, warning that the Lone Star demands unity, discipline, and service as the nation marked 179 years of its flag.

By Emmanuel Weedee-Conway

Speaking at the official program marking this year’s National Flag Day, President Boakai said the flag is more than a national symbol. The event was held at the Executive Pavilion on Ashmun and Broad Streets in Monrovia.

‘’It is beyond the cloth and the recognizable colors of our flag lies a powerful expression of our national identity, our national history, and the struggles and aspirations of our people,” President Boakai told a crowd of government officials, diplomats, students, and citizens.

From Independence to Identity

The President noted that this year’s Flag Day, which follows last month’s 179th Independence Anniversary under the theme: “Strengthening National Identity Through Liberian-Led Historical Leadership,” must give Liberians one national identity – a visible, enduring symbol.

“It reminds us of who we are, where we come from, and the Liberia we must continue to build.”

He recalled the role of the seven women led by Susanna Lewis who sewed the first flag in 1847.

“Our national flag derives from the courage and determination to give physical form to the aspirations of our people as a nation in the making,” he stated.

Say No to Drugs – A Warning To The Students

Directing part of his remarks to young people, President Boakai called on students to live by the Flag Pledge by rejecting vices that destroy the future such as drugs.

“Learn the words of the pledge, but more importantly, understand and live by them. Loyalty to Liberia means respecting your fellow citizens, obeying the laws of the Republic, rejecting violence, protecting our national symbols, working hard and preparing yourself to serve your country,” he urged.

“In particular, I urge you to say no to drugs. Drug trafficking and the use of our country as a transit and operational center pose a serious threat, especially to our young people. Do not let anyone steal your future. Stay focused, disciplined, and determined to become the citizens that Liberia needs.”

The President praised students who participated in the parade, noting: “I saw discipline. I saw precision. I saw confidence and patriotism in the eyes of our young people. I am very proud of them.” He congratulated schools recognized as Best Salute, Most Disciplined, and Best Dressed.

Lead by Example – A Message To Adult Liberians

President Boakai challenged adults and public officials to match their words with action.

“We cannot ask our children to love Liberia while we undermine its institutions. We cannot ask them to respect the law while we disregard it. We cannot demand patriotism while we place personal, ethnic, religious, or partisan interests above the national good,” he declared.

As the head policymaker of the country, the Liberian leader announced the reintroduction of civic education in primary schools and the launch of standardized civic textbooks nationwide as a step toward restoring knowledge of the Constitution, history, and citizenship.

Commemoration, Not Complacency

Calling for national unity and development, the President intoned that the flag demands action against division and corruption.

“Our flag calls on us to action. It demands that we reject division, hatred, corruption, violence, and every force that threatens our national fabric,” he said.

“It calls on us to build a Liberia where our roads connect our people, electricity reaches more communities, healthcare improves, education is transformed, opportunities expand, our young people are not subjected to drugs, and every citizen can take pride under the Lone Star,” the President asserted, emphasizing that the flag belongs to every Liberian.

“To the elder in the village and the leader in the city, to the farmer in Lofa, the fisherman on the coast of Maryland, the worker in Monrovia, and to every Liberian at home and abroad. It belongs to all of us.”

One People, One Destiny

President Boakai called on Liberians to honor the sacrifices of the past and build for the future.

“May our flag continue to fly proudly over land and sea, and across the world, where for nearly two centuries it has served as a beacon of hope… May it remind us always that we are one people, one nation, with one destiny,” he said.

“As we always say, in all that we do: let us think Liberian, love Liberia, and together build Liberia. God bless the Lone Star. God bless the Republic of Liberia.”

Meanwhile, Education Minister, Dr. Jarso Maley Jallah, said the reintroduction of civil and the launch of its textbooks will help propel Liberian young learners into responsible leadership and love for nation.

The Minister extolled President Boakai for his stewardship of the country that continues to bring improvement in the educational sector of the country.

World.title: Judiciary Statements on Presidential Petition Leave Key Question Unresolved
World.content:
Zambia’s Judiciary has confirmed that Chief Justice Dr Mumba Malila received an email, sent to his private address by a member of the public, containing documents described as “the people’s presidential petition” challenging Hakainde Hichilema’s re-election. In a statement, the Judiciary’s communications office described this mode of communication as “highly irregular,” but confirmed the Chief Justice referred the documents to the Constitutional Court for a determination on whether they constitute a valid filing.

A separate letter from Chief Administrator Nalishebo Imataa to the Secretary to the Cabinet states that, as of 18:00 hours on 24 August, no petition had been recorded at the Constitutional Court Registry. The letter references Article 103(1) of the Constitution, which allows a candidate seven days from the declaration of a President-elect to petition the court. Hichilema was declared winner between 02:00 and 06:00 on 18 August, placing the deadline at 25 August. Imataa’s letter reflects the Registry position as at the close of business the day before that deadline.

Taken together, the two statements address different channels: one confirms a submission reached the Chief Justice directly, while the other reports no filing through the formal Registry as at a stated point in time. Neither statement addresses reports, raised separately by the opposition, that access to court premises was restricted around the same period.

The Tonse Pamodzi Alliance has said the government’s position that no petition was filed should be read alongside those access reports. In a statement, Media Director Brian Matambo said armed security personnel were present at court premises and that access was limited in the period before the petition deadline. He argued that if the ordinary filing channel was unavailable, the use of an alternative channel to reach the Judiciary should not be treated as invalidating the attempt to petition.

Matambo also placed the petition question within the Alliance’s wider account of the 13 August election, referencing the Electoral Commission’s temporary suspension of the results process, the involvement of security services during the count, and what he described as discrepancies between presidential and parliamentary turnout figures. He said Cabinet Secretary Patrick Kangwa’s announcement that the inauguration would proceed came before the Constitutional Court had ruled on whether a valid petition exists.

The government has not yet issued a further response to the Alliance’s statement. Kangwa’s original announcement was made on the basis that no petition had been received within the prescribed period.

The Constitutional Court has not indicated a timeline for its determination on whether the documents received by the Chief Justice amount to a valid filing. That ruling is expected to clarify whether a substantive challenge to the election result will be heard before the planned inauguration.

World.title: The State Cannot Block the Courts and Then Claim No Petition Was Filed
World.content:
By Brian Matambo | Media Director – Tonse Pamodzi Alliance



The Tonse Pamodzi Alliance has taken note of the statement attributed to Secretary to the Cabinet, Patrick Kangwa, announcing that no presidential petition had been received within the prescribed period and that the inauguration of Hakainde Hichilema would therefore proceed.

Kangwa should not pretend to suffer from selective memory. Zambians are not in a trance. They are watching, they remember what happened, and they understand the sequence of events that brought us here.

Less than 24 hours before that announcement, court premises were surrounded by armed security personnel and access to court facilities was blocked at the very time when a presidential election petition was due to be filed.

The question Kangwa must answer is simple: how do you physically obstruct access to the courts and then announce that nobody filed a petition?

The petition was eventually transmitted to the Chief Justice under admittedly irregular circumstances. But those circumstances cannot be separated from what happened at the courts. When citizens are prevented from using the ordinary avenue provided for filing their case, they cannot subsequently be condemned for finding another means of placing their petition before the Judiciary.

Indeed, the Judiciary has now confirmed that Chief Justice Dr Mumba Malila received documents designated as “The People’s Presidential Petition” and has referred them to the Constitutional Court for consideration of the filing issue. The Constitutional Court must therefore be allowed to deal with that question without political or administrative interference.

This latest development must also be understood against the wider sequence of events surrounding the disputed August 13 election. ECZ suspended the results process. Thereafter, we witnessed an extraordinary involvement of the military in an electoral process that should ordinarily be administered by civilian institutions. Results subsequently emerged containing serious inconsistencies which we have already begun placing before the Zambian people, including discrepancies between presidential and parliamentary turnout figures.

Then came the constitutional opportunity to challenge those results. And what happened? The courts were blocked.

This is why we find Kangwa’s rush to pronounce the inauguration more troubling than the irregular manner in which the petition reached the Chief Justice. The fundamental issue before Zambia is not whether an email was conventional. The fundamental issue is whether Zambians will be permitted to exercise their constitutional right to challenge a disputed presidential election.

Kangwa must also understand that his conduct as a senior public officer is being watched and recorded. His role and public pronouncements surrounding the late President Edgar Chagwa Lungu remain fresh in the minds of many Zambians. His comments following the death of Hon. Mutotwe Kafwaya during this election period have also been noted. His present rush to pronounce the presidential transition concluded, while the Judiciary itself says the Constitutional Court will consider the petition’s filing, raises further serious questions.

We therefore repeat the question we have asked before: if Hakainde Hichilema genuinely believes that he won the August 13 election freely and fairly, why should anybody be afraid of a petition?

A petition is not an insurrection. It is not terrorism. It is not an attack on the State. It is a constitutional process through which disputed elections are tested before a court of law. If the declared results are genuine, let them withstand judicial scrutiny.

Zambia desperately needs the truth. Zambia needs healing. That healing will not come from soldiers outside courtrooms, administrative pronouncements or attempts to shut down legitimate constitutional questions. It will come when every democratic process is allowed to reach its lawful conclusion and every institution is permitted to perform its constitutional duty.

The Constitutional Court must therefore be allowed to determine the question now placed before it. No public officer should attempt to prejudge that process.

And when all this is over, everyone who exercised public power during this extraordinary period must be prepared to account for his or her decisions in accordance with the law. That includes those commanding the military and police, those administering the electoral process, and senior officials within the Executive and Judiciary. Public office does not extinguish personal responsibility for unlawful conduct.

Let the petition be heard. Let the evidence be examined. Let the truth come out. That is not too much to demand in a constitutional democracy.

Brian Matambo

Media Director, Tonse Pamodzi Alliance

World.title: North-Western PS calls for development cooperation
World.content:
The Department of National Registration, Passport and Citizenship (DNRPC) in Mwinilunga district is making steady progress in issuance of birth certificates to children below the age of five.

District Registrar, Gradson Kamanga, says the department under the UNICEF supported Enhanced Chances for Human Development (EC4HD) programme, is registering and issuing close to 800 birth certificates monthly.

Speaking when he handed over birth certificates to parents at Chibwika Rural Health Centre as well as Chibwika and Mudyanyama Primary Schools, Mr Kamanga explained that the department has a target of issuing 2,500 birth certificates quarterly.

“For this quarter, we have again already passed our target because our CBVs who have been trained are really doing their job, so in every month we are targeting to issue out 833 birth certificates and more,” said Mr Kamanga.

He said the department is ensuring that every child in school and those in the community are registered and given birth certificates by working with teachers, health workers and community based volunteers such as Safe Motherhood Groups (SMAGs), Community Welfare Assistance Committees (CWACs).

Mr Kamanga added that through health staff and volunteers, the department is making sure that all children born at health facilities are registered before they are discharged and issued with birth certificates within a week.

He called on all parents and guardians in the district to ensure that their children acquire birth certificates as the document is important for determining the age of the child, enrollment in school, acquisition of National Registration Cards (NRCs).

Meanwhile, Gift Chilomba, a Community Health Assistant at Chibwika Rural Health Centre said every mother who delivers from the health facility is encouraged to carry the child’s birth record which is a key requirement in registration of birth certificates.

“So we receive the forms from our district office and we make sure to fill them in and send them back to our district offices where they are handed over to the registration department for printing the certificates,” she said.

And Florence Ngolofwana, who received birth certificates for her two children, said she was happy to have the birth documents because they will be easily identified as citizens of Zambia and will not struggle to have them registered for various government services and programmes.

“So I am very happy to receive these certificates especially after receiving the knowledge about the importance of registering our children for birth certificates” said Ms Ngolofwana.

She has since encouraged fellow parents around Chibwika satellite to avail their children so that they can be registered and issued with birth certificates.

World.title: Chief Mumena toasts President Hichilema’s victory
World.content:
North-western Provincial Council of Chiefs Chairperson, Chief Mumena has congratulated President Hakainde Hichilema and the United Party for National Development (UPND) on winning the 2026 general elections.

Speaking during a media briefing in Kalumbila District, Chief Mumena expressed gratitude for the peaceful manner in which the elections were conducted, describing them as among the most peaceful elections the country has witnessed.

Chief Mumena said although there were a few isolated incidents of differences, these could be addressed collectively as a nation.

He commended the peace that characterised the electoral process and called for continued investment in peace, dialogue and national unity.

The traditional leader also commended all political parties and political players who participated in the elections, saying their participation was essential to the growth of democracy.

“For those who took part, political parties and political players, whether as individual parties or as alliances, we are grateful for aspiring to lead this great nation,” Chief Mumena said.

He further congratulated the Electoral Commission of Zambia (ECZ) for the manner in which it conducted the electoral process, saying the successful elections were an indication that Zambia’s democracy continues to grow.

“For those elected, the election is over. We also want to congratulate the Electoral Commission of Zambia for the manner in which they conducted their business leading to the successful succession. At least we can see that our democracy is growing,” he said.

Chief Mumena urged all elected leaders, from Members of Parliament to councillors, to focus on delivering their mandate, pursue dialogue and address areas requiring improvement.

“Many hearts were broken, but we can work together to heal and move on as a nation. Pursue dialogue, peace and unity, and show leadership so that those that are led should be able to say we have leaders in place,” he said.

Chief Mumena stressed that effective leadership requires followers, urging elected leaders to remain connected to the people they serve.

“If you have no following, then you are not a leader. So as you pursue and move with your programmes, always look behind and see whether your followers are still with you, lest you continue on a journey alone. Success is shown by the leadership following that you have,” he said.

The traditional leader also congratulated newly elected Lumwana Member of Parliament, Mathews Mashimamgo, urging him to continue working with the team that supported his campaign and remember their contribution.

Chief Mumena also welcomed the increased number of independent candidates elected to various positions, saying they had a responsibility to serve the people who voted for them.

“Those that are coming as independents, we are very grateful. This is the only time Zambia has seen so many independents. As much as you are independent, remember that people voted for you ,so you are not alone. You are answerable to the people,” he said.

He said all elected leaders had a responsibility to work towards growing the economy and developing the country.

“Above all, let us grow the economy, let us grow the nation,” Chief Mumena said.

World.title: No petition filed, President Hichilema to be sworn-in – Kangwa
World.content:
Secretary to the Cabinet, Patrick Kangwa has announced that President-elect Hakainde Hichilema will be sworn into office on Tuesday, September 1, 2026.

In a statement issued to the media today, Mr Kangwa said the Judiciary had not received any petition at the expiration of the seven days provision allowed for filing in of petition challenging a presidential election.

“This serves to inform the Nation that at the expiration of the seven days provision allowed for filing in of a petition challenging a Presidential election, the Judiciary had not received any petition,” Mr Kangwa said.

He said the swearing-in ceremony of the President-elect will therefore proceed on September 1, 2026, in accordance with the provisions of Article 105 of the Constitution of Zambia Act No. 2 of 2016.

Mr Kangwa said the venue for the inauguration ceremony will be communicated in due course.

World.title: Driver dies in Kazungula accident
World.content:
A 32-year-old man identified as Andrew Edwin Simwimba of Kabanana Site and Service, Lusaka who was a driver for City Frontiers in Lusaka died yesterday in Kazungula after being run over by an unknown truck.

The accident which claimed the life of the victim occurred between 04:00 hours and 07:00 hours at the Kazungula Bridge Point Truck Park on August 24, 2026.

Mr Simwimba sustained fatal injuries and was pronounced dead upon arrival at Kazungula District Hospital and his body has been taken to Batoka Hospital Mortuary in Livingstone awaiting post-mortem examination.

This is according to a statement issued by Southern Province Commanding Officer, Moono Namalongo.

Mr Namalongo disclosed that preliminary investigations indicate that the pedestrian, who was reportedly under the influence of alcohol or drugs, was lying in the truck park when he was run over by an unknown truck bearing an unknown registration number and being driven by an unknown driver.

“The circumstances surrounding the accident are subject to further investigation. The Zambia Police Service is appealing to the driver involved or anyone with information that may assist in identifying the vehicle and driver to report to the nearest police station,” Mr Namalongo said.

World.title: Chinsali Council relocates roadside traders
World.content:
The Lamba Lima Council of Elders has congratulated President Hakainde Hichilema on his re-election as Republican President.

Council of Elders Member, Josphat Nsundwe, says the victory obtained in the August 13, 2026 general elections has cheered the Lamba people on the Copperbelt Province and other areas.

Mr Nsundwe said the Lamba people on the Copperbelt, Central and Northwestern Provinces have praised President Hichilema for winning another term in office.

He added that the Council of Elders has noted a number of projects that the President has undertaken in the past five years.

Mr Nsundwe said programmes such as free education have seen a number of children going back to school.

He added that the school feeding programme, is also helping in improving the lives of school going children.

World.title: IBA renews 16 broadcasting licenses
World.content:
The Independent Broadcasting Authority (IBA) Board has renewed sixteen broadcasting licenses across the country.

The renewed licenses include 14 radio stations and two in the television category, comprising seven community radio stations, six commercial and two religious stations respectively.

And the Board has approved applications for three broadcasters to change their licence categories and station names.

IBA Director General Webster Malido disclosed this in a press statement issued today.

Mr Malido said the renewals and approvals were granted during its 46th Ordinary Board Meeting held recently.

He said that the approvals and renewals of the licenses are a statutory and regulatory requirement in accordance with Section 28 of the Independent Broadcasting Authority (Amendment) Act No. 26 of 2010.

He named the stations whose licenses were renewed as Shekinah Community Radio of Chingola district, Namwianga Community Radio in Kalomo, Salvation Army Radio in Chikankata, Breeze FM Radio in Chipata, Kwenje Community Radio in Chama and Nyimba FM Radio.

Others are PASME Community Radio of Petauke, 945 Metro Sports Radio of Lusaka, Tuta FM Radio in Mansa, Bangweula FM Radio in Samfya, Direct Connect Talk Radio in Lusaka, Kokoliko Radio in Chingola, Kanchibiya FM Radio in Kanchibiya and Chipata’s Radio Maria.

Lumen Television and Strong Technologies Subscription Management Service both of Lusaka are in the television category.

Mr Malido, who also serves as Board Secretary, said all renewed licenses are valid for a period of five years, subject to payment of prescribed fees and continued compliance with the IBA Act, broadcasting guidelines and Standard Operating Procedures.

He stated that the Authority reminds all broadcasting licensees that applications for license renewal, together with all required documentation and prescribed fees, should be submitted at least six months before the expiry of their licenses in accordance with the law.

Meanwhile, the Board, pursuant to Section 27 of the Independent Broadcasting Authority (Amendment) Act No. 26 of 2010, approved applications by three broadcasters to change their broadcasting license categories.

Chisamba FM was approved to change its broadcasting licence category from Community to Commercial, while Blessings Miracle Television and Miracle FM Radio changed from Religious Community to Commercial categories.

Mr Malido revealed that Chisamba FM in Chisamba district changed its name to Mwomboshi FM while Blessings Miracle Television in Lusaka district also changed its name to Beacon Media Television.

He said the IBA reiterates its commitment to promoting a professional, diverse and accessible broadcasting sector in the country.

He urged all broadcasting licensees to continue operating in compliance with their licence conditions, the IBA Act, broadcasting regulations, guidelines and programming standards.

World.title: Africa: All of Africa Today - August 25, 2026
World.content:
Two UN Peacekeepers Killed in South Sudan Ambush

Two UN peacekeepers have been killed and seven others injured after unidentified gunmen ambushed a UNMISS patrol in South Sudan's eastern Jonglei state. The injured include three peacekeepers, two national police officers and two civilian staff. UNMISS chief Anita Kiki Gbeho condemned the attack and called for a prompt investigation, warning that attacks on peacekeepers may constitute war crimes. The incident comes as renewed violence puts South Sudan's fragile peace process under increasing strain. The country remains one of the world's most dangerous places for aid workers, with at least 36 humanitarian workers killed since January.

Prince Harry Steps Down from African Parks Board

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Prince Harry has stepped down from the board of African Parks, an African wildlife charity he supported for 10 years. However, he remains a supporter of its conservation mission. His departure follows an independent investigation into allegations that rangers managed and funded by the organisation committed human rights abuses, including beatings, rape and torture, against indigenous people in Congo-Brazzaville. African Parks admitted the abuses last year and said it had since strengthened its safeguarding measures and governance. Harry's exit comes as he and Meghan prepare to relocate with their children from California to the UK.

Kagame Slams 'One-Sided' US Sanctions Over DR Congo Conflict

Rwandan President Paul Kagame has criticised US sanctions imposed over Rwanda's alleged involvement in the conflict in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo. He said that they add to existing problems without addressing the root causes of the crisis. The US sanctioned the Rwanda Defence Force and four senior commanders in March, accusing them of supporting AFC/M23. Kigali described the measures as one-sided. Kagame said international pressure should also address the role of the FDLR, the Congolese government and other actors, arguing that the conflict cannot be blamed solely on Rwanda. He said Rwanda would continue pursuing peace while taking measures it considers necessary to protect its security.

Former DP Gachagua Vows to Contest 2027 Presidential Election

Former Kenyan Deputy President Rigathi Gachagua has said that his impeachment does not automatically prevent him from contesting the 2027 presidential election. Gachagua is challenging the decision in the Court of Appeal and potentially the Supreme Court. Gachagua argued that the High Court acknowledged his right to a fair hearing was violated. However, they still upheld his removal from office, which he called a constitutional "absurdity". Gachagua insists he remains a presidential contender, declaring that he is not a "kingmaker" but a potential candidate himself. He said that his opposition to President William Ruto is driven by concerns over governance rather than personal bitterness.

Close 

Tanzania Commission Begins Probe Into Election Violence

The Presidential Commission of Inquiry into the Individuals Involved in Violence and Violations of the Law during and after the October 2025 General Election has officially begun preparations to investigate those responsible. Commission chairperson retired Court of Appeal Judge Shaban Ali Lila said it will collect evidence from the public and other stakeholders. He said the commission would receive oral testimony, examine documents, and visit locations identified as connected to the incidents under investigation. The commission, established by President Samia Suluhu Hassan, will assess the evidence in accordance with Tanzanian laws and regulations.

US Seeks Wider UN Arms Embargo on Sudan

The United States has proposed expanding the UN arms embargo on Darfur to cover all of Sudan, as the country's civil war enters its fourth year. US Envoy Massad Boulos told the UN Security Council that weapons and financial support from outside powers were fuelling the conflict and proposed including drones and related technology under the embargo, as well as increasing monitoring. Sudan has backed a technical extension of the existing embargo but warned against measures that could weaken its army. Russia has expressed concerns about expanding the sanctions. The war between Sudan's army and the Rapid Support Forces has killed tens of thousands and displaced millions, with Darfur among the areas worst affected by violence.

World.title: South Africa: Businessman Seeks Bail in Trafficking Case - South African News Briefs - August 25, 2026
World.content:
KwaZulu-Natal Businessman Seeks Bail in Trafficking Case

A KwaZulu-Natal businessman accused of human trafficking and sexual exploitation is set to apply for bail at the Durban Magistrates Court, reports EWN. The 65-year-old, whose identity is protected by law, was arrested by the Hawks. He is accused of being the ringleader of a trafficking operation in which four women were allegedly lured from Johannesburg to Durban with promises of sales jobs before being forced into prostitution and pornography. His alleged accomplice, a 48-year-old man, is also expected in court. The businessman has also been linked to senior police officers and politicians through testimony at the Madlanga Commission.

Two Killed, 12 Injured in Eastern Cape Crash

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Two people have been killed and 12 others injured in a collision involving a car and a minibus taxi in Duncan Village in KuGompo City, Eastern Cape, reports SABC News. The crash occurred as the two vehicles were travelling in opposite directions. The provincial Transport Department has said that reckless and negligent driving is suspected to have contributed to the collision. The injured passengers were taken to Cecilia Makiwane and Frere hospitals, while a case of culpable homicide has been opened at Duncan Village SAPS.

Limpopo Lawyer, Cop Husband Seek Bail in R4m Fraud Case

A Limpopo lawyer and her Tshwane Metro Police officer husband are set to continue their bail application over allegations that they defrauded three deceased estates of more than R4 million, reports EWN. Charlotte Tibana, who runs a law firm in Polokwane, is accused of unlawfully transferring money from trust accounts. Acting as executor, while Peter "Gagash" Nonyane is alleged to have been involved in the fraud. The State is opposing bail and has expanded the allegations from an initial R1.75 million to more than R4 million. Tibana faces three counts of fraud and two of money laundering. Nonyane faces two counts each of fraud and money laundering. Both deny the allegations.

World.title: Liberia: Former VP Howard-Taylor Sent to Prison as Court Rejects Bail Request
World.content:
MONROVIA — Former Vice President Jewel Howard-Taylor was sent to jail Wednesday after the Monrovia City Court denied a request from her lawyers to release her on humanitarian grounds, days after she suffered a medical emergency in police custody.

Stipendiary Magistrate Ben Barco issued a writ of arrest naming Howard-Taylor and three foreign nationals on charges including unlicensed importation of controlled drugs, illicit trafficking, abuse of office, criminal conspiracy, criminal facilitation, criminal solicitation, money laundering and aiding the consummation of a crime.

Howard-Taylor, who was vice president from 2018 to 2024, was stopped at Roberts International Airport on Aug. 19 as she prepared to board a flight to Ghana, and held at Liberia National Police headquarters. She suffered a medical emergency in custody and was taken under police escort to the Gomez Institute of Medical Sciences. Her lawyers said at the time that the hospital transfer did not release her from government custody.

Her legal team has rejected the allegations, calling them baseless and politically motivated, and has said it will defend her vigorously.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

The writ traces the case to 2021, alleging that three foreign nationals, Sheik Bashiru Kante, Taras Zadereiko and Mihovil Vrovac, conspired to move cocaine into and out of Liberia for onward shipment to Europe. It alleges that Kante introduced the other two to Howard-Taylor in 2022, while she was vice president, and that the four later met at her residence in Congo Town.

The foreign nationals then invited her to Dubai to meet Nikola Ivancic, a Croatian national the complaint identifies as the head of the network, according to the writ.

The writ alleges that in Dubai she received US$45,000 from Ivancic, described as money for shopping, in the presence of the other three, and that after returning to Liberia she requested and received a further US$75,000. It alleges the group discussed using Liberia as a transit route for cocaine bound for Europe.

The government said last week that Howard-Taylor faces charges under the Controlled Drug and Substance Act, the Penal Law and the Anti-Money Laundering and Terrorist Financing Law. The Ministry of Justice said three foreign nationals have been charged in absentia.

None of the allegations has been tested in court, and Howard-Taylor is presumed innocent unless convicted.

World.title: Clinton-appointed judge triggers appeal after blocking key voter citizenship law
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

A Clinton-appointed judge in Ohio is blocking the implementation of an Ohio law that requires voting registrants to provide photo ID proof of their citizenship before enrollment.

In a decision delivered on Tuesday, Judge Solomon Oliver Jr. stayed the law, citing what he saw as a conflict with federal requirements.

"The court grants plaintiff’s motion for preliminary injunction … from relying on House Bill 54’s amendment to require any driver’s license or renewal to produce documentary proof of citizenship before offering the opportunity to register to vote," Oliver wrote.

The decision is just the latest development in the national debate over state-level voting requirements designed to prevent non-citizens from participating in U.S. elections — and how far those requirements can go without overarching federal reforms.

FEDERAL APPEALS COURT RESTORES TEXAS MAIL BALLOT ID REQUIREMENTS IN MAJOR ELECTION INTEGRITY RULING

Most immediately, the decision means that voter registrants in Ohio can once again enroll without a passport, a current driver’s license, a certification of naturalization, or a birth certificate.

Ohio Secretary of State Frank LaRose announced on Tuesday that his office plans to appeal the decision.

"We strongly disagree with that decision, and I’ve asked our legal team to file an immediate appeal. I will vigorously defend our legal authority to safeguard our voter rolls and protect the integrity of Ohio’s elections," LaRose said in a statement.

In the case of Red Wine & Blue v. the Ohio Secretary of State, the court was asked to weigh whether requirements under the new Ohio law conflict with the National Voter Registration Act (NVRA), also known as the "Motor Voter Act."

That law, passed in 1993 under the Clinton administration, instructs states to give voters the opportunity to register to vote using the same information they use when applying for a driver’s license. The bill was originally intended to increase voter participation.

NEW JERSEY REMOVES 6,600 PEOPLE FROM VOTER ROLLS WHO WERE ELIGIBLE TO CAST A BALLOT FOR 2024 ELECTION

It states that "the voter registration application portion … for a driver’s license may not require any information that duplicates information required in the driver’s license portion of the form."

Notably, the NVRA doesn’t explicitly prohibit states from requiring proof of citizenship. But because virtually all driver's license forms ask about citizenship status, Oliver believes further proof amounts to redundancy.

He laid out his view in Tuesday’s decision.

"As the rest of Ohio’s voter registration scheme demonstrates, election officials do not need documentary proof of citizenship to assess a voter registration applicant’s citizenship because signed attestation of citizenship is enough," Oliver wrote.

LaRose, the secretary of state, disagreed. He cited instances of known voter fraud that have escaped detection because of the current enforcement mechanisms.

MEXICAN NATIONAL CONVICTED OF ILLEGALLY VOTING IN US AFTER FALSE CITIZENSHIP CLAIMS FACES REMOVAL: DHS

"Earlier this year, an Ohio woman admitted to voting illegally as a lawful permanent resident in 2018 because, according to the judge in the case, ‘a [Bureau of Motor Vehicles] clerk, a government official, told her to register.’ The court found her not guilty by reason of entrapment. The judge specifically noted that the voter admitted she knew she was not a citizen when she voted, but he found that the BMV employee misled her into violating the law by implying she was eligible to vote."



"The Franklin County case proves it’s not enough to just have a person’s attestation," LaRose added. "Ohio has a constitutional requirement to ensure that only U.S. citizens are voting in our elections."

A former Norfolk, Virginia, police officer filed a lawsuit against the city and its police chief earlier this month after the police department allegedly allowed a biological male to use the women's locker rooms.

According to the documents obtained by Fox News Digital, the Aug. 10 legal complaint stemmed from an August 2024 incident in which former Norfolk police officer Meghan Grabow was changing in the women's locker room and stripped down to her underwear when a recruit described as a "biological male who identifies as a woman" entered the room wearing a suit and tie. Grabow said that the recruit looked at her "as a man would look at a woman" before moving to another part of the locker room.

Grabow claimed that when she spoke to her superiors about her discomfort, she was told to "learn to deal with it" and "find another locker room" if she was uncomfortable.

SAN FRANCISCO YMCA CHANGES LOCKER ROOM RULES AFTER TRANSGENDER CONTROVERSY: REPORT

In addition to this incident, Grabow said that she and other concerned officers were told by police chief Mark Talbot that the "woman" hired by the department "will use the restroom that's appropriate for her gender" and were repeatedly instructed to refer to the recruit as "she."

Other officers also voiced concerns that they were not warned about sharing facilities with a biological male, something Talbot acknowledged could have been handled "better."

APPEALS COURT REVIVES LAWSUIT BY ALASKA AIRLINES FLIGHT ATTENDANTS FIRED AFTER OPPOSING PRIDE MESSAGE

Grabow later received an indefinite suspension pending termination in 2025 over a minor traffic violation committed prior to the incident after attempting to voice a complaint. Other officers have since left the department over their backlash to the transgender policy, the complaint states.

Grabow is seeking $15 million in compensatory damages, claiming Talbot and the police department were guilty of intentional infliction of emotional distress as well as violating her religious freedoms by forcing her to share a changing facility with a biological male and validate transgender ideology against her Catholic beliefs.

CHRISTIAN LIFEGUARD WHO REFUSED PRIDE FLAG DUTIES AND WAS SUSPENDED IS NOW HEADED TOWARD TRIAL

The Norfolk Police Department declined to comment to Fox News Digital, saying that it "cannot comment on pending litigation or personnel-related matters."

World.title: New research finds 1 in 4 NFL players could develop CTE in their lifetime: 'Should be a call to action'
World.content:
The NFL continues to make a concerted effort for safe play for all players, especially when it comes to head injuries.

But since chronic traumatic encephalopathy, better known as CTE, was found to be heavily linked to former professional football players, there has been ongoing discussion about how current and future NFL players could be affected.

New data published in The BMJ from a recent six-year research period provided some harrowing discoveries.

ZERO BS. JUST DAKICH. TAKE THE DON'T @ ME PODCAST ON THE ROAD. DOWNLOAD NOW!

The study found that at least one in every four people who have played in the NFL might expect to end up with CTE at some point in their lives.

For the study, 878 former NFL players who died from 2016-21, which varied from players in their 20s to their 80s and in between, at least 215 of them had CTE in some stage.

That’s 24.5%, with the actual prevalence likely being higher considering there were 643 of those brains that were not examined.

ALDON SMITH'S FAMILY DONATING HIS BRAIN TO CTE RESEARCH AS ATTORNEYS INVESTIGATE DEATH

If these results were applied to the NFL today, which consists of 1,696 players on the active roster combined for all 32 teams — this doesn’t include practice squad players and those not on the roster due to other injury reasons — around 415 would be diagnosed with CTE.

One of the main problems of the degenerative brain disease is that it can only be confirmed as a diagnosis post-death once the brain is examined.

The neurodegenerative disease is caused by repeated blows to the head as well as severe head trauma. The symptoms found in those with CTE include memory loss, mood swings, erratic behavioral actions and more.

While the disease was first found in boxers, it has become associated with football players in this modern era due to the repeated blows to the head sustained on every snap of the ball. It has, however, also been found in athletes participating in hockey, rugby and other sports.

But its connection to football became public when beloved players like Junior Seau, Mike Webster, Frank Gifford and others were diagnosed with CTE after their deaths. Webster was dubbed "Patient Zero" after Dr. Bennet Omalu examined his brain and became the first to diagnose an NFL player with CTE, jump-starting a concussion crisis within the game.

Dr. Julian Bailes, a neurosurgeon and chief medical advisor for Q-30 Sports Science, has spent decades studying the disease as well as concussion and repetitive subconcussive impacts. He helped pioneer the early investigation into CTE, being portrayed by Alec Baldwin in the popular film, "Concussion." He has also authored more than 300 publications and previously advised the NFL Players Association, NCAA and Pop Warner Football.

Seeing this study, Dr. Bailes believes it "should be a call to action for everyone involved in football."

SUPER BOWL CHAMPION STEVE MCMICHAEL, WHO DIED LAST YEAR, REVEALED TO HAVE CTE

"We have made tremendous progress in recognizing and managing concussions, but the science increasingly tells us that diagnosed concussions are only part of the equation," Dr. Bailes said in a statement provided to OutKick. "Repetitive head impacts accumulated over years of play matter, and we need to bring the same urgency we’ve applied to understanding CTE to preventing and reducing the forces experienced by the brain in the first place.

"That means continuing to advance rules, training, equipment and new approaches to brain protection at every level of the game. This should not be approached as an all or nothing assignment. The next frontier in athlete safety must be proactive brain protection."

A simple proactive action would be eliminating repeated blows to the head, which researchers know prevents CTE. Obviously, the game of football would forever be changed and there’s much more complexities there, especially at the professional level.

"The NFL continuously strives to make the game of football safer, including by implementing strategies to reduce concussions and head impacts," the league told The Athletic in a statement. "The NFL remains committed to ensuring that the NFL community has access to robust — and expanding — set of resources to enhance their physical and mental well being."

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

The NFL Players Association also told the outlet, "The finds should serve as a call to action across the entire football ecosystem."

There were 168 documented in-game concussions during the 2025 NFL season, which was a 30% increase from the 129 record during the 2024 campaign. There were a total of 538 evaluations and 26 medical timeouts as well.

World.title: Newsom promises new legal fight after Trump gets Supreme Court victory on mail-in voting
