“It is necessary to reframe the dialogue between the north and south of the Americas in more equal terms,” said the meeting's coordinator, David Adler, at the closing session held at the Teatro Solís. Conclusions were organised around regional integration, peace and security, care policies and welfare systems.

The congress was marked by one notable absence: former Colombian president Gustavo Petro, who promoted the first edition, held in Bogotá in 2024. Organisers cancelled his participation as a precaution to avoid exposure to sanctions, since Petro has been listed since October 2025 by the Office of Foreign Assets Control of the US Treasury Department, along with the then first lady, his eldest son and his interior minister. The designation, administrative rather than judicial in character, cited an alleged role in illicit drug trafficking. There has been no trial or conviction, and the Colombian government at the time described it as political persecution.

Among the subjects debated was the militarisation of public security in several countries in the region. Brazilian senator Humberto Costa warned that the inclusion of two organisations from his country on the US list of terrorist groups affects national sovereignty and could serve as an argument for military intervention under the justification of combating drug trafficking. He called for particular attention to Brazil ahead of October's presidential elections.

US lawmakers present referred to the midterm elections due in November in their country. Representative Jesús García called for prioritising the wellbeing of working people and respect for the sovereignty of Latin American nations.

The gathering, held from Friday to Sunday with both public sessions and closed-door debates, also included an address by Macarena Gelman, granddaughter of Argentine poet Juan Gelman, whose identity was taken from her at birth during Argentina's dictatorship and who was located years later by the Grandmothers of the Plaza de Mayo. The figure of the late Uruguayan president José Mujica was repeatedly invoked in speeches.

The forum began in Bogotá in 2024 and held its second edition in Mexico City in 2025. With Brazil chosen as host, the meeting moves to the region's largest country in the year following its presidential elections.

World.title: Man detained in Buenos Aires after driving a stolen bus, saying it was his dream
World.content:
Man detained in Buenos Aires after driving a stolen bus, saying it was his dream

24th Monday, August 2026 - 21:44 UTC Full article

The situation came to light when the bus scraped another vehicle belonging to the same company

A man was detained on Sunday in the western part of the Buenos Aires metropolitan area after driving a city bus for several kilometres, having taken it without authorisation from a depot, following the line's regular route and picking up passengers at stops.

The episode began at around 6:30am at the depot operated by Empresa 216 in Pontevedra, in the district of Merlo. According to investigators' reconstruction, the man boarded a vehicle that was parked there and drove it away. He covered Pontevedra and central Morón, two districts of greater Buenos Aires, keeping to the established route and stopping to let passengers board, none of whom noticed anything irregular. He was wearing a shirt bearing the company logo.

The situation came to light when the bus scraped another vehicle belonging to the same company. Its driver alerted colleagues and, once it was confirmed the unit had left the depot without its assigned driver, a union representative filed a theft report at the police station.

A patrol car located the bus in southern Morón. An officer from the fourth precinct of Gervasio Pavón went to a stop a few metres from the station, raised his arm as though he were a passenger and, when the vehicle stopped, boarded, identified himself and told the driver he was under arrest.

The case is being handled by Prosecutor's Office No. 2 in Morón, headed by Fernando Capello, which ordered a psychiatric evaluation of the detainee to determine whether he is fit to face charges. On being detained, the man said: “I wanted to fulfil my dream of being a bus driver.” According to the newspaper Perfil, officers seized a knife from him. No injuries have been reported.

The bus sustained bodywork damage as a result of the collision and was handed to the company for repairs before returning to service. The detainee has not been publicly identified and has not been convicted.

Urban bus lines, known locally as colectivos, are the main form of transport in greater Buenos Aires, a metropolitan area of around ten million people surrounding the Argentine capital. The route the man covered extended for more than eleven kilometres, according to some local reports.

World.title: Colombia orders deportation of irregular migrants after a decade as the main host country
World.content:
Colombia orders deportation of irregular migrants after a decade as the main host country

24th Monday, August 2026 - 21:37 UTC Full article

“The order to Migration is clear: first those committing crimes, second those who have not regularised their status, who in due course will have to be deported,” he said

Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella has ordered coordinated operations between the migration authority and the police to begin this week to identify and deport foreigners without regular migration status, marking a shift from the policy the country has maintained for more than a decade as the main destination for Venezuelan migration.

“The order to Migration is clear: first those committing crimes, second those who have not regularised their status, who in due course will have to be deported,” he said during a security council meeting held on Sunday in Barranquilla, the alternate seat of his government. The remarks became known through a leaked video of that meeting. “I will not accept illegal migration. First Colombians, second Colombians and third Colombians,” he added.

Figures on the scope of the measure differ. The Venezuela Observatory at Universidad del Rosario puts the number of Venezuelans without regular status at 848,000, of whom 193,000 would be minors. Migración Colombia data as of January 2026, cited by the outlet La Silla Vacía, indicate that around 82% of Venezuelan migrants hold regular status and close to 500,000 do not. The United Nations refugee agency estimated three million Venezuelans living in Colombia in 2025.

The announcement calls into question the Temporary Protection Statute for Venezuelan Migrants, created by decree in March 2021, which provides a free temporary protection permit and made the country an international reference point on migration regularisation. Colombia took in almost a third of the 7.8 million people who have left Venezuela since 2015, under governments of differing political persuasions.

“A person in irregular status is not a criminal,” said Ronal Rodríguez, a researcher at the observatory, warning against linking irregularity with crime. Congresswoman María Fernanda Carrascal, of the Pacto Histórico, called the measure “an affront to human rights” and said it lacked evidence. Academic Andrés Sampayo estimated the Venezuelan population's contribution to the Colombian economy at around 3 billion dollars a year in consumption, taxes and entrepreneurship.

Implementation faces practical obstacles. Colombia shares a 2,219-kilometre land border with Venezuela, and any mass deportation would require cooperation from the government of acting president Delcy Rodríguez, in a country undergoing a US-backed negotiated transition.

At the same security council meeting, De la Espriella ordered the activation of a rewards system, the strengthening of the informants network and prison transfers to prevent jails from operating as bases for extortion.

World.title: Milei links Lula to the case of the Argentine former adviser detained in Bolivia
World.content:
Milei links Lula to the case of the Argentine former adviser detained in Bolivia

24th Monday, August 2026 - 21:26 UTC Full article

The remarks come during the worst diplomatic crisis between the two countries since the return to democracy

Argentine President Javier Milei has attributed the criminal case against his former adviser Fernando Cerimedo, detained in Bolivia over an attempted femicide, to a regional plot in which he included Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, former Bolivian president Evo Morales and Argentine lawmaker Marcela Pagano. He offered no evidence to support the claim.

“Let's not rule out that behind this is the whole rabble,” he said on Saturday in an interview with Radio Mitre, before listing those names and referring to “castrochavismo,” a term used in the region to describe governments seen as aligned with Cuba and Venezuela. He said it was “a band of castrochavista criminals operating in the region.” In previous days he had accused Lula of running an “anti-Argentine campaign” and of “interfering in electoral processes across the region.”

The remarks come during the worst diplomatic crisis between the two countries since the return to democracy. Brasília recalled its ambassador in Buenos Aires for consultations on July 26 and on August 4 downgraded relations to chargé d'affaires level, after Milei took part in a campaign event for Brazilian presidential candidate Flávio Bolsonaro at which he referred to Lula in terms the Brazilian government deemed offensive.

In the same interview, Milei distanced himself from Cerimedo. “He is someone who is not part of our movement, who has no link of any kind with us, and with whom we stopped having contact in 2023,” he said. Casa Rosada visitor records examined by the newspaper La Nación show at least thirteen entries by the consultant to the seat of government between December 2023 and June 5, 2024. The logs record who enters and who authorises access, but do not establish meetings with the president. Then interior minister Lisandro Catalán appears as the official who most often approved the visits.

Cerimedo co-founded the digital outlet La Derecha Diario, took part in the communications strategy of Milei's 2023 campaign and advised the campaign of Bolivian President Rodrigo Paz. A judge in Santa Cruz de la Sierra on Friday ordered 180 days of pre-trial detention on a charge of attempted femicide. He denies the accusations and has not been convicted. His business partner in the outlet, Spaniard Javier Negre, told the newspaper Clarín that Cerimedo had agreed to give up his stake before the arrest.

Last week Milei reposted messages on social media questioning the severity of the injuries suffered by Nadia Beller, Cerimedo's former partner. The medical report from the clinic where she was treated records an open, comminuted fracture of the right humerus with metal fragments, requiring emergency surgery.

World.title: Some 25,000 people are seeking housing in Cali two weeks after Colombia's earthquake
World.content:
Some 25,000 people are seeking housing in Cali two weeks after Colombia's earthquake

24th Monday, August 2026 - 21:08 UTC Full article

Among those seeking accommodation, the prevailing perception is of a generalised rise in prices

The municipal survey in Cali, Colombia's third city with more than two million inhabitants, now covers 10,000 families affected by the magnitude 7.4 earthquake of August 10 and estimates around 25,000 people have been left without adequate housing. Many have spent recent days in shelters or with relatives while searching for a rental, in a market strained by the sudden loss of supply.

The city government has carried out detailed assessments of 920 buildings, of which 56 collapsed. Technical analyses place the greatest concentration of damage in commune 19, where close to 200 properties may end up being demolished.

Among those seeking accommodation, the prevailing perception is of a generalised rise in prices. “Rents have gone up in every neighbourhood,” says Laura del Mar Villada, 29, who left her flat in the El Limonar district on the day of the quake and has not yet been able to retrieve her belongings. Manuel Alejandro Molina, 40, who lived with his wife and three-month-old son in the south of the city, says properties that previously cost 2.8 million pesos a month are now being advertised at up to 3.8 million.

Available data, however, point to a localised effect. Economist Sebastián Súlez, a former finance secretary of Jamundí, compiled listings from sixteen portals and estate agencies across 63 neighbourhoods up to August 19 and compared them with a partial snapshot from August 9, the day before the earthquake. Of the eleven comparable neighbourhoods, six recorded falls, one held steady and four rose. In Bellavista, in the affluent western area, the median went from 4.1 to 4.8 million pesos, a rise of 17.1%; in Ciudad Meléndez, in the harder-hit south, prices fell 6.3%. These are asking prices set by landlords, not amounts finally agreed.

Property adviser Harold Andrés Millán observes that owners managing their own properties are asking between 25% and 30% more, while rents on company-managed stock have not changed. Along the corridor where buildings collapsed, he adds, supply and demand have fallen alike.

Mayor Alejandro Eder said days after the earthquake that rents in some areas had doubled and asked the national government for a temporary rent freeze. He also acknowledged a gap in support programmes aimed at middle-income households.

The Colombian Federation of Real Estate Boards clarified that the earthquake does not automatically terminate leases or exempt tenants from payment, though the Civil Code allows termination to be sought if a property becomes uninhabitable. According to the national statistics institute, four in ten Colombian households were renting in 2025, the highest share since at least 2019.

World.title: Despite a Q2 dip, first-semester Foreign Direct Investment was Mexico’s highest ever
World.content:
Mexico attracted US $34.968 billion in Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) between January and June 2026, marking the highest amount ever recorded for a first semester, the Economy Ministry (SE) reported.

The figure represents a 2.1% year-on-year increase compared to the same period last year and confirms Mexico’s continued appeal as a destination for established international companies.

Going back further, foreign investment practically doubled, with an accumulated growth of 89.7%, compared to the first half of 2021, when Mexico attracted US$18.433 billion,

The 2026 advance lost momentum, however, during the second quarter, when revenues reached $10.464 billion, 3.5% less than the $10.848 billion originally recorded during the same period in 2025.

The SE attributed the contraction to last year’s high base of comparison and indicated that it does not represent a change in trend. Despite the year-on-year decline, the result for the second quarter of 2026 was the second highest in the last 16 years.

Who received the foreign investment?

The manufacturing industry was the primary recipient of the arriving resources, receiving $13.482 billion, equivalent to 38.6% of total FDI. The figure represents a 9.3% year-over-year increase for manufacturing.

Financial and insurance services ranked second, with $10.15 billion, followed by the transportation, postal, and warehousing sectors, which registered the strongest growth, attracting $2.65 billion.

Mexico City came in as the top destination for foreign investment, receiving $16.862 billion, or 48.2% of the national total. It was followed by Nuevo León, with $3.712 billion; México state, with $2.114 billion; Baja California, with $1.743 billion; and Jalisco, with $1.406 billion.

Together, these five states accounted for 73.9% of all FDI received during the first half of the year.

Where did the first semester FDI come from?

In the first half of 2026, the United States remained the leading source of FDI in Mexico, with a flow of $16.871 billion, equivalent to 48.2% of the total.

Spain ranked second with $4.954 billion, followed by Canada ($1.741 billion), Australia ($1.698 billion) and Germany ($1.647 billion).

According to the SE, the positive FDI numbers are attributed to the country’s macroeconomic and institutional fundamentals and the guidelines of Plan México, the government’s flagship economic and policy strategy.

Mexico News Daily

World.title: MND Local: Is the tourism outlook in Los Cabos improving?
World.content:
Spring was a poor season for tourism in Mexico. International air arrivals — the driver of 80% of all tourism revenue in the country, with two out of every three passengers hailing from the U.S. — were down nationwide in March, April and May.

That trend continued in June, as spring turned to summer, despite Mexico’s role as a host for the 2026 FIFA World Cup. But outside of the host cities, which received a boost from the event — albeit not to the extent expected — high-value tourism to traditional beach tourism destinations in Mexico like Los Cabos continued to plummet. International air arrivals fell 7.1% in Los Cabos in March, 9.7% in April, 10.5% in May and 14.2% in June, relative to the same months in 2025.

July was even worse, with international air arrivals falling by 16.6%. That means that in the first seven months of the year, international tourism fell by 7.2% in Los Cabos, with overall tourism declining by 5.4%. Unfortunately, things don’t look much better for the second half of the year, with U.S. air bookings for the next six months down 13% from 2025.

That said, there are some signs of a brightening outlook for Los Cabos.

Domestic tourism is beginning to improve

After seeing falling numbers for 10 straight months — from July 2025 to April 2026 — the domestic travel market has recently shown signs of life in Los Cabos. Domestic arrivals nosed into positive numbers in May and were up 7% in July, with nearly 20,000 more Mexican nationals visiting the destination relative to the same month in 2025.

Low season rates are part of the appeal. High season prices typically peak in April (US $470 per night for hotels in 2026), with summer seeing lower average hotel room rates in Cabo San Lucas (US $336 as of the most recent numbers from May) and San José del Cabo (US $339), as well as for the destination as a whole (US $414).

But since airline bookings for the next six months are up 5.4% domestically, with a better than 9% increase in passengers from Mexico City expected through the end of the year, it appears that this isn’t just a seasonal spike, but rather a welcome return to form for what has traditionally been an important market, accounting for over one-third of overall tourists to Los Cabos.

Tourism from Canada is on the uptick

The Canadian tourism market is not as robust as the U.S., at least not in Los Cabos. Last year, for example, over two million tourists from the U.S. visited Los Cabos, versus 215,000 from Canada. So even though tourism from Canada is up 8.8% in 2026, that doesn’t make up for U.S. tourism being down by more than 7%.

Still, it’s significant that numbers are up this year for visitors from Canada, as well as for visitors from Europe, the Caribbean, and Central and South America. This diversification is important to the local economy, especially if U.S. tourism to Mexico continues to slump.

Cruise tourism continues to boom

The reason international arrivals are considered “high-value” is because these tourists, on average, spend more than US $1,300 each. Cruise ship tourists, by contrast, traditionally spend less than US $100 per person. Every little bit helps, however, especially when it comes to keeping businesses alive in downtown Cabo San Lucas.

Last year, the Land’s End city set a record, surpassing one million cruise ship tourists for the first time. This year, that record will almost certainly be broken, as through June, cruise ship arrivals were up by 64.5% through June; 789,919 through the first six months of 2026, compared to 480,198 during the same timeframe in 2025.

If this pace continues, Cabo San Lucas will top 1.5 million cruise ship passengers for the year, cementing its position as the nation’s fourth largest cruise ship destination, behind only Cozumel, Mahahual and Ensenada.

New air routes added to replace those that have been lost

Airline capacity cuts due to rising jet fuel costs, combined with a declining demand for seats to Mexican beach destinations, have led to the cancelation of several Los Cabos-bound routes this year, including the loss of Southwest flights from Baltimore, Chicago and Indianapolis, and a Delta flight from Seattle.

Fortunately, though, new flights have been added this summer to make up for, or at least mitigate, previous tourist losses. Southwest added its first nonstop flight from Las Vegas to Los Cabos during the first week of June, the same week a new domestic route was added by Volaris connecting Puebla to Los Cabos.

Once high season returns this fall, expanded service to Los Cabos will also be offered by several airlines, including Volaris in Mexico; American, Southwest and United in the U.S.; and Air Transat, Porter and WestJet in Canada.

Chris Sands is a writer and editor for Mexico News Daily, and the former Cabo San Lucas local expert for the USA Today travel website 10 Best and writer of Fodor’s Los Cabos travel guidebook. He has also contributed to numerous other websites and publications, including The San Diego Union-Tribune, Marriott Bonvoy Traveler, Forbes Travel Guide, Porthole Cruise and Travel, and Cabo Living.

World.title: Former Sinaloa state official arrested in Utah with more than 100,000 fentanyl pills
World.content:
A former Sinaloa state official was arrested this month in a Utah hotel room with more than 100,000 fentanyl pills in his possession, U.S. authorities said.

Ricardo Verduzco Bernal, former head of the high-performance program at the Sinaloa Institute of Physical Culture and Sport, was detained in Salt Lake County on Aug. 12, according to an Aug. 20 statement released by the U.S. Attorney’s Office in the District of Utah. He is currently in preventive detention awaiting trial.

Over 200,000 Fentanyl Pills Taken Off Utah Streets During Two Separate Unrelated Seizures PRESS RELEASE: 🔗https://t.co/J4P7GFf1GC pic.twitter.com/m9luPFOsax — US Attorney Utah (@USAO_UT) August 20, 2026

In its statement, the U.S. Attorney’s Office said that “according to allegations contained in court documents, in August 2026, the FBI Wasatch Metro Drug Task Force initiated a criminal investigation on Bernal and co-conspirators, both known and unknown, associated with a drug trafficking organization believed to be distributing large quantities of fentanyl and other narcotics in the District of Utah.”

The suspect is referred to as Bernal throughout the statement, although his first surname is Verduzco.

The U.S. Attorney’s Office said that in August 2026, FBI agents “conducted a controlled purchase of fentanyl from Bernal.”

“As a result of the controlled purchase, agents obtained and executed a search warrant on a hotel room in Salt Lake County, Utah. On August 12, 2026, agents executed the search warrant, and Bernal was alone inside the room where agents located and seized approximately 11,160.65 grams of field-tested positive fentanyl,” the Attorney’s Office said.

“Agents estimated the fentanyl evidence to be approximately 111,000 fentanyl pills. According to U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, Bernal is in the United States on a visitor visa.”

At the start of its statement, the U.S. Attorney’s Office said that Bernal and another Mexican national “were indicted by a federal grand jury after they were arrested and charged in two separate and unrelated cases that led to the seizure of approximately 204,000 fentanyl pills in one week.”

“Jesus Alexis Cecena Cota, 22, of Mexico, residing illegally in West Jordan, Utah; and Ricardo Verduzco Bernal, 54, of West Valley City, Utah, were charged in two separate complaints August 13, 2026,” the statement said.

The U.S. Attorney’s Office said that “Bernal is scheduled for a jury trial on August 26, 2026, before a U.S. Magistrate Court Judge at the Orrin G. Hatch United States Courthouse in downtown Salt Lake City.” He is accused of “possession of fentanyl with intent to distribute.”

During a court appearance last Wednesday, the suspect maintained his innocence despite the discovery of the fentanyl in the hotel room where he was arrested.

Verduzco’s civil service career

Verduzco served as head of the high-performance program at the Sinaloa Institute of Physical Culture and Sport, a state government institute, during the governorship of Rubén Rocha Moya, who is also accused of drug trafficking by U.S. prosecutors. He left that position on July 31, according to the newspaper Milenio.

Verduzco previously served as the director of the Municipal Institute of Sport in Guasave, a city in Sinaloa around 150 kilometers northwest of the state capital, Culiacán. He occupied that position between 2022 and 2024. Before taking up that role, Verduzco was a manager with the Guasave water authority.

With reports from Milenio and Reforma

World.title: US issues security alert concerning area of Mexicali
World.content:
U.S. officials have expressed concern that a recent drug bust in the northern border city of Mexicali could result in retaliatory violence by the “Los Rusos” crime gang.

In a tersely worded alert issued on Monday, the U.S. Embassy in Mexico urged U.S. citizens to be aware of the potential threat, adding that all “U.S. government activities in, and travel to, Mexicali have been suspended on August 25.”

The statement encouraged U.S. citizens to be aware of their surroundings at all times, to avoid local government buildings in Mexicali and to “notify friends and family of your safety in the event of an incident.”

The U.S. Consulate in Tijuana — about 180 kilometers (112 miles) east of Mexicali — shared the warning, but did not provide any details about the supposed threat.

On Tuesday morning, President Claudia Sheinbaum said the alert was issued due to the possibility that a criminal group could pose a danger, though she said “there is no specific issue.”

The Baja California state government said it has reinforced security in the entire municipality of Mexicali with the cooperation of federal agents and members of the armed forces.

“Prevention, patrol and surveillance efforts continue on a permanent basis to protect the peace of mind of Mexicali families,” Baja California Governor Marina del Pilar said on social media.

She urged members of the public to call 911 in case of emergency, or to make an anonymous report by calling 089.

State Security Minister General Laureano Carrillo said that “rigorous, continuous and coordinated work” is being carried out by state and federal authorities “to prevent and contain any type of contingency in Mexicali.” Mexico’s federal security cabinet released a statement saying it had not identified evidence confirming “a specific or imminent risk to the public” at midday on Tuesday.

El Gabinete de Seguridad informa: pic.twitter.com/43Qwwxr7O1 — Gabinete de Seguridad de México (@GabSeguridadMX) August 25, 2026

Last week, Mexican authorities — with the help of the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) — seized 120 kilograms of fentanyl pills in a joint operation carried out in Mexicali by federal and state agents.

The raid occurred at a property linked to “Los Rusos” — a cell operating as part of the Los Mayos faction of the Sinaloa Cartel — and resulted in the seizure of approximately 4 million opioid doses.

According to reporting by Luis Chaparro, U.S. authorities decided to issue the security alert after the DEA intercepted at least one call in which alleged members of Los Rusos appeared to be planning an attack on the Municipal Police and the offices of the Federal Attorney General’s Office in Mexicali.

With reports from El Financiero, El País and La Jornada

World.title: Sheinbaum puts out more fires in the Morena party: Tuesday’s mañanera recapped
World.content:
Sheinbaum’s mañanera in 60 seconds

⚖️ Rocha’s fate hinges on evidence : Sheinbaum reiterated that no one can be arrested or extradited from Mexico without evidence proving they committed a crime. Her remarks came after Sinaloa Governor Rubén Rocha Moya requested leave again amid U.S. drug trafficking accusations.

: Sheinbaum reiterated that no one can be arrested or extradited from Mexico without evidence proving they committed a crime. Her remarks came after Sinaloa Governor Rubén Rocha Moya requested leave again amid U.S. drug trafficking accusations. 🚪 Other accused officials should follow suit : Asked whether Senator Enrique Inzunza — named in the same U.S. indictment as Rocha — should also step aside, Sheinbaum said she believes other accused officials still in office should go on leave as investigations continue. However, she stressed that “everyone has to make their own decisions.”

: Asked whether Senator Enrique Inzunza — named in the same U.S. indictment as Rocha — should also step aside, Sheinbaum said she believes other accused officials still in office should go on leave as investigations continue. However, she stressed that “everyone has to make their own decisions.” 🤝 New interim governor praised as “honest” : Sheinbaum said she doesn’t know Graciela Domínguez well but called her “an honest woman” who has long fought for social justice. The Morena deputy and former Sinaloa education minister was designated interim governor by the state Congress on Tuesday.

: Sheinbaum said she doesn’t know Graciela Domínguez well but called her “an honest woman” who has long fought for social justice. The Morena deputy and former Sinaloa education minister was designated interim governor by the state Congress on Tuesday. ✈️ Lezama pressed on private jet travel: Responding to a Reforma report alleging Quintana Roo Governor Mara Lezama took 97 private plane flights while in office, Sheinbaum said it’s up to Lezama to clarify the details. Lezama denied the figures and said she never used public funds for the flights.

Why today’s mañanera matters

The case of Sinaloa Governor Rubén Rocha Moya — who U.S. prosecutors accuse of drug trafficking and weapons offenses — continues to be a hot topic in Mexico.

Rocha went on leave in early May, but returned to the governorship last Friday. However, under pressure from President Claudia Sheinbaum and Morena governors and lawmakers, he requested leave again on Saturday and the Sinaloa Congress approved his request on Sunday.

Another return to the governorship of Sinaloa appears highly unlikely for Rocha, a 77-year-old Morena politician who has essentially been disowned by his own party. Whether he can ultimately avoid extradition to the United States remains unclear. His fate appears to largely depend on U.S. authorities’ ability to submit evidence to Mexican authorities that convinces them that there is probable cause to believe the governor committed the crimes he is accused of.

At her Tuesday morning press conference, Sheinbaum stressed, once again, that no one can be arrested in Mexico or extradited from Mexico without evidence supporting an accusation that they committed a crime.

Her remarks came in response to a question about whether a Morena senator named in the same U.S. indictment as Rocha should also go on leave. The U.S. accusations against Rocha and other officials affiliated with Morena are a major headache for Sheinbaum, the leader of the “fourth transformation” political movement, of which Morena is a central part.

Also of note at today’s mañanera were Sheinbaum’s remarks about Sinaloa’s new interim governor, who is slated to govern the state until a new elected governor takes office in late 2027.

In addition, the president briefly commented on Quintana Roo Governor Mara Lezama’s reportedly extensive travel on private planes, revealed by the newspaper Reforma on Monday.

Should Enrique Inzunza go on leave?

A reporter asked the president whether Senator Enrique Inzunza should go on leave ahead of the Senate’s legislative period in September.

Inzunza, a senator for Sinaloa, is one of 10 current and former officials accused by U.S. prosecutors of drug trafficking in league with the Sinaloa Cartel.

Sheinbaum noted that she offered an opinion on the case of Governor Rocha on Monday, before declaring that she believed that other accused officials who are currently in office and under investigation in Mexico should also go on leave.

“But everyone has to make their own decisions,” she said.

Sheinbaum subsequently reiterated that “in Mexico Mexicans decide” whether a person accused of wrongdoing by U.S. authorities has a case to answer.

“When there is an investigation by the U.S. Department of Justice and it is asking for an extradition or an arrest, there has to proof,” she said.

“We’re always going to defend that [position],” Sheinbaum said.

“… It’s a matter of the law, of the constitution,” she said.

Sheinbaum: Interim governor of Sinaloa is an ‘honest woman’

A reporter noted that Graciela Domínguez, a federal Morena deputy, appeared likely to be appointed as interim governor of Sinaloa. Domínguez, who previously served as education minister in Sinaloa during Rocha’s government, was proposed for the job by the Sinaloa Congress and designated as interim governor on Tuesday morning during the president’s mañanera.

Sheinbaum said that she doesn’t know Domínguez well, but added: “I do know she is an honest woman.”

“… She’s a woman who has been fighting for social justice and people’s well-being for many years,” she said.

Sheinbaum said that the federal government would support Domínguez as interim governor. Her task, she said, will be to “work for the peace, security and well-being of the people of Sinaloa,” a violence-plagued state where rival factions of the Sinaloa Cartel are engaged in a long-running and very bloody war.

After a reporter noted that there were calls for a person not linked to Rocha to be appointed as interim governor, Sheinbaum highlighted that the decision corresponded exclusively to the Sinaloa Congress.

“It’s not a decision for the president, it’s a decision for the state Congress,” she said.

Sheinbaum: Lezama has to explain her extensive travel

A reporter asked the president about Lezama’s reported travel on private planes to Mexican and international destinations, including Orlando and Vail in the United States.

According to Reforma, Lezama — a Morena governor who took office in Quintana Roo in September 2022 — has taken 97 flights on private planes while serving as a public official. Her husband and children accompanied her on many of those flights.

Sheinbaum said that it’s up to the governor to explain her travel.

“That’s the first thing,” she said. “It comes out in the media, but we don’t know how true it is,” Sheinbaum said.

“… [Lezama] has to clarify whether she used these planes and under what conditions,” she said.

In a social media post on Tuesday morning, the Quintana Roo governor said that she had taken flights on private planes, but asserted that she never paid for them with public money.

Lezama rejected Reforma’s reporting regarding the number of flights she has allegedly taken on private planes.

“It would mean being on vacation a whole year, it would be impossible,” she wrote.

“My commitment is to work 24/7, without rest, without neglecting my responsibility at any time,” Lezama said.

World.title: Inside the amphibious history and identity of Tenochtitlán-Mexico City
World.content:
The place we recognize today as Mexico City — known in pre-Hispanic times as Tenochtitlán — has always been fascinating and cosmopolitan. Modern Mexico City is defined by its various hotspots, the different languages that drift across its streets, and cultural exchange on every corner.

But 500 years ago, the landscape was not that different.

Before the Spanish ever set foot in the Mexica capital, it was already lauded as one of the most important cities in the Americas, and it remained so after the conquest. In short, half a millennium ago, a city built in the middle of a lake fell so that an amphibious, metaphorical city could rise.

As the commemorative plaque at Tlatelolco states: “On August 13, 1521, heroically defended by Cuauhtémoc, Tlatelolco fell to Hernán Cortés. It was neither a triumph nor a defeat; it was the painful birth of the mestizo people that is the Mexico of today.”

An aquatic city

Everyone who has been to Mexico City during the rainy season knows that a trip across downtown is something of an odyssey. The city’s weather has not changed for thousands of years; what has changed is its inhabitants’ approach to it.

Tenochtitlán’s settlement on an islet in the middle of a lake made it unique, requiring the Mexicas to develop technology that remains innovative to this day: chinampas and a complex freshwater system.

These conditions allowed crops to be cultivated around the city, boosting trade between different neighborhoods and establishing a symbiosis between humans and the natural environment. What we now call “bad weather” was eagerly awaited 600 years ago: the storms that made crops grow and the lake level rise.

The unveiling of a treasure

Drs. Antonio Rubial and Jessica Ramírez conducted extensive research on the city’s transformation, distinguishing Mexico-Tenochtitlán from any other major American city where the Spaniards chose to settle.

Given its impressive organization, Tenochtitlán was one of the most attractive urban centers in the Americas for the Spanish; however, the choice was not random. The city already possessed a perfectly coordinated political, social, economic and cultural system.

“Unlike Peru, where Lima, the Spanish city, and Cuzco, the Indigenous one, occupied two distinct sites, the founding of Mexico City on top of Tenochtitlán created a dual society within the same space: a Spanish center and an Indigenous periphery,” the authors state in their book, “Amphibious City: Mexico-Tenochtitlan in the 16th Century.”

As the experts describe, beyond precious materials, the Spanish found something far more valuable: an organized society they could leverage to extract resources from a new land — the direct ancestor of the city we inhabit today.

An amphibious city

Tenochtitlán’s grid layout reveals that it was a city of hierarchies. Its neighborhoods were carefully planned, featuring their own markets, schools and workshops. Canals were maintained to facilitate the transport of people and goods, while causeways and bridges stitched the whole thing together.

Ramírez looks to the past to remind us that today’s challenges stem from the dissolution of the environmental dynamics that locals maintained before the conquest. According to the researcher, the transformation was radical.

With these changes, the landscape underwent a profound metamorphosis. Massive logging to provide wood for colonial construction became a decisive factor in weakening the soil, which historically propped up lighter, balanced structures. What had once been crop fields became cathedrals in less than a century.

Likewise, a lack of understanding regarding water management played a fundamental role in mutating the ecosystem where the imperial capital had thrived. The destruction of the Nezahualcóyotl dike was a major blow, as it was a crucial mechanism for separating fresh and salt waters. Once this system ceased to function, food production changed completely.

A heart that beats, even after the conquest of the Americas

Despite the dramatic shifts the capital of the Mexica empire underwent throughout its existence, the identity of Mexico-Tenochtitlán survived the passage of centuries.

More than 500 years after the fall of Tenochtitlán, chinampas still survive, albeit with difficulty, on the city’s outskirts; markets remain filled with dozens of languages; and a city that once thrived over a lake continues to defy ever-growing urban development.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by arca tierra (@arca.tie

Ancient canals became the avenues traversed today by thousands of cars, while public squares remain gathering spots for surrounding communities. Its physical structure was altered, but its spirit never disappeared.

Where to find the ancient city

As the plaque at Tlatelolco reminds us, the fall of Tenochtitlán was “neither a triumph nor a defeat; it was the painful birth of the mestizo people that is the Mexico of today.”

This relationship between what’s dying and what’s being born is a classic dichotomy in Mesoamerican philosophy. We have to feed the deities of death in order to create life. In this symbiotic relationship, something always remains.

That’s why we can still see evidence of the old Tenochtitlán, not only as pieces in museums but as archaeological windows throughout the city. So, it is no surprise that the Museo de la Ciudad de México is guarded in one of its corners by a pre-Hispanic Quetzalcóatl, and the Centro Cultural de España en México holds an underground calmécac (the school for young nobles).

Despite much of the ancient city being swallowed up by conquest, its roots, much like its ancient waterways, run deep underground while also being reflected in the city’s surface, reminding us of the duality that defines the amphibious Mexico City.

Lydia Leija is a linguist, journalist and visual storyteller. She has directed three feature films, and her audiovisual work has been featured in national and international media. She’s been part of National Geographic, Muy Interesante and Cosmopolitan.

World.title: Isaac del Toro wins his first Tour of Germany
World.content:
Mexican cyclist Isaac del Toro once again put Mexico at the forefront of international cycling after winning the 40th Deutschland Tour (Tour of Germany), one of the most prestigious stage races on the European calendar.

At 22 years old, this victory makes Del Toro the first Latin American cyclist to win the Tour of Germany, following his recent milestone of becoming the first Mexican cyclist in 36 years to win a stage of the Tour de France.

😱 75 Meter fehlen 🇲🇽 Isaac del Toro zum zweiten Etappensieg! 🇫🇷 Paul Magnier gewinnt in Heilbronn vor 🇳🇱 Danny van Poppel und 🇩🇪 Tim Torn Teutenberg. 👕 Isaac del Toro ist der Gesamtsieger der 🇩🇪 #DeineTour 2026! 🏆#DeutschlandTour pic.twitter.com/8iWFYttYv1 — Tour de France – DE (@letour_de) August 23, 2026

The star cyclist finished the four-stage race with an accumulated time of 17 hours, 39 minutes and 48 seconds, while Frenchman Louis Barré finished second, 53 seconds behind. Swiss rider Marc Hirschi completed the podium, 1:08 back.

Sunday’s final stage covered 156.5 kilometers around Heilbronn, with a route marked by constant climbs and descents.

With the German championship, Del Toro, originally from Ensenada, secured his twentieth professional title since winning his first in 2013 at the Tour de l’Avenir. In 2016, he also won the UAE Tour, Tirreno-Adriatico and Tour Auvergne-Rhône-Alpes.

The Tour of Germany, which ran from Aug. 19 to Aug. 23, also saw the participation of Edgar “Chucky” Cadena, 26, originally from Mexico City.

Chucky was Mexico’s national champion before Del Toro, and is part of a broader generation of athletes working to bring Mexican cyclists back to major competitions.

Participating in Team Storck-MRW Bau, Chucky tried to surprise with an attack 1.5 kilometers from the finish line. With a steady pace in the mountain stages, Chucky’s stamina on the toughest climbs allowed him to quietly climb the standings, securing the No. 10 spot overall.

With reports from Infobae and ESPN

World.title: University of Guadalajara scientists discover 6 ant-killing ‘zombie fungi’
World.content:
Six newly documented species of “zombie fungi” — parasites that hijack the behavior of ants and drive them to their deaths — have been identified in western Jalisco, marking the first scientific record in Mexico of the unusual fungus.

One of the new described species, Ophiocordyceps deltoroi, was named for Guadalajara-born filmmaker Guillermo del Toro, whose work often blends horror and fantasy.

Researchers from the University of Guadalajara (UdeG) found the fungi in a tropical forest near the Haravéri Botanical Garden in San Sebastián del Oeste, Jalisco.

Their study was published online late last year, then drew wider attention this month after reports highlighted the species named for Del Toro.

The six species belong to the Ophiocordyceps unilateralis complex, a group of ant-parasitizing fungi found in tropical forests worldwide.

After infecting an ant by penetrating its outer cuticle, the fungi produce metabolites that alter the ant’s behavior.

The infected ants ultimately clamp their mandibles onto tree bark, leaves or rocks in the forest. After the ant dies, the fungus grows from its body and releases spores, helping infect new hosts.

“It’s both monstrous and beautiful at the same time,” César Ballesteros Aguirre, the UdeG mycologist who led the work, said in a university news release.

The discovery is the first scientific record in Mexico of the so-called “zombie-ant fungi,” according to the university. The team is also studying fungi near metropolitan Guadalajara and parasites of butterflies and wasps.

The fungi are not known to pose a threat to people. Their highly specialized relationships with insect hosts differ sharply from portrayals such as “The Last of Us,” a fictional HBO series in which a mutated Cordyceps fungus spreads to humans and turns them into violent, zombie-like creatures.

Beyond the taxonomy, the UdeG work establishes a baseline for studying Mexico’s fungal biodiversity, the parasites’ relationships with their ant hosts and the chemical compounds they produce.

Their discovery provides a starting point for researchers to catalog the fungi’s metabolites and test them for biological activity.

Some related insect-pathogenic fungi have produced compounds of interest to researchers studying potential biomedical applications and pest control.

However, the new Jalisco species have not been shown to treat any disease, and any potential scientific applications would require substantially more study.

With reports from TV Azteca, Tribuna de México and Infobae

World.title: Dominican Republic Tourism Push: Fitpar Honor and Luxury Hotels

Dominican Republic · TOURISM

Key Facts — What happened The Dominican Republic was named guest-partner country of honor for FITPAR 2026, the 21st edition of Paraguay’s international tourism fair in Asunción.

— How big The tourism ministry is promoting US$4 billion, about RD$250 billion, in expected investment, including a US$500 million hotel complex in Miches.

— The catch The fair’s official launch is 26 August 2026 at the Unión Industrial Paraguaya, with the event itself in October.

— Who pays Private developers back the headline projects, with local bank BHD financing the first phase in Miches.

— What comes next A three-day Dominican presence in Asunción in October, with operators engaging the local trade and public.

Guest-of-honor status at Paraguay’s tourism fair pairs with a US$4 billion luxury investment pitch.

The Dominican Republic will be the guest-partner country of honor at FITPAR 2026, Paraguay’s international tourism fair, taking place on 16-18 October 2026 at the Centro de Convenciones Mariscal in Asunción. The honor gives Dominican Republic tourism officials a prominent three-day platform as they push a luxury investment agenda anchored by US$4 billion in expected projects.

Punta Cana anchors the Dominican Republic’s record tourism numbers. (illustrative)

FITPAR 2026 Names Dominican Republic Partner Country

FITPAR, the Feria Internacional de Turismo del Paraguay, will hold its 21st edition on 16-18 October 2026 at the Centro de Convenciones Mariscal in Asunción. The Dominican Republic will attend as guest-partner country of honor.

The fair is organized by ASATUR, Paraguay’s tourism association, with backing from SENATUR, the national tourism secretariat. The official launch is set for 26 August 2026 at the Unión Industrial Paraguaya.

As partner country, the Dominican Republic will hold a prominent presence across the three days. Its delegation and operators will engage directly with the Paraguayan trade and the general public.

The role is a showcase for Dominican Republic tourism in a South American market the country has been working to grow.

FITPAR’s 21st edition continues a fair that has become Paraguay’s main meeting point for travel agencies, tour operators and destinations. Landing the guest-of-honor slot gives the Dominican delegation top billing in programming and exhibition space.

How the Role Was Formalized

The guest-of-honor role was formalized by a letter of intent signed on 15 October 2025 in Santo Domingo. The signatories were Tourism Minister David Collado and Paraguay’s Tourism Minister Angie Duarte de Melillo.

The signing took place during a UN Tourism event, giving the agreement an international frame. Paraguay and the Dominican Republic have both raised their profiles in the organization.

For the Dominican Republic, the FITPAR slot is one piece of a broader strategy that mixes trade promotion abroad with investment attraction at home.

The sequence of events is deliberate: the letter of intent in October 2025, the FITUR luxury pitch in January 2026, the official FITPAR launch on 26 August 2026, and the fair itself in October.

Paraguay, in turn, gets a headline partner with one of the strongest tourism brands in the Americas for its flagship fair.

Luxury Push Anchors Dominican Republic Tourism Strategy

The luxury focus was set out at FITUR in Madrid on 21-25 January 2026. There, Mitur, the tourism ministry led by David Collado, centered its pitch on US$4 billion, roughly RD$250 billion, in investment expectations.

Vice Minister Jacqueline Mora described luxury as “a driver for tourism real estate”, tying high-end hotels to property development.

The strategy builds on record arrivals: the country received 11.7 million visitors in 2025, and 1,219,606 in January 2026 alone, up 5.5% year on year.

Dominican Republic tourism officials argue that moving upmarket raises spending per visitor rather than relying only on volume growth.

The January 2026 figure is striking because it shows the record pace continuing into the new year. A base of more than a million visitors in a single month gives investors confidence that new rooms can be filled.

Flagship Projects: Miches, Cap Cana and Punta Cana

The largest concrete deal is a US$500 million JW Marriott and Autograph Collection complex at Playa Esmeralda in Miches. It will have 650 rooms, with a first phase of US$300 million financed by BHD.

Miches, on the country’s northeastern coast, has been positioned as the next major resort pole after Punta Cana, and the Marriott commitment is one of the largest hotel investments announced for the area to date.

The Miches property will be the country’s and the region’s first all-inclusive luxury hotel under the JW Marriott brand, extending a luxury brand into a format the Dominican Republic pioneered.

A second project brings Archipelago International together with Tonino Lamborghini in a luxury alliance. Its first development will be in Cap Cana, backed by Duna Development Group.

In Punta Cana, the Grand Aston Coral Golf Resort represents US$160 million. With 200 rooms and 325 residences, it is billed as the country’s first fully tokenized hotel, adding a novel financing twist to the luxury wave.

Together the three projects show the range of the current cycle: global brands entering all-inclusive, fashion-branded hospitality alliances, and digital-asset financing structures, all within the same US$4 billion pipeline.

Execution risk remains, as investment expectations are not completed hotels. But the record arrival figures, 11.7 million visitors in 2025, give developers a demand story that few Caribbean competitors can match.

For Asunción in October, the message will be simple: the Dominican Republic is open for both tourists and investors.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the Dominican Republic’s role at FITPAR 2026? It is the guest-partner country of honor at the fair in Asunción on 16-18 October 2026, with a prominent three-day presence and operators engaging Paraguay’s trade and public. How much luxury investment is Dominican Republic tourism promoting? Mitur is promoting US$4 billion, about RD$250 billion, in expected investment, including a US$500 million JW Marriott and Autograph Collection complex in Miches and a US$160 million tokenized resort in Punta Cana. What visitor numbers back the luxury push? The country received a record 11.7 million visitors in 2025 and 1,219,606 in January 2026 alone, up 5.5% year on year.

World.title: El Salvador Submarine Cable Consultancy Tender Opens With CAF
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

The morning intel from across Latin America. Free.

El Salvador · TECHNOLOGY

Key Facts — What happened CAF opened a tender for consultancy studies supporting SIGET; bids close on 4 September 2026 and are open to national and foreign firms and consortia.

— How big SIGET signed a turnkey contract above US$130 million with Liberty Networks in December 2025 for a roughly 1,800 km cable to Panama.

— The catch Deployment is set to start in late 2026 and the cable is due in service only in the second half of 2028.

— Who pays A US$145 million CAF loan approved in July 2024 and ratified by the Legislative Assembly in August 2024 and again in October 2025.

— What comes next National capacity is expected to rise from 4-5 Tbps to 16-20 Tbps within five years, with the cable designed for a 25-year life.

Bids for consultancy studies close 4 September 2026 as the US$130 million-plus Liberty Networks cable to Panama advances.

CAF, the development bank of Latin America, has opened a tender for consultancy studies supporting El Salvador’s electricity and telecommunications regulator SIGET, with bids due on 4 September 2026. The technical, economic, financial and regulatory studies relate to the country’s first El Salvador submarine cable, a roughly 1,800-kilometer link to Panama now under contract with Liberty Networks.

El Salvador’s first submarine cable will run about 1,800 km to Panama. (illustrative)

What the CAF Tender Covers

The El Salvador submarine cable tender seeks consultants to produce technical, economic, financial and regulatory studies supporting SIGET, the Superintendencia General de Electricidad y Telecomunicaciones.

National and foreign firms may bid, and consortia are also welcome. Offers must be submitted by 4 September 2026.

The studies will underpin the institutional side of the El Salvador submarine cable project as it moves from contract signing toward deployment.

Opening the consultancy to international bidders suggests the government wants specialized submarine-cable expertise that is scarce in the local market.

CAF’s role as tender organizer also reflects its position as the project’s lender. Running the consultancy competition through the bank adds a layer of procurement oversight to the El Salvador submarine cable program.

The Liberty Networks Contract Behind the Cable

In December 2025, SIGET signed a contract with Liberty Networks valued at more than US$130 million. The deal is turnkey, meaning the contractor delivers the system ready to operate.

The cable will run approximately 1,800 kilometers from El Salvador to Panama. It is the country’s first submarine cable project.

Deployment is scheduled to begin in late 2026, with the cable entering service in the second half of 2028. The system is designed for a 25-year life.

A turnkey structure transfers construction risk to the contractor, an important consideration for a country executing its first marine cable project without prior in-house experience.

Panama’s position as a regional cable hub makes it the logical landing partner for the link.

Once live, the El Salvador submarine cable is expected to lift national capacity from the current 4-5 Tbps to 16-20 Tbps within five years.

How the Project Is Financed

The financing backbone is a US$145 million loan from CAF. The bank approved the credit in July 2024.

El Salvador’s Legislative Assembly ratified the loan in August 2024 and again in October 2025, completing the required approvals.

That loan comfortably covers the US$130 million Liberty Networks contract and leaves room for associated costs such as the consultancy studies now out to tender.

The structure means the state, through SIGET, owns the project while a private operator builds it, a model common for strategic infrastructure in the region.

The two ratification votes, more than a year apart, also show the project has maintained legislative backing across an extended approval process rather than slipping through in a single session.

Why El Salvador’s First Cable Matters

El Salvador has never landed its own submarine cable. Its international connectivity has depended on terrestrial fiber links crossing neighboring countries to reach cable landing stations abroad.

That dependence carries costs: transit fees, longer routes and exposure to any disruption along the path. Landing a cable directly changes the economics of connectivity.

A direct link to Panama, a major hub for submarine cables in the Americas, gives Salvadoran traffic a short route to global networks.

Policymakers expect the added capacity, from 4-5 Tbps to as much as 16-20 Tbps, to lower data costs and support data centers, cloud services and digital businesses.

For ordinary users, the effects would arrive indirectly: more wholesale capacity tends to translate into cheaper and faster retail internet over time. For businesses, a direct landing reduces dependence on routes through third countries and improves redundancy when a terrestrial link fails.

Timeline to 2028

The near-term milestone is the consultancy tender, closing 4 September 2026. Deployment work with Liberty Networks is set to start in late 2026.

Cable manufacturing and marine installation typically take well over a year, which is why service is targeted for the second half of 2028.

With a 25-year design life, the system is intended as long-lived national infrastructure rather than a stopgap.

Until it enters service, El Salvador’s international traffic will keep flowing over the terrestrial routes the El Salvador submarine cable is meant to complement and eventually supersede.

Each phase has a public checkpoint: the tender result after 4 September 2026, the start of deployment in late 2026, and commissioning in 2028. Those dates give observers clear points to measure progress against.

Frequently Asked Questions

What did CAF tender for El Salvador’s submarine cable? Consultancy studies, technical, economic, financial and regulatory, supporting SIGET. Bids close on 4 September 2026 and are open to national and foreign firms and consortia. Who is building El Salvador’s first submarine cable? Liberty Networks, under a turnkey contract above US$130 million signed with SIGET in December 2025. The cable runs about 1,800 km to Panama and is due in service in the second half of 2028. How is the submarine cable financed? Through a US$145 million CAF loan approved in July 2024 and ratified by the Legislative Assembly in August 2024 and October 2025.

World.title: El Salvador Workday Plan for 11-Hour Shifts Draws Union Rejection
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

El Salvador · SOCIETY

Key Facts — What happened The Consejo Superior de Trabajo is studying an option of four 11-hour days plus three rest days, keeping the 44-hour legal week.

— How big No law has changed; the Labor Code still sets eight hours a day and 44 hours a week under Article 161.

— The catch The Movimiento de Trabajadores Despedidos says the El Salvador workday plan concentrates the same hours rather than reducing the weekly workday.

— Who pays Workers would carry longer daily shifts; the MTD counter-proposes a six-hour day with no pay cut.

— What comes next The idea remains at discussion stage, and the MTD has asked the International Labour Organization to monitor the process.

The 11-hour day is one option under tripartite study, not a bill; a workers’ movement wants a six-hour day instead.

A proposal to let Salvadorans work 11-hour days over four days, with three rest days, is under study in the Consejo Superior de Trabajo, the tripartite body that brings together government, employers and workers. The El Salvador workday option would keep the same 44-hour legal week, and it is not a formal government bill, but it has already drawn sharp rejection from the Movimiento de Trabajadores Despedidos.

Factory and garment workers are among those who would feel any change to El Salvador’s workday rules. (illustrative)

What the Labor Council Is Actually Studying

The 11-hour day is one option under study in the Consejo Superior de Trabajo, or CST, El Salvador’s tripartite labor body. The council includes representatives of government, employers and workers.

Under the option, employees would work four days of 11 hours each and then take three rest days. The total would remain the 44 hours per week set by current law.

Crucially, this is not a formal government bill. It is a concept being examined inside a consultative body, and no draft legislation has been presented.

In practical terms, a worker on such a schedule would start earlier or finish later than the conventional eight-hour shift, in exchange for a third full day away from work each week.

That distinction has been blurred in public debate. The El Salvador workday discussion is at an early, exploratory stage, and nothing has been decided.

Tripartite study is the standard first step for labor reform in the country. Ideas examined in the CST only move forward if the three sides, government, employers and workers, find common ground, and even then they must be turned into legislation.

Why the MTD Rejects the El Salvador Workday Option

The rejection has come from the Movimiento de Trabajadores Despedidos, or MTD, a movement of dismissed workers. In a statement on 22 August 2026, it expressed “profunda preocupación y rechazo”, deep concern and rejection, toward the proposal.

The group’s central argument is that the option does not shorten working time. “No existe una reducción de la jornada semanal, sino una concentración de las mismas horas,” it said, meaning there is no reduction of the weekly workday, only a concentration of the same hours.

For the MTD, packing 44 hours into four days raises the daily burden on workers without giving them any net time back. Long shifts, it argues, affect health, family life and safety.

The movement has asked the International Labour Organization to monitor the discussion, seeking outside scrutiny of whatever emerges from the CST.

The MTD organizes workers who lost their jobs, which shapes its focus on the quality and length of working time rather than on employer flexibility. Its public rejection makes it the clearest organized voice against the option so far.

The Six-Hour Counter-Proposal

Instead of longer days, the MTD is pushing in the opposite direction. It proposes a six-hour workday with no cut in pay.

The group argues that a genuinely shorter day, rather than a rearranged week, is what would improve workers’ lives. Its position turns the debate from scheduling flexibility into a question of total working time.

A six-hour standard day would imply a 30-hour week at the same pay, a far deeper change to labor costs than the compressed schedule under study. Neither side has published estimates of what either model would cost employers.

That counter-proposal is also far from becoming law. It sets the MTD’s negotiating line as the CST continues its study of the El Salvador workday options.

Employer and government positions within the council have not produced any agreed recommendation so far.

Supporters of compressed schedules elsewhere argue that four-day arrangements can cut commuting and raise morale. The MTD’s objection is narrower: compressing 44 hours is not the same as working less.

Where the Debate Stands Legally

El Salvador’s Labor Code currently sets the standard workday at eight hours and the week at 44 hours, under Article 161. Nothing in that framework has changed.

Any move to an 11-hour day, even within the same weekly total, would require legal reform. That process has not started.

The CST’s role is to study and recommend. Until a formal bill exists and passes the Legislative Assembly, the eight-hour day remains the rule.

For now, the 11-hour option is a talking point inside tripartite talks, one that has already exposed a clear split between a workers’ movement and the idea’s backers.

Any eventual El Salvador workday reform would also have to define overtime rules, since 11-hour days sit well above the current eight-hour standard. None of that detail exists yet, which is why both supporters and critics are arguing over a concept rather than a text.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is El Salvador adopting an 11-hour workday? No. The 11-hour day is one option under study in the tripartite Consejo Superior de Trabajo. It is not a government bill, and the legal workday remains eight hours and 44 per week under Article 161. Who rejected the 11-hour workday proposal? The Movimiento de Trabajadores Despedidos. On 22 August 2026 it expressed deep concern and rejection, saying the plan concentrates the same hours rather than reducing the weekly workday. What alternative does the MTD propose? A six-hour workday with no pay cut. The movement also asked the International Labour Organization to monitor the discussion in the labor council.

World.title: Chevron Panama Solar Project Breaks Ground at Colón Fuel Terminal
World.content:

The morning intel from across Latin America. Free.

Panama · ENERGY

Key Facts — What happened Chevron laid the first stone for a solar plant at its Bahía Las Minas fuel terminal in Colón on 20 August 2026.

— How big The plant has 4.03 MWp of capacity, will generate an estimated 5.15 GWh per year and avoid 1,809.3 tonnes of CO2 annually.

— The catch Chevron has not disclosed how much it is investing in the project.

— Who pays Chevron is the offtaker; Celsia, a Grupo Argos company, is the partner installing 6,714 panels over four hectares under a March 2024 agreement.

— What comes next Construction proceeds toward a plant designed for a roughly 30-year operating life.

The 4.03 MWp plant with Celsia will power Panama’s largest fuel-storage facility for roughly 30 years.

Chevron laid the first stone on 20 August 2026 for a solar power project at its fuel terminal in Bahía Las Minas, Colón, the largest fuel-storage facility in Panama. The 4.03 MWp Chevron Panama solar installation is expected to generate about 5.15 GWh of renewable electricity a year and cover 100% of the power used by terminal operations.

Chevron’s Bahía Las Minas terminal in Colón will run fully on solar power. (illustrative)

Chevron Panama Solar Plant to Power Entire Terminal

The Chevron Panama solar project will be built at the company’s fuel terminal in Bahía Las Minas, in the province of Colón on Panama’s Caribbean coast. The site is the largest fuel-storage facility in the country.

With 4.03 MWp of capacity, the plant is expected to produce an estimated 5.15 GWh of electricity each year. That output is designed to cover 100% of the power consumed by the terminal’s operations.

The installation is planned for a service life of roughly 30 years. Once running, it will also avoid about 1,809.3 tonnes of CO2 emissions per year.

For an industrial site that moves fuel around the clock, fully covering its own power demand with on-site renewables is a notable operational shift.

The first-stone ceremony marks the formal start of construction, a milestone the company chose to celebrate publicly with government officials present. Site preparation and panel installation will follow.

Celsia Partnership and Project Design

Chevron’s partner on the project is Celsia, the energy company of Colombia’s Grupo Argos. The two companies reached their agreement in March 2024.

Under that agreement, Celsia will install 6,714 solar panels spread over four hectares of terminal land. The design matches the 4.03 MWp capacity announced at the groundbreaking.

Celsia has built a regional business in distributed generation and renewables for industrial clients. The Chevron Panama solar plant adds a high-profile fuel-sector customer to that portfolio.

The arrangement lets Chevron decarbonize its terminal operations without building and operating the plant on its own.

The March 2024 agreement predates the groundbreaking by more than two years, reflecting the engineering and permitting work required before construction could formally begin.

Officials Attend First-Stone Ceremony

The 20 August 2026 ceremony drew both company leadership and government officials. Chevron was represented by Mike Vomund, its vice president for fuels sales, and by Doriana Hun, Chevron’s general manager in Panama.

From the government side, Panama’s National Energy Secretary Rodrigo Rodríguez attended, along with Vice Minister of Domestic Commerce and Industries Omar Torres.

Their presence signals official support for private renewable generation at industrial sites. Panama has been working to broaden its energy mix beyond hydroelectric power.

No completion date was announced at the ceremony. Chevron also did not disclose the investment figure for the project.

The Bahía Las Minas location places the solar array next to tank farms and loading infrastructure, underlining that the power is intended for the terminal itself rather than for sale into the national grid.

A Long Operating History in Panama

Chevron has operated in Panama since 1936, making it one of the longest-established foreign fuel companies in the country. Its retail network includes more than 80 Texaco service stations.

That 90-year presence gives the solar project symbolic weight: a company built on fossil fuels is now generating renewable power at the heart of its Panamanian operations.

The Bahía Las Minas terminal has long been central to that business, storing and distributing fuels for the domestic market and the canal corridor.

The Chevron Panama solar investment fits a wider pattern of oil and fuel companies adding renewables at their own facilities to cut operating emissions and power costs.

Because the terminal is Panama’s largest fuel-storage site, its switch to solar is likely to be watched by other industrial energy users in the country.

What the Project Signals for Industrial Solar

Large industrial consumers in Panama have traditionally drawn power from the grid or from on-site fossil generation. A terminal that can run entirely on its own solar output offers a template for similar facilities.

The project’s numbers are modest by utility standards but meaningful at site level. Generating 5.15 GWh a year against full operational demand shows the terminal’s load can be matched by a four-hectare array.

The avoided emissions, 1,809.3 tonnes of CO2 a year, give Chevron a measurable figure for its sustainability reporting over the plant’s roughly 30-year life.

If the Chevron Panama solar installation performs as designed, it could accelerate similar agreements between fuel, logistics and port operators and renewable developers such as Celsia.

Colón’s industrial corridor concentrates exactly that kind of energy user, making the province a natural test bed for on-site renewables at critical infrastructure.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the Chevron Panama solar project? A 4.03 MWp solar plant at Chevron’s Bahía Las Minas fuel terminal in Colón, expected to generate about 5.15 GWh a year and cover 100% of the terminal operations’ power. Who is building the solar plant for Chevron? Celsia, a Grupo Argos energy company, is Chevron’s partner. Under a March 2024 agreement it will install 6,714 panels over four hectares, avoiding 1,809.3 tonnes of CO2 a year. How much is Chevron investing in the solar plant? Chevron has not disclosed the investment figure. The company announced the capacity, expected output and roughly 30-year life, but no cost, at the 20 August 2026 ceremony.

World.title: Panama Hotel Investment: Mercan Unveils US$200 Million in Projects

Panama · BUSINESS

Key Facts — What happened Mercan Group launched a 300-key Pullman Hotel & Casino and the 200-unit Santa Maria Luxury Apartments in Panama City, while the commerce ministry reported a successful Caribbean trade mission.

— How big The two Mercan projects carry a combined development value above US$200 million; the trade mission produced over B/.17 million (US$17 million) in business intentions.

— The catch Mercan’s government partnership dates to October 2025, the projects only launched in March 2026, and construction still lies ahead.

— Who pays Foreign investors buying through Panama’s Qualified Investor Program, which requires a minimum of US$300,000, are the target buyers.

— What comes next Mercan is selling units with investor visas, a guaranteed five-year buyback on hotel units and estimated returns of 3% to 6% across the two projects, while 60 exporters work to convert 650 trade meetings into orders.

A Portuguese developer enters Panama with two investor-visa projects as exporters log US$17 million in Caribbean business intentions.

Portugal’s Mercan Group has launched two Panama City developments with a combined value above US$200 million, the company’s first Panama hotel investment after decades focused on Portugal and Greece. In a separate boost for the economy, the Ministry of Commerce and Industries reported more than US$17 million in business intentions from a trade mission to four Caribbean markets, a result it announced on 24 August 2026.

Panama City, where Mercan Group is developing a Pullman hotel and a luxury apartment tower.

Mercan Makes Its First Panama Hotel Investment With Two Projects

Mercan Properties Portugal, founded in 1989, has built a portfolio of 34 hospitality projects in Portugal and Greece. The Panama launch marks the group’s first hotel venture outside those two countries.

The company, led by President Jordi Vilanova and Group CEO Jerry Morgan, launched the projects in March 2026. Together, the Panama hotel investment projects carry a development value above US$200 million.

The first is the Pullman Hotel & Casino, a five-star property branded by Accor with 300 keys. The second is Santa Maria Luxury Apartments, a 44-floor residential tower with 200 units.

The scale of the launch makes it one of the more visible Panama hotel investment announcements of the year. It also tests whether the country’s residency-for-investment framework can keep attracting European developers.

Investor Visas Anchor the Sales Pitch

Both projects are tied to Panama’s Qualified Investor Program, which grants residency to foreigners who invest at least US$300,000. Units are being sold with that visa route as a central part of the offer.

For hotel units, Mercan is marketing a guaranteed buyback after five years and estimated returns of 5% to 6% per year, while the apartments are offered with estimated returns of 3% to 5%. Those terms are aimed at buyers who want residency plus a defined exit rather than a pure real-estate play.

The partnership with Panama’s government was first announced at IMI Connect in Rome on 7-9 October 2025, alongside Vice Minister of Commerce and Industries Eduardo Arango. The projects themselves were only launched in March 2026, and construction is still ahead.

That timeline matters for buyers: the Panama hotel investment is at an early stage, with sales and permitting well before any hotel opens its doors.

Trade Mission Delivers US$17 Million in Business Intentions

While developers court foreign capital, Panamanian exporters are pushing into nearby island markets. The Ministry of Commerce and Industries, known as MICI, led a trade mission with buyers and distributors from Curaçao, Aruba, Bonaire and Sint Maarten.

The mission generated more than B/.17 million, equivalent to US$17 million at Panama’s dollar-parity exchange rate, in business intentions. Sixty Panamanian companies took part and held more than 650 business meetings.

The strongest sectors were fruits, construction materials, personal-hygiene products and poultry. The results were reported on 24 August 2026.

Business intentions are not firm contracts, so the final export value will depend on follow-through. Still, 650 meetings give the participating companies a wide pipeline of potential orders.

The four target markets are small but import-dependent, which makes them realistic destinations for Panamanian food and consumer goods. Proximity keeps freight costs low and delivery times short.

Minister Sees Real Opportunity in Caribbean Markets

Minister of Commerce and Industries Julio Moltó framed the results as proof of untapped demand close to home. The Caribbean islands import much of what Panama already produces.

“More than B/.17 million in business intentions and 650 business meetings show there is a real opportunity for our exporters in Caribbean markets,” Moltó said.

The mission fits a broader government strategy of pairing investment attraction, such as the Mercan projects, with export promotion in the region.

Officials argue that both tracks reinforce each other: a stronger export base supports jobs, while foreign-funded construction adds hotel and housing capacity.

What the Twin Announcements Mean for Panama

Taken together, the two stories sketch Panama’s current economic playbook: attract foreign capital into tourism real estate and help local firms sell more abroad.

The Mercan entry shows the Qualified Investor Program remains a working magnet for a Panama hotel investment, even if returns are estimated and construction has yet to begin.

The trade mission shows smaller, incremental wins in nearby markets where logistics are short and Panamanian goods are competitive.

The risks are real on both sides. Investor-visa projects depend on delivery, and business intentions must become signed orders before they move the trade balance.

For now, the numbers point in the same direction: foreign developers are willing to price a Panama hotel investment at nine figures, and local exporters are finding buyers within a short sail of the country’s Caribbean coast.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is Mercan Group launching in Panama? Two Panama City projects worth over US$200 million combined: the five-star Pullman Hotel & Casino with 300 keys, and the 44-floor Santa Maria Luxury Apartments with 200 units. How are the Mercan projects linked to residency visas? They are sold through Panama’s Qualified Investor Program, which requires a minimum US$300,000 investment. Hotel-unit buyers are offered a five-year buyback and estimated returns of 5% to 6%; the apartments carry estimated returns of 3% to 5%. What did Panama’s Caribbean trade mission achieve? The MICI mission to Curaçao, Aruba, Bonaire and Sint Maarten produced over US$17 million in business intentions, with 60 Panamanian companies holding more than 650 meetings.
