World.title: Paraguay Sets Labor Equity Roadmap with 2030 Targets
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

The morning intel from across Latin America. Free.

Paraguay · SOCIETY

Key Facts — What happened The MTESS presented the Estrategia Nacional Tripartita de Equidad Laboral 2026-2030 on 24 August 2026, led by Minister Mónica Recalde.

— How big The strategy runs to 2030 with annual action plans, mid-term and final evaluations, and four thematic axes.

— The catch Gender gaps persist in Paraguay’s labor market, from informality to unequal care responsibilities.

— Who pays Government, employers and workers share implementation, with technical support from the ILO.

— What comes next The National Tripartite Commission on Equal Opportunity, reactivated in 2024, will be strengthened as the plan’s anchor.

The first tripartite labor equity strategy, backed by the ILO, sets four axes and measurable goals through 2030.

Paraguay’s Ministry of Labor presented the Estrategia Nacional Tripartita de Equidad Laboral 2026-2030 on Monday 24 August 2026, the country’s first tripartite labor-equity strategy built by government, employers and workers with technical support from the International Labour Organization. Led by Minister Mónica Recalde, the plan sets goals, indicators and monitoring to 2030 and marks a new institutional push for Paraguay labor equity.

Women workers on a maquila production line, the kind of formal-sector jobs at the center of Paraguay’s 2026-2030 labor equity strategy (illustrative).

First Tripartite Strategy of Its Kind

The Ministry of Labor, known as MTESS, presented the strategy on Monday 24 August 2026. Minister Mónica Recalde led the launch of the plan.

It is the first Paraguayan labor-equity strategy built through tripartite dialogue. Government, employer organizations and worker organizations all took part in its design.

The International Labour Organization provided technical support for the process. That backing links the plan to international labor standards.

Minister Mónica Recalde headed the presentation on behalf of the MTESS. Her leadership places the labor ministry at the center of the equity agenda through 2030.

The launch places Paraguay labor equity on the formal institutional agenda, with a defined roadmap rather than isolated initiatives.

Officials described the document as a hoja de ruta, a road map, for the coming years. Its tripartite origin means all three actors share ownership of the commitments.

Four Axes of the Strategy

The first axis promotes decent work for women. It covers formalization, social protection, and training and certification programs.

The second axis focuses on preventing discrimination, violence and harassment in the workplace. It aims to build safer conditions across the labor market.

The third axis addresses work-family conciliation and care co-responsibility. It recognizes that care duties still fall disproportionately on women.

The fourth axis strengthens the National Tripartite Commission on Equal Opportunity. That body was reactivated in 2024 after roughly six years of inactivity.

The commission gives the strategy a permanent forum. Its revival in 2024 restored the space where government, employers and workers discuss equal-opportunity policy.

Each axis carries its own lines of action within the 2026-2030 framework. Together they cover employment quality, workplace safety, family life and institutional capacity.

Goals and Monitoring to 2030

The strategy sets goals, indicators and monitoring mechanisms that run through 2030. Each commitment is tied to measurable targets.

Implementation will proceed through annual action plans. These plans translate the broad axes into yearly tasks for each actor.

A mid-term evaluation will review progress partway through the period. A final evaluation in 2030 will assess the strategy’s overall results.

Between those two checkpoints, the annual action plans keep the work on a fixed and public calendar year after year.

This monitoring architecture is designed to keep Paraguay labor equity commitments verifiable rather than aspirational.

The mid-term review creates a checkpoint to correct course before 2030. If indicators lag, the annual plans can be adjusted without abandoning the strategy’s goals.

The Gaps the Plan Must Close

Paraguay’s labor market shows persistent gender gaps. Women participate less in formal employment and are more concentrated in unprotected work.

Care responsibilities weigh heavily on women’s working lives. Time devoted to unpaid care limits access to formal jobs and career advancement.

These gaps are structural rather than new. The 2026-2030 strategy is the first attempt to address them through a single, monitored national framework.

The strategy’s decent-work axis responds directly to that reality. Formalization and social protection expand the floor of rights for women workers.

Training and certification programs under the same axis aim to open higher-skilled occupations. Better credentials improve access to formal, protected employment.

The conciliation axis addresses the distribution of care between men and women, and between families, employers and the state.

Violence and harassment in the workplace also fall within the plan’s scope. The prevention axis treats safe working conditions as a condition for equal participation.

What Comes Next

Implementation begins with the first annual action plan under the 2026-2030 framework. Each year will add new commitments and review past ones.

The strengthened National Tripartite Commission on Equal Opportunity will serve as the governance anchor. Its reactivation in 2024 ended about six years without a functioning forum.

ILO technical support will accompany the process. That includes help with indicators, monitoring and alignment with international conventions.

The strategy’s tripartite design also spreads responsibility for results. Employers and worker organizations are co-authors of the plan, not merely its audience.

For the MTESS, the launch on 24 August 2026 closes the design phase. Attention now shifts to execution, where annual plans will test the commitments in practice.

Whether the strategy delivers will be judged at the mid-term and final evaluations. For now, Paraguay labor equity has a roadmap, an institutional home and a deadline.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is Paraguay’s new labor equity strategy? The Estrategia Nacional Tripartita de Equidad Laboral 2026-2030, presented on 24 August 2026. It is the country’s first tripartite labor-equity plan, with four axes and goals monitored to 2030. Who designed the Paraguay labor equity strategy? Government, employers and workers designed it jointly through the MTESS, led by Minister Mónica Recalde, with technical support from the International Labour Organization. How long does the strategy run? From 2026 to 2030, with annual action plans, a mid-term evaluation and a final evaluation at the end of the period.

World.title: Paraguay Faces Fiscal Crossroads as Deficit Cap Slips to 2028
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

The morning intel from across Latin America. Free.

Paraguay · ECONOMY

Key Facts — What happened The MEF projects deficits of 3.2% of GDP in 2026 and up to 3.9% in 2027, with the 1.5% legal cap postponed to 2028.

— How big A one-year correction from 3.9% to 1.5% equals 2.4 percentage points of GDP, roughly US$1.5 billion.

— The catch H1 2026 tax revenue grew 2.4%, well below the 8.5% official forecast, and arrears to suppliers exceed US$1 billion.

— Who pays A concentrated 2028 cut could shave 1.5 to 2.5 percentage points off growth that year, hitting the wider economy.

— What comes next Options include gradual correction, comprehensive tax reform, protected public investment and escape clauses in the fiscal law.

With revenue below forecast and the 1.5% cap postponed, Paraguay must choose between gradual adjustment and a sharp 2028 cut.

Paraguay’s deficit is projected at 3.2% of GDP in 2026 and could reach 3.9% in 2027, returning to the 1.5% Fiscal Responsibility Law cap only in 2028, according to projections from the Ministry of Economy and Finance. The outlook, framed by Prensa Mercosur on 25 August 2026 citing economist Wildo González, captures what analysts describe as a Paraguay fiscal crossroads: correct gradually starting now, or concentrate a painful adjustment in a single year.

Paraguay’s Congress in Asunción, where lawmakers will shape the deficit path the government has mapped through 2028.

Deficit Cap Formally Postponed to 2028

The Ministry of Economy and Finance projects a fiscal deficit of 3.2% of GDP for 2026. For 2027, the projection rises to as much as 3.9% of GDP.

The government announced the postponement of the return to the 1.5% deficit target on 7 August 2026. Under that decision, the Fiscal Responsibility Law cap would bind again only in 2028.

The 1.5% ceiling is the anchor of Paraguay’s fiscal framework. Deferring it for two more years marks a significant loosening of the country’s budget rule.

The original rule was designed to keep deficits small and predictable. Pushing compliance to 2028 means two more years, 2026 and 2027, will pass with deficits well above the cap before the rule binds again.

Prensa Mercosur framed the situation on 25 August 2026, citing economist Wildo González. His reading describes a Paraguay fiscal crossroads in which the timing of the correction matters as much as its size.

Revenue Falls Short of Forecast

Tax revenue grew just 2.4% in the first half of 2026. The official forecast had projected growth of 8.5% for the period.

That shortfall complicates the consolidation path. Slower revenue growth means the deficit must be closed more through spending restraint than through rising income.

The state has also accumulated arrears to pharmaceutical and construction firms above US$1 billion. Those unpaid bills represent hidden pressure on future budgets.

Public debt stood at US$21.947 billion at the end of the first half of 2026. Servicing that debt adds a fixed cost that narrows room for maneuver.

The combination of weak revenue, supplier arrears and a rising debt stock defines the fiscal starting position. Each element limits the options available for the correction ahead.

The Cost of a One-Year Adjustment

Correcting the deficit from 3.9% to 1.5% of GDP in a single year implies an adjustment of 2.4 percentage points. That is equivalent to roughly US$1.5 billion.

With fiscal multipliers estimated between 0.7 and 1.2, such a cut could reduce 2028 growth by 1.5 to 2.5 percentage points. The economy would feel the contraction across consumption and investment.

A gradual correction starting earlier would spread that cost over several years. Each step would be smaller, and the cumulative drag on growth would be easier to absorb.

That trade-off sits at the heart of the Paraguay fiscal crossroads: pay a moderate price over time, or a heavy price all at once.

González’s analysis, as presented by Prensa Mercosur, stresses that postponing the adjustment does not eliminate it. The arithmetic of 2.4 percentage points of GDP remains on the table regardless of when the correction begins.

Options on the Table

One named option is a comprehensive tax reform. The agenda would broaden the tax base, review exemptions and strengthen tax administration.

Paraguay’s tax burden stands at roughly 14% of GDP, low by regional standards. Each additional point of tax pressure is equivalent to about US$600 million.

Another recommendation is to protect public investment, currently between 1.5% and 2.5% of GDP. Cutting capital spending would deliver savings today at the cost of growth tomorrow.

A third path would add escape clauses or a cyclical rule to the Fiscal Responsibility Law. Such mechanisms would let the deficit breathe in bad years without abandoning the anchor.

None of these options excludes the others. A gradual correction could run alongside tax reform, protected investment and a redesigned fiscal rule, combining revenue, spending and institutional fixes.

Markets Still Open for Asunción

Despite the fiscal slippage, Paraguay retains access to international capital markets. The sovereign reopened its 2055 bond at a yield of 6%.

That continued access gives the government room to choose a gradual path. Financing remains available while credibility holds.

But the revenue underperformance and the stock of arrears narrow the margin for delay. Each year of drift adds to the eventual adjustment bill.

Market access at 6% is a resource, not a guarantee. Sustained investor confidence depends on a credible path back to the 1.5% cap.

The path chosen in the coming months will determine whether the Paraguay fiscal crossroads ends in orderly consolidation or in an abrupt 2028 shock.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the Paraguay fiscal crossroads? It is the choice between correcting the deficit gradually starting now or concentrating a US$1.5 billion adjustment in 2028, when the 1.5% of GDP legal cap returns. When will Paraguay return to the 1.5% deficit cap? In 2028. The government announced the postponement of the target on 7 August 2026, with deficits projected at 3.2% of GDP in 2026 and up to 3.9% in 2027. How large is the adjustment Paraguay needs? Closing the gap from 3.9% to 1.5% of GDP in one year equals 2.4 percentage points, about US$1.5 billion, and could cut 1.5 to 2.5 points off 2028 growth.

Paraguay · TRADE

Key Facts — What happened Rediex, the promotion agency of the Ministry of Industry and Commerce, reported 75 products reaching 43 new destinations in January-July 2026.

— How big Biodiesel to Singapore is the top new flow, at US$5 million.

— The catch The list counts only products with more than US$50,000 exported in 2026 and none above that threshold between 2019 and 2025.

— Who pays Paraguayan exporters opened the new destinations, backed by Rediex promotion programs.

— What comes next Officials frame the results as part of an export-diversification drive to reduce reliance on a few commodities and buyers.

Rediex reports 75 products reaching 43 new destinations as the country’s diversification drive gains ground.

Paraguay sent 75 products to 43 new destinations between January and July 2026, the export and investment promotion agency Rediex reported on 24 August 2026 through the state news agency IP. Eight of those products entered world markets for the first time, a result officials presented as fresh evidence that Paraguay exports new markets beyond its traditional buyers.

Soybeans and other farm goods anchor the export basket Paraguay is expanding into 43 new markets with 75 products (illustrative).

75 Products, 43 New Destinations

Rediex reported the figures through Agencia IP on 24 August 2026, drawing on data from the Ministry of Industry and Commerce. Between January and July 2026, Paraguayan goods reached 43 destinations where they had not been sold in recent years.

Eight products entered world markets for the first time during the period. That group stands out even within the broader diversification effort, because it reflects goods Paraguay had never exported before.

The announcement fits the country’s long-running strategy to widen both its product basket and its buyer base. Officials argue that Paraguay exports new markets most effectively when promotion, logistics and private initiative align.

Rediex is the export and investment promotion agency of the Ministry of Industry and Commerce. It works with Paraguayan firms to identify buyers, attend trade fairs and clear market-entry hurdles.

The data released on 24 August 2026 cover only the first seven months of the year. Officials treat the mid-year snapshot as a progress report on the diversification agenda rather than a final balance.

Asia Leads the New Flows

Nepal emerged as a destination for sunflower oil, mung beans and cotton fiber. Malaysia, meanwhile, took Paraguayan sunflower oil for the first time in the period covered.

The standout new flow was biodiesel to Singapore, worth US$5 million. It is the single largest of the new market openings reported for January-July 2026.

These Asian openings show Paraguay exports new markets for both farm goods and processed products. The Singapore biodiesel shipment, in particular, points to diversification beyond raw commodities into processed energy products.

For a landlocked exporter, reaching buyers in South and Southeast Asia marks a notable extension of commercial geography.

The Nepal opening is especially varied, covering three distinct product lines in a single new destination. Sunflower oil, mung beans and cotton fiber each cleared the US$50,000 threshold there in 2026.

From Uruguay to Ukraine and Sweden

Closer to home, Uruguay received safflower oil and modular electrical containers from Paraguay during the period. The containers represent a manufactured, higher-value product in the new-destinations list.

Guyana took aluminum conductors, adding a Caribbean market for Paraguayan industrial goods. The sale fits the pattern of niche manufactured exports finding buyers abroad.

Ukraine imported salted bovine casings, a traditional animal-product line finding a new buyer. Sweden, meanwhile, received Paraguayan wood veneers.

Taken together, the list spans agro-industrial goods, processed foods and manufactured products. That range is central to the argument that Paraguay exports new markets across sectors, not just in its traditional commodity lines.

How Rediex Counts a New Market

The agency applied a strict criterion to build the list. A destination counts as new only if the product shipped more than US$50,000 worth of goods there in 2026.

In addition, the same product cannot have exceeded that threshold in that destination at any point between 2019 and 2025. This filter excludes reactivated trade relationships.

The US$50,000 floor also screens out symbolic or one-off sample shipments. Only commercially meaningful flows make the count.

That methodology makes the 43-destination figure a conservative reading of how Paraguay exports new markets, rather than an inflated one.

The same criterion explains the eight first-time products. Those goods had no recorded shipments above the threshold anywhere in the world during the 2019-2025 reference period.

Why Diversification Matters for Paraguay

Paraguay’s export earnings have long depended on a narrow set of commodities and a handful of large buyers. Concentration of that kind leaves the economy exposed to price swings and demand shocks.

The diversification drive led by Rediex aims to spread that risk across more products and more destinations. Each new market opening, however small, adds an option for exporters.

The January-July 2026 results suggest the strategy is producing measurable outcomes. Officials presented the data as evidence that promotion work converts into real shipments.

Each of the 43 destinations passed the same strict test. That consistency gives the headline number weight when officials argue the model is working.

With five months left in the year, the agency expects the map of Paraguayan exports to keep widening.

The 24 August 2026 report gives exporters a benchmark. Firms weighing new destinations can point to concrete cases, from Singapore biodiesel to Swedish veneers, where market entry already succeeded in 2026.

Frequently Asked Questions

What did Paraguay export to new markets in 2026? Highlights include biodiesel to Singapore (US$5 million), sunflower oil to Nepal and Malaysia, aluminum conductors to Guyana, salted bovine casings to Ukraine and wood veneers to Sweden. What counts as a new market for Rediex? A product-destination pair with more than US$50,000 exported in 2026 and no shipments above that threshold between 2019 and 2025. Who reported the Paraguay exports new markets figures? Rediex, the export and investment promotion agency of the Ministry of Industry and Commerce, reported them through the state news agency IP on 24 August 2026.

World.title: Imari Young keeps bail after missing court date, trial set for October
World.content:
Imari Young keeps bail after missing court date, trial set for October

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Fresh Pond resident Imari Young, who is before the Belize City Magistrate’s Court on a burglary charge, was allowed to remain on bail Friday after being brought before the court on a bench warrant for failing to attend a previous court date.

Young appeared unrepresented before Magistrate Neeshad Rohammad, who asked him to explain why his bail should not be revoked after he failed to appear in court on July 22.

Young told the court that he had been sick at the time. He also said his mother is hospitalized and that his father recently died. Young claimed that he had obtained a doctor’s document explaining his absence, although the court reportedly had no record of receiving it.

Despite the missed appearance, the Magistrate did not revoke Young’s bail and allowed him to remain free while his case continues.

Young is charged with burglary and is now scheduled to return to the Belize City Magistrate’s Court on October 14, 2026, when his trial is expected to begin.

World.title: International News: Caribbean urged to prepare as strengthening El Niño raises heat and drought concerns
World.content:
International News: Caribbean urged to prepare as strengthening El Niño raises heat and drought concerns

By Zoila Palma: Across the Caribbean, leaders, farmers and businesses are being urged to strengthen preparations for potentially severe climate conditions as a strengthening El Niño threatens to worsen the hot and dry weather already affecting parts of the region.

The Caribbean Institute of Meteorology and Hydrology (CIMH) and the University of the West Indies Climate Studies Group Mona (UWI CSGM) issued the warning as the region enters its peak heat season from August through October.

Climate officials say El Niño conditions strengthened rapidly from weak levels in May to moderate levels by July, with forecasts indicating a high likelihood of very strong conditions between October and December 2026.

Below-normal rainfall could persist into 2027, while extreme heat may become particularly severe during the next heat season from March through May. Drought conditions could worsen across parts of the Eastern and Greater Caribbean as reduced rainfall combines with increased evaporation.

The impacts are expected to extend across several sectors, including agriculture, water, health, energy and tourism.

Rain-fed farming, including in Belize and Jamaica, is considered particularly vulnerable as longer and more frequent dry spells could reduce crop production and threaten food security.

Professor Michael Taylor, co-director of UWI CSGM, described the developing situation as a “slow-moving crisis,” stressing that preparations should begin immediately despite expectations for a relatively quiet Atlantic hurricane season.

Weather experts warned that reduced rainfall could also affect regional supply chains and increase food costs, while higher temperatures could raise demand for water and electricity.

World.title: Sandhill cook Sherise Moralez remanded to prison for alleged unlawful sexual intercourse with 15-year-old boy
World.content:
Sandhill cook Sherise Moralez remanded to prison for alleged unlawful sexual intercourse with 15-year-old boy

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A 37-year-old chef from Sandhill Village is currently on remand at the Belize Central Prison after being accused of having sexual intercourse with a 15-year-old boy twice in one day.

Sherise Shelmadine Moralez, a resident of Mile 19 on the Philip Goldson Highway, appeared before the Chief Magistrate in Court #1 on Tuesday, August 25, 2026. She was formally read two indictable counts of unlawful sexual intercourse (USI).

According to police reports, the alleged incidents occurred on July 30, 2026, at Moralez’s home, where she reportedly had sexual intercourse with the boy twice in a single day—once in her bathroom and once in her bedroom. The matter was reported to the Ladyville Police Station on August 6 by the 15-year-old minor in the company of his 46-year-old mother.

Following an investigation, Ladyville Police detained Moralez on August 23. During an interview under caution in the presence of a Justice of the Peace on August 24, Moralez denied all allegations. She was officially charged later that day.

In court, no plea was taken due to the indictable nature of the charges. Defense attorney Orson “OJ” Elrington argued for court discretion regarding bail, contending that the specific act under which Moralez was charged references carnal knowledge of a girl rather than a boy. However, the prosecutor submitted that under the Crime Control and Criminal Justice Act, the minor remains a victim and bail should be withheld.

The Chief Magistrate agreed with the prosecution and denied bail, remanding Moralez to the Belize Central Prison until November 16, 2026, when she is scheduled to receive disclosure in the case. The court noted that if bail is not granted by the High Court within 90 days, the lower court may revisit the bail application at that time.

World.title: Belize City man fined $505 for almost 2 ounces of weed
World.content:
Belize City man fined $505 for almost 2 ounces of weed

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A 38-year-old Belize City man was fined a total of $505 on after pleading guilty to possession of 56.9 grams of marijuana.

Niven Orin Anthony Flowers, a resident of Marigold Lane, appeared unrepresented before Magistrate Neeshad Mohammed in the Belize City Magistrate’s Court last week, where he pleaded guilty to a single charge of possession of a controlled drug.

Police say Flowers was found with 56.9 grams of marijuana, an amount significantly above the quantity permitted for personal possession but 3.1 grams below the 60-gram threshold referenced by authorities for the more serious drug-trafficking charge.

Flowers was fined $500 plus $5 cost of court and was given until January 29, 2027, to pay. In default of payment, he faces four months’ imprisonment.

During sentencing, the Magistrate reportedly reminded Flowers that the law permits possession of no more than 10 grams of marijuana under specified circumstances. The court also took into consideration that Flowers had a previous drug-related conviction and therefore could not be treated as a first-time offender.

According to police, officers conducted a search at a Marigold Lane property at about 6:45 a.m. Friday. During the search, officers allegedly found a green plastic bag containing suspected cannabis inside a double-door refrigerator located in the yard.

The substance was subsequently identified as marijuana, leading to Flowers being charged and brought before the court later that day.

World.title: Statistical Institute of Belize hosts sensitization session on draft National Data and Statistical Systems Act
World.content:
Statistical Institute of Belize hosts sensitization session on draft National Data and Statistical Systems Act

By Zoila Palma: Today, the Statistical Institute of Belize (SIB) held a one-day sensitization session for data-producing agencies within the National Statistical System (NSS) to review the draft National Data and Statistical Systems Act, 2026.

The session, held at the Best Western Belize Biltmore Plaza in Belize City, brought together senior representatives who examined key provisions of the proposed legislation and provided feedback before it is finalized.

The draft Act seeks to address a gap in Belize’s existing legal framework. While the SIB currently operates under the Statistical Institute of Belize Act, there is no comprehensive legislation governing the wider National Statistical System. The proposed law would establish a unified framework for agencies involved in producing official data, with technical support from the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) through the KOICA-funded “Enabling of Belize’s Statistical System” project.

The proposed legislation aims to strengthen cooperation and coordination among data-producing agencies while clearly defining their roles and responsibilities within the National Statistical System. It also includes provisions governing the production, sharing, protection and use of data for statistical purposes, reflecting changes in the data environment and the growing demand for timely and reliable official statistics.

During the session, participants received presentations on the background and key provisions of the draft Act before taking part in small-group discussions. Officials reviewed the proposed changes in relation to their agencies, identified areas requiring clarification and made recommendations, which were later discussed in a plenary session.

The meeting concluded with a question-and-answer session and discussions on the next steps toward finalizing the proposed legislation.

World.title: Melroy Pelayo granted bail after three months on remand
World.content:
Melroy Pelayo granted bail after three months on remand

By Breaking Belize News Staff: After spending exactly three months on remand, Melroy Mathew Pelayo, 27, has been granted bail while awaiting trial on a charge of aggravated assault with a firearm.

Pelayo, a fisherman and barber from the Fabers Road area of Belize City, appeared unrepresented before Magistrate Neeshad Rohammad on Friday and requested bail after spending approximately 90 days at the Belize Central Prison.

The court granted him bail in the sum of $3,000, with either one surety for the full amount or two sureties of $1,500 each.

Pelayo must report to the Raccoon Street Police Station every Friday between 6:00 a.m. and 6:00 p.m. He was also ordered not to contact the virtual complainant or any prosecution witnesses directly or indirectly, remain at least 100 feet away from the complainant, continue residing at his Swanka Street address, and not be charged with any other offence while on bail.

Pelayo was initially arraigned on May 21, 2026, along with 21-year-old Demarion Lamb. The two men pleaded not guilty to aggravated assault with a firearm and were initially remanded.

The charge stems from an incident on March 16, 2026, on Neal’s Pen Road Extension. A man told police that he and his 17-year-old nephew were in the yard of an abandoned building when two men arrived on a red motorcycle.

Police allege that the motorcycle stopped near the property and the passenger produced a firearm and pointed it in the direction of the complainant and his nephew. The two reportedly ran behind the building for cover and shortly afterward heard what sounded like gunshots.

According to the report, a police mobile subsequently intercepted the motorcycle. Police allege that Pelayo was apprehended and was seen with a firearm in his hand, while the other suspect initially escaped.

Pelayo and Lamb, who has also since been granted bail, are scheduled to return to the Belize City Magistrate’s Court on September 2, 2026.

World.title: International News: U.S. issues security alert for Mexicali, suspends consular activities
World.content:
International News: U.S. issues security alert for Mexicali, suspends consular activities

By Zoila Palma: The United States government has issued a security alert for Americans traveling to Mexicali, Mexico, and temporarily suspended consular activities in the northern border city because of what officials described as a potential threat.

The U.S. notice did not provide details about the nature of the threat or who may have been targeted, AP reports.

The alert, issued Monday night, advised U.S. citizens to avoid government buildings, remain aware of their surroundings and seek shelter if a security incident occurs. Mexicali is the capital of Baja California and sits directly across the border from Calexico, California, making it an important crossing point between the two countries.

Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum said Tuesday that the alert was linked to information about the possible actions of a criminal group. She said the information came from U.S. agencies but that Mexican authorities had not received additional details about what the threat might involve. Sheinbaum urged residents to remain alert while authorities increased surveillance in the city.

Despite the alert, Mexicali remained calm throughout Tuesday.

Mexico’s security cabinet later said authorities had found no evidence of a specific or imminent threat to the population, while increased patrols and surveillance were being carried out as a precaution.

World.title: Weather experts monitor 2 disturbances in Atlantic
World.content:
Weather experts monitor 2 disturbances in Atlantic

By Zoila Palma: Forecasters at the National Hurricane Center (NHC) are monitoring two areas of disturbed weather over the Atlantic Ocean, with both systems showing potential for tropical development in the coming days.

One system is located northeast of Bermuda, while the other is several hundred miles south-southeast of the Cabo Verde Islands.

The first system AL95 is associated with a broad area of low pressure several hundred miles northeast of Bermuda.

It is moving north-northeastward at approximately 15 to 20 miles per hour, but its shower activity remains disorganized.

The NHC noted that the system could briefly develop into a tropical depression or tropical storm before encountering unfavorable conditions by early Wednesday.

The second system, AL96, is located in the eastern tropical Atlantic and is producing showers and thunderstorms around a low-pressure area south-southeast of the Cabo Verde Islands.

Forecasters say environmental conditions around AL96 appear favorable for gradual development, and the system could become a tropical depression within the next day or two as it moves westward to west-northwestward across the Atlantic.

AL96 has a 70 percent chance of development over both the next 48 hours and 7 days.

World.title: ‘Baddies build furniture too’
World.content:
Carpenter Sydonie Miller at her shop in DunKirk, Kingston (Photo: Garfield Robinson).

With work hard to find and financial constraints mounting during the coronavirus pandemic, one Jamaican woman discovered a hidden talent that opened an unexpected livelihood for her in a labour-intensive trade not often pursued by local females – carpentry.

Twenty-nine-year-old Sydonie Miller had been finding it difficult to secure a job in 2020, during the heights of COVID-19, despite having a bachelor’s degree in business management and secretarial skills.

Miller, who was a new mother at the time, said her husband, a taxi operator, was the only one working and she was determined to find a way to contribute to her family.

Her journey to carpentry began with a desire to own a padded bedhead and being quoted what she considered an exorbitant price to have one made.

“At the time, it was padded bed did run the place. When I go to ask the price, them a give me an arm and a leg for it. Me say me nah pay that,” Miller told Observer Online.

So, she decided to build it herself.

Seeking the guidance of a carpenter friend on Charles Street and gathering the necessary materials, Miller went on to make her first bedhead.

After completing the project, Miller’s curiosity and determination pushed her to learn more. She eventually made her way to Oxford Street, where veteran carpenters such as Chucky, Paul, Max, Abi Doll and Warren took her under their wings and taught her how to build a wider range of furniture, including dressers, chests of drawers and beds.

But for Miller, learning the trade was not difficult because she has always been a practical learner. She quickly grasped the skills being taught to her.

“If you’re going to do something, I see what you’re doing. If you show me one time, you don’t have to show me again. Just the one time, I know what to do,” she explained.

But the mother of three said her entry into carpentry was about more than simply learning how to build furniture. She believes the skill was placed in her path for a reason.

“At the time, I was at work and I can’t forget the day. The almighty say I give you a skill, go and use it. I have business management, secretarial skills. I thought it was that skill but I never knew it was this skill. So when him say I give you a skill, go and use it, me just say alright me ago just go deal with the bed head. Me see say me can build dresser and me just a build. Me go under the wings of the veterans,” she said.

Miller, who now owns her very own furniture business, Luxurious Furnitures by Syd, said her client base now ranges from individual customers to stores in the downtown Kingston area.

When Observer Online visited her shop on Banana Street in the McIntyre Villa community of East Kingston, Miller was seen working on a bedhead and bed bottom for one of her customers.

While her skills have helped her build a business, Miller said being a woman in a male-dominated trade has presented its own challenges.

“Some of them, when them see a woman come and say you know say me build this, them don’t believe it” she explained.

Miller said some customers only become convinced that she builds the furniture herself after seeing a male carpenter deliver one of her pieces.

Despite the doubters, Miller said she has also encountered customers who appreciate the fact that she is a woman in the trade and are willing to give her the time needed to complete their furniture.

“To be honest, it’s a bittersweet moment, but at the end of the day there are some people that really love me, who are really happy that I’m a woman and I do this. You have some patient ones, big up on unu self. Them say alright then, I’ll give you time,” she added.

The carpenter said each piece of furniture requires patience and attention to detail, with the process involving several stages before a finished product is ready.

“For me its patience, to really put in the work, because remember, furniture building takes time. It has different layers, different processes to build. So to build a bed head like this, it takes time. I have a lot of different grades of sanding to do,” she said.

She further explained: “I have to start the sanding from, like, 80, and I go down to 180. Then I go down to 200. Then I go down to 220. It’s patience. And you have to get all the nooks and crannies. You can’t just sand off just the bigger parts. You have to sand from the corners, from underneath, behind, everything. So it’s just patience.”

Of all the furniture she has made since entering the trade, Miller said one particular piece remains her favourite, a king-size mahogany bed set. She said the piece holds special significance because it challenged her skills when she was still new to furniture building.

Miller is now encouraging other women not to allow traditional perceptions about certain professions to prevent them from pursuing their interests.

“Don’t follow the stigma say a man work. Woman can do it, too. Once you see something that you want to do just do it. Learn the skill, do it, because at the end of the day, it’s not who do it. It’s really how you set your mind to do it or if you have the determination to do it,” Miller said. “So don’t follow them a man work. Baddies build furniture too. Baddies build furniture too.”

World.title: More vacancies than advertised
World.content:
Numerous schools are scrambling to fill permanent and temporary teaching posts.

With the new academic year just days away numerous schools are scrambling to fill permanent and temporary teaching posts. But Jamaica Association of Principals of Secondary Schools (JAPSS) President Anniona Jones says the influx of s across various media do not reflect the full picture of the staffing needs.

According to Jones, while some vacancies have been caused by teachers embarking on well-earned vacation breaks, others are the result of educators leaving the system, some without proper notice.

“Some of these resignations do not reach the regional office, and sometimes we fill [vacancies] based on old resumes and not necessarily place all of it in an ad because not every school has the fiscal position to even run an ad. So what you’re seeing in the paper is the tip of the iceberg of the actual gaps in schools because many of us do not place in the national papers the s for teachers. We use a lot of social media, word of mouth, our teachers’ groups, Jamaica Teachers’ Association groups, and so on. That’s what’s happening. So we really don’t have a good picture nationally on what is really happening on the ground,” Jones told the Jamaica Observer on Monday.

The educator, who was responding to queries by the Observer about what accounts for the almost perennial influx of s yearly during the summer break, explained that the system itself is partly accountable.

“The education system asks all members of the academic staff to apply for their leave by November of the first term, for the following academic year. So leave applications are made almost a year in advance. Usually, by June we would get notification from the Ministry of Education indicating which teachers’ leave application is approved. This year it came a little later in July, and we see where a priority was placed on approving leave applications, certainly in Region One, which is Kingston and St Andrew, for persons who would have applied for eight months,” Jones outlined.

She said while the leave amounts might seem staggering, a little known fact is that “it takes a regular classroom teacher or vice-principal five years of service in order to qualify for four months of leave”.

“So, unlike many people’s workplace where they will get two weeks’ vacation leave, we don’t do that in education, and there are a lot of reasons for that. However, that’s how the system is set up. So teachers will get leave of four months or eight months. They’d apply for study leave, and they would know at that period of time,” she said.

Jones noted that because of the late approvals, principals were not made aware, until July, of how much their staffing levels would be affected for September.

“Usually that’s when many principals know how many of the teachers who have applied for leave have had their leave approved, and whether or not it is for four months, eight months, a year study leave, two years, or so on. So that means that July and August of every year, obviously, you’re going to see a large number of applications in the media, and we will have to fill these positions for smooth start of school for September,” Jones said.

She noted that teacher migration and not just vacation entitlements have also influenced the s of vacancies.

“There are several factors causing teacher migration. It’s not a national problem only, it’s not a regional problem only, it’s an international problem; and if you look at many of the international bodies, such as Education International, some projections go as high as 40 million teachers may be needed within the next decade globally. There are lots of reasons why teachers are leaving the education system: terms and conditions of service, salary, moving on to other interests, and so many other reasons. But we do have a significant shortage in some areas, the industrial arts [for example]. Obviously, persons can earn far more money in the private sector than in teaching,” she told the Observer while noting that Jamaican educators are in high demand by other territories.

The recruitment, she said, is also driven by the fact that there are “shortages in some areas that are undersubscribed like history, geography, the foreign languages like French, Spanish” in addition to the fact that some schools are located in remote areas, or in communities where Zones of Special Operations are in force, or areas that experience high levels of crime or violence, therefore “not many people may want to work in some of those areas”.

According to Jones, the discontinuation of a special hazard allowance — a grant that made to teachers who worked in very remote or rural situations, or in high-risk areas — as an incentive is also a contributor to some schools finding it difficult to fill vacancies.

“So there are many factors that would influence how fluid the system is. And then, of course, if we only have four months available, and that teacher gets a position that is potentially permanent, a teacher may go in that regard. So the short-term vacancies may also be difficult to fill,” the JAPSS president stated.

She said it is difficult to provide a total number of all schools with unfilled vacancies.

“If you look in the papers you will find that even schools that would have advertised before, they may have conducted interviews and even made an offer to a teacher. A teacher may rescind that offer from one school and move to another school where they did interviews because teachers are applying for multiple jobs, they’re doing many interviews, and then they’re picking once they’re offered. So, because of how fluid the system is, you may also find that you may think that you have filled a vacancy, and a teacher calls back to say, ‘I am so sorry. Instead of working at your school for four months or eight months, I’ve just been offered a position for a year, or a clear vacancy at another school, and so I’m going to take that offer instead’. So even though you may think that you filled the vacancy, it now becomes available again because the teacher is moving in the direction of what is best for them and their families,” Jones said.

Asked to say whether this meant the association still has no clear picture as to readiness for the new school year Jones said, “We have filled most of the vacancies… but many schools will have at least one or two positions that they’re hoping to fill this week, with some schools having as many as six or eight positions that are yet to be filled”.

Jones, in the meantime, had this message for parents, guardians, and students: “Every Jamaican child deserves high-quality education, and conditions of work for the teacher are conditions of learning for the children. So if it is that we want the best for our children, then it means we should want the best for the teachers. So, please help us to advocate for the conditions that will be required for us to be able to attract the best and the brightest, retain the most experienced teachers, so that our children can ultimately benefit.”

Added Jones, “Let’s celebrate those who have gone on their well-earned leave; [working] five years to get four months is a lot [and working] 10 years to get eight months is a lot. So let’s celebrate with those who are taking well-deserved breaks. But let us work together to advocate for a better education system.”

World.title: Celene Hall takes Miss Universe Jamaica 2026 crown
World.content:
Celene Hall makes her first walk as Miss Universe Jamaica 2026.

Despite winning five sectional prizes, the newly crowned Miss Universe Jamaica 2026 titleholder, Portland native Celene Hall said she had no idea that she would have emerged the winner.

Hall competed with 32 other ladies for the coveted title and to represent Jamaica at the Miss Universe finals in Puerto Rico in November.

he coronation show took place on Sunday night inside a jam-packed ballroom at AC Hotel Kingston.

“I know I received a lot of sectional awards, but honestly, it wasn’t until the crown was placed on my head that I really knew that I was Miss Universe Jamaica 2026,” Hall told the

Jamaica Observer shortly after she was crowned.

This marked the start of a new journey and the end of countless days and nights of practice, rehearsals, and training.

Hall first entered the Miss Universe Jamaica Portland pageant, which she won a few months ago.

According to Parish Director Shanique Rogers, Hall was transformed during the process.

“From the beginning, she listened, she understood what the crown represented, and, most importantly, she was willing to learn… She is not the same woman who entered the competition in Portland. The Miss Universe Jamaica Portland platform challenged her, developed her, and helped shape her into the queen she is today,” Rogers, a former Miss Universe Jamaica finalist, told the Observer.

She added: “Seeing Celene win makes me incredibly proud, because I know the amount of hard work, dedication, and behind-the-scenes effort that went into preparing her for this moment. To see that hard work pay off is truly rewarding.”

Hall concurred that the pageant challenged her.

“I knew the space would challenge me more to grow into the absolute best version of myself, and that is the reason why I entered in the first place,” she shared.

From Passley Gardens in Port Antonio, she attended Titchfield High School.

Her beaming parents, three sisters and two brothers were on hand to witness her success.

“She started modeling from primary school and she just kept going, and we have been supportive of her,” said her mother, Sonia Hall.

Father Victor said, “Celene has been a queen from ever since. I told her mother from the beginning that Celene had what it takes.”

The coronation show started more than an hour late, and once it got going there was no turning back. The 33 contestants opened the show but they were quickly reduced to a top 20.

The ladies then moved into swimwear before the top 14 were announced.

The evening gown competition resulted in the final six spots being filled.

After being interviewed, the final three were revealed to be Kadejah Anderson, Celene Hall, and Tianna McDaniel.

Hall won the Essence of Style Award, Best in Swimwear, Best in Evening Gown, Most Aware, and the Altruism Award.

Tianna McDaniel was adjudged Most Photogenic; Andrea Hill – Most Congenial; Marcie Lee Smith – Best Personality; Alanda Newman – Runway Star Award; and Marsha Roberts, Alanda Newman and Channon Smith made a three-way tie for Spirit of the Pageant award.

At the end of the night second runner-up was determined to be Anderson, while McDaniel, a medical practitioner, finished in the first runner-up position, as Hall snagged first place.

World.title: ‘Cricket isn’t dead!’
World.content:
Jamaica Kingsmen opener Kirk McKenzie hits the ball during the Caribbean Premier League T20 match against Trinbago Knight Riders at Sabina Park in Kingston on August 15, 2026.

JAMAICA Cricket Association President Dr Donovan Bennett believes the Jamaica Kingsmen have already made a strong impression on the island is optimistic they can play a key role in developing grassroots cricket locally.

The Caribbean Premier League (CPL) returned to Sabina Park for the first time since 2019 as the new Jamaica franchise hosted four games which concluded last Tuesday.

Tens of thousands of Jamaicans turned out for the four matches against the Barbados Tridents, Trinbago Knight Riders, Guyana Amazon Warriors and St Kitts and Nevis Patriots with some of the Caribbean’s top players on display including the Kingsmen’s own Rovman Powell and Andre Russell as well as regional stars Nicholas Pooran, Shimron Hetmeyer and Sunil Narine.

It continued the trend of growing crowd interest shown by local fans following last summer’s series between the West Indies and Australia, as well as Sri Lanka’s visit in June.

Bennett believes the Kingsmen’s home leg is a good reflection of the state of cricket in Jamaica.

“I have heard many persons who are or were cricket fans saying that cricket is dead in Jamaica but what both the Sri Lanka tour and the CPL that followed have clearly said is that cricket is not dead in Jamaica,” he told the Jamaica Observer.

“In fact, cricket is still one of the most popular sports in the country and that as long as the people are fed the right diet, they get what they want to see, they will come out and support us and it was clear to everybody from the crowds. It was a fantastic atmosphere, not just the numbers, but the participation because the crowds were a behind the team with almost every ball that was bowled. It was really something electric and really a pleasure to sit and observe.”

Although pleased with action on the pitch, Bennett says he was impressed by the Kingsmen’s early investment in youth cricket.

The team’s ownership sponsored the All-Grace Shield and All-Headley Cup exhibitions tournament in July, which saw some of the best high school cricketers from the urban and rural areas go head to head in a 50 over match and a T20 match over two days. The

Observer understands the Kingsmen handed over $3.1 million to the JCA to execute the matches.

“As I made a presentation to them, it was a yes and I can tell you, the amount that was literally given to us for the two games is a significant amount of money which comfortably put both games on,” Bennett said. “I think it is something that should encourage the schools to participate on a wider basis and for players to have something substantive to look forward to at the end of the season. It should be the responsibility of ISSA but in a situation where ISSA does not have an interest, then I think the JCA has got to take up the responsibility and get those games on a yearly basis.”

While happy with the progress the Kingsmen have made, Bennett wants them to do more to help develop the next generation of Jamaican cricketers.

“As soon as the CPL is concluded, hopefully we can sit down with the Kingsmen to discuss other development programmes because I am not one of those who sees development from above downwards. I think that is one of the problems with West Indies Cricket over the years is that a lot of money has been spent at the top and very little at the bottom,” he said.

“We have had initial discussions, we haven’t had any decisions as yet. But certainly things like our under-13 programme has got to be put on the table because we really want to do an extended, comprehensive under-13 programme. Every year, we need to have an Under-13 Jamaica team and then from that, we need to extract the best players out of that group every year and put them into a specialised, continuous programme so that in a couple of years’ time, we can have a large cadre of players who, from an early age, have been taught the right things, the right attitudes and also the seriousness at which they should take the cricket, both representing Jamaica and the West Indies.”

The Kingsmen, who have four games remaining in the league stage, are currently just outside the play-off spot in fifth on four points. They return to action on Thursday against the Patriots at Warner Park in St Kitts.

World.title: Before You Book: Questions You Should Ask Your Hotel Wedding Venue
World.content:
Finding a beautiful hotel venue is exciting. You can already picture the décor, the guests arriving, the food being served and everything coming together perfectly.

But before you sign the contract or pay that deposit, there are a few important conversations you need to have.

When planning a wedding at a hotel, what you don’t ask can sometimes cost you just as much as what you do. A venue may look perfect during a walkthrough, but the details behind the scenes — from additional fees and set-up times to catering restrictions and technology — can have a major impact on your event.

Here are some things you should know before saying yes to a hotel venue.

What Exactly Is Included in the Venue Cost?

Never assume that everything you see during your tour is included in the quoted price. You should also ask about taxes, service charges, overtime charges and any additional fees that may appear on the final bill. The goal isn’t simply to know the rental price; it’s to understand the true cost of hosting your event there.

Will the Space Really Work for Your Wedding?

Capacity is about more than the maximum number of people allowed in a room. A ballroom might accommodate 300 people theatre-style but significantly fewer once you add banquet tables, a stage, dance floor, buffet stations, décor and audiovisual equipment.

Explain exactly what you’re planning and ask the hotel how many guests the space can comfortably accommodate with your preferred layout.

Think Beyond the Start and End Time

Your invitation might say 6:00 pm, but your event begins long before the first guest arrives. Decorators, florists, entertainers, photographers and production teams may need several hours to prepare. Ask when vendors can access the venue, where they can load and unload, and how much time is allowed for breakdown afterward. If additional set-up or breakdown time comes at an extra cost, that’s something you want to know well in advance.

Understand the Food and Beverage Details



If the hotel provides catering, don’t stop at choosing a menu. Ask about food-and-beverage minimums, service styles, what’s included in the per-person price and how dietary requirements and allergies are handled. If you’re hoping to bring a special cake, outside caterer or another food or beverage item, confirm whether it’s permitted and whether additional fees apply.

These small details can have a surprisingly big impact on both your plans and your budget.

Ask About Vendors, Technology and Entertainment

If you already have a favourite decorator, DJ, photographer or production company, confirm that they’re allowed to work at the hotel. Some properties have preferred or exclusive vendors, while others may require outside suppliers to provide insurance or meet specific requirements.

Technology deserves the same attention. Ask what’s available for microphones, speakers, screens, projectors, lighting, electrical connections and Wi-Fi. And before planning candles, elaborate installations, confetti, hanging décor or late-night entertainment, ask about the hotel’s restrictions. There may be rules around open flames, wall or ceiling installations, amplified music and the time entertainment must end.

Consider the Guest Experience

Walk through the experience from your guests’ point of view. Where will they park? How easy is it to find the event space once they enter the hotel? Accessibility matters too. Ask about ramps, elevators, accessible restrooms and step-free access for guests who may need them.

A beautiful venue means very little if getting into it — or moving around it — is difficult for your guests.

What Happens When Plans Change?

Guest counts rarely remain exactly the same from the day you book until the day of your wedding. Find out when the final guaranteed number is due and what happens if attendance increases or decreases.

If your wedding booking includes overnight accommodation, discuss room blocks, booking deadlines and any commitments attached to those rooms.

You should also understand the hotel’s cancellation and rescheduling policies. Are there cancellation charges? And what happens if circumstances outside your control affect the event?

Is there a back-up location secured for you if you are outdoor and it rains?

These aren’t the most exciting questions to ask, but they’re some of the most important ones to have answered in writing.

Know Who Will Be Looking After You



The person who shows you the ballroom and prepares your proposal may not be the person managing your event on the day. Ask who your main contact will be throughout the planning process and who will be responsible for your function once event day arrives. Knowing exactly whom to call when you need an answer or something changes can make the planning process considerably easier.

And Finally, Ask the Question People Often Forget



After you’ve gone through everything on your list, ask your hotel representative: “Based on the type of event I’m planning, is there anything else you think I should know before I book?”

It’s a simple question, but an experienced event professional may immediately identify something you haven’t considered.

Before You Sign



Choosing a hotel event venue isn’t only about finding the prettiest ballroom or the most attractive package. You’re choosing a partner that will play a significant role in your guests’ experience.

The right venue shouldn’t just look good in photographs. It should have the space, team, policies and resources to help your event run smoothly — from the first vendor arriving for set-up to the final guest heading home.

Because when it comes to wedding planning, the questions you ask before you book can save you from the surprises you don’t want later.

World.title: Honorary consul to Atlanta Elaine Grant-Bryan ‘humbled’ by OD recognition
World.content:
Elaine Grant-Bryan

When Elaine Grant-Bryan settled in Atlanta in 1990, that city was long acknowledged as the mecca of black empowerment in the United States. She joined a growing Jamaican community which has made an impact in commerce and community politics.

Grant-Bryan has been Jamaica’s honorary consul to Atlanta since 2018. Currently in her third term, she has been awarded the Order of Distinction (Officer class) by the Jamaican government for service to the diaspora.

That award will be presented during the National Honours and Awards ceremony on October 19 at King’s House in Kingston.

In an interview with Observer Online, Grant-Bryan spoke of being “deeply humbled” by recognition of her work. Like New York City and South Florida, she said Jamaicans have made their mark in Atlanta and neighbouring areas such as Decatur and Stone Mountain.

“This region has grown significantly, especially after COVID-19 as Jamaicans moved from colder regions in the United States in great numbers. Our community has doubled, and many have successfully assimilated in the Georgia culture and made significant contributions to Jamaica and this region,” Grant-Bryan stated.

An educator and real estate broker, she points to initiatives started with her husband Gregory as major achievements of her tenure. These include the Elaine Bryan Foundation which drives the Jamaican Pioneer Programme and STEAM (Science, Technology, Engineering, Arts, Mathematics).

The pioneer programme allows Americans of Jamaican heritage to gain citizenship in their family’s homeland. Once that is secured, they increase their contribution to Jamaica’s education system by mentoring and assisting needy students.

STEAM is an enrichment curriculum she developed with her husband, a programmer and Information Technology expert. It teaches coding/programming and offers career assessments, internships, entrepreneurships, and scholarships to Jamaican students completing degrees in STEAM fields.

Empowerment was a buzz word in Elaine Bryan’s home in Kingston, where she was born to a father who was an engineer and her mother, a nurse. A past student of Excelsior and Kingston Technical high schools, she was head girl at the latter.

Staying true to her profession, education is the thrust of upcoming projects by the Elaine Bryan Foundation.

“We will continue to include additional students who are completing degrees in the STEAM fields in Jamaica. The projection for 2026-7 is to extend mentorship programmes in Jamaica, study abroad and exchange programmes,” she disclosed.

World.title: Khadija Shaw crowned PFA women’s player of the year
World.content:
Khadijah 'Bunny' Shaw (Instagram Photo: PFA)

MANCHESTER, United Kingdom (AFP)—Reggae Girl and Manchester City’s Khadijah ‘Bunny’ Shaw was crowned the Professional Footballers’ Association (PFA) women’s player of the year for the second time on Tuesday as Manchester United’s captain Bruno Fernandes scooped the men’s award.

Portuguese international Fernandes broke the all-time record for Premier League assists during an outstanding individual 2025/26 season, setting up 21 goals as he surpassed Thierry Henry and Kevin De Bruyne’s previous mark.

The 31-year-old also scored nine times as United overcame a poor start to finish third in the Premier League under Michael Carrick and earn a return to the Champions League.

Fernandes also won the Football Writers’ Association footballer of the year award in May.

“It is obviously a very proud moment. They are the ones you go on the pitch against and it’s probably not easy to vote for someone you play against, so it is a very good moment,” said Fernandes.

Shaw was rewarded for scoring 21 goals on the way to a third straight Golden Boot and securing City’s first Women’s Super League title for a decade.

There was further success for City as Nico O’Reilly was named the men’s young player of the year.

The 21-year-old scored twice in the League Cup final as City beat Arsenal and was part of the side that also won the FA Cup last season.

“I’m very proud of the season I had,” said the England international. “I won two trophies with my club and managed to play at the World Cup with my country. I’m over the moon how it turned out.”

O’Reilly was joined by City teammates Erling Haaland, Rayan Cherki and Antoine Semenyo in the team of the year.

Champions Arsenal had five representatives in David Raya, Gabriel, William Saliba, Jurrien Timber and Declan Rice, with Fernandes and Brentford’s Igor Thiago completing the XI.

World.title: Nigel Farage wants to scrap GDPR for the UK
World.content:
“[T]he GDPR has strangled small businesses and tech firms alike in a web of unnecessary regulation ... Ten years after the Brexit referendum we should not still be following ridiculous EU privacy laws that hurt British businesses,” Reform UK MP Robert Jenrick said in a statement.

The EU GDPR provides for a wider set of individual rights around personal data (including the “right to be forgotten”) than New Zealand's Privacy Act does.

However, Reform UK stressed in its press release that following the New Zealand model would preserve the U.K.'s EU data adequacy status, meaning personal data would still be allowed to flow freely between the U.K. and EU.

The European Commission only grants adequacy to countries that provide an essentially equivalent level of data protection to that of the EU.

The U.K. has already diverged from Brussels on privacy laws with the passage of the Data (Use and Access) Act last year, which relaxed some aspects of the U.K. GDPR in a bid to boost economic growth.

World.title: Trains between Britain and Europe on track to run every 15 minutes
World.content:
Using this new facility will allow Trenitalia to bypass capacity limits at the Temple Mills International depot in east London, where Eurostar keeps its fleet and where Virgin is also expected to do so. The U.K. regulator allocated the last space in the facility to Virgin last year.

Mark Smith, a former rail manager who runs the popular Man In Seat 61 travel website, told POLITICO: “Both contenders appear to have the ability and financial backing to make this happen, but there are many steps in a long process before any train runs. Trenitalia are in pole position with a 2029 start date, helped by having ordered trains of a type already approved for France and a continuation of an existing production line.”

Travellers check their phones while standing next to a Eurostar train at St. Pancras station in London on December 30, 2025. | Carlos Jasso/AFP via Getty Images

“I see no reason why experience in Italy or Spain should not be repeated, where competition has raised standards, increased capacity and lowered average fares. The whole market has gown, in Italy Trenitalia is carrying more passengers than it did before competition from Italo arrived. Passengers have won, the biggest loser has been short haul flights.”

Reasons to be cautious

There’s still plenty of time for it all to go wrong — as it has before.

German state railway Deutsche Bahn once planned services through the tunnel, going so far as to send a promotional train to St Pancras for a photo op in October 2010. The operator was ultimately stymied by Brexit and backed away from the idea, although it has since shown some renewed interest.

There is also room for the new entrants to revise their plans. Operators don’t necessarily have to run every service they get authorization to operate from the ORR. Each operator also needs separate authorizations in each country and for the Channel Tunnel itself, meaning there are still regulatory hurdles to clear.

World.title: Sánchez’s ministers clash over whether Madrid missed Ceuta migrant warnings
World.content:
“Our armed forces, intelligence services, and, of course, the National Intelligence Center carried out the work that was and is required of them, and shared and analyzed this information with the state security forces and the staff of the government delegation,” the minister told lawmakers, defending the work of the agents she oversees.

Robles’ statement directly contradicts the Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska’s version of events. For weeks, he has insisted the national government did not reinforce the border in Ceuta because it had no way of anticipating the sudden migrant surge.

The minister underscored this point during an extraordinary meeting of the bloc’s interior ministers on Aug. 4, in the aftermath of the influx, where he emphasized Spain’s status as a “strong, reliable partner.”

On Tuesday, Grande-Marlaska hit back directly at Robles’ statement during a press conference, insisting that neither Spain’s intelligence services nor any foreign intelligence agents had detected or warned of anything unusual near Ceuta.

“There was no report that foreshadowed what ultimately transpired on July 30,” he said, adding that it was a matter of “common sense” that any warning would have been taken seriously and handled accordingly.

After lawmakers informed Robles that Grande-Marlaska had denied her statement, the defense minister doubled down and said the country’s intelligence services had warned authorities on July 29, a day earlier than she had originally stated, adding that it was “common knowledge, public knowledge, that people were swimming into Ceuta.”

World.title: Polish prosecutors charge MEP with Holocaust denial over Auschwitz ‘fake’ claim
World.content:
The MEP was summoned as a suspect to the Kraków branch of Poland’s Institute of National Remembrance, a state body empowered to prosecute crimes related to the Nazi occupation and communist eras.

The case stems from two interviews he gave in July 2025. In one, he declared that “Auschwitz with its gas chambers is unfortunately a fake”; in another, he described accounts of their use as a “propaganda narrative” underpinning a “quasi-religious cult.”

The existence and use of gas chambers at Auschwitz-Birkenau is extensively documented. Around a million Jews were killed in the camp, along with around 100,000 Poles, Roma, Soviet prisoners of war, gay people, Jehovah’s Witnesses and criminals.

Poland sought to strip Braun of his parliamentary immunity over the remarks, and the European Parliament approved the request in March. Braun, who has a long record of antisemitic rhetoric, is already on trial over separate alleged offenses, including his use of a fire extinguisher to disrupt a Hanukkah celebration in the Polish parliament in 2023.

Braun did not immediately respond to POLITICO’s request for comment.

His legal troubles come as his party emerges as a potentially consequential force ahead of Poland’s October 2027 parliamentary election. A CBOS poll published Monday, after allocating undecided voters, put Braun’s party at 10.2 percent, compared with 21.3 percent for the conservative Law and Justice party and 14.9 percent for the far-right Confederation.

PiS leader Jarosław Kaczyński has repeatedly ruled out an alliance with Braun’s party. But PiS prime ministerial candidate Przemysław Czarnek has drawn a narrower line: He has said Braun himself would “200 percent” not serve in a PiS-led government, while declining to exclude a coalition with his party categorically.

That distinction could matter after October 2027, when Poland’s fragmented right may need every available seat to assemble a governing majority.

World.title: UN chief tells countries to rein in autonomous weapons
World.content:
Guterres and ICRC chief Mirjana Spoljaric underlined that targeting civilians in war is a violation of international humanitarian law, and said they fear that machines won't be able to tell the difference between combatants and non-combatants.

Both called for a ban on autonomous weapons which produce unpredictable results and anti-personnel weapons that deliberately target human beings.

The UN is set to hold a conference in Geneva in November to review its treaty on conventional weapons. Lethal autonomous weapon systems are expected to be a subject of that gathering. The UN has long been pushing countries to progress on legally binding rules.

"When we speak about AI, we want human oversight," European Commission spokesperson Thomas Regnier told reporters on Tuesday when asked about the Commission's assessment on whether humans should be kept in the loop of military applications.

Human oversight is a key concept of the bloc's Artificial Intelligence Act, which doesn't apply, though, to defence or security applications.

World.title: Armenia detains former President Kocharyan on corruption charges
World.content:
Former Armenian President Robert Kocharyan and his eldest son were detained Tuesday after law enforcement officers conducted searches at dozens of locations linked to the family, the country's Anti-Corruption Committee said.

 

Armenia's Prosecutor General's Office said it initiated criminal prosecution against Kocharyan, 71, on charges of abuse of authority, bribery, and large-scale money laundering.

The office said it detained four other people besides Kocharyan and his eldest son Sedrak as part of the investigation.

Armenia's Anti-Corruption Committee said it was investigating allegations that state assets were illegally sold to private companies below market value during Kocharyan's time in office from 1998 to 2008. It further said the case included nine other people besides Kocharyan.

Former President Serzh Sargsyan, who served as Kocharyan's prime minister from 2007 to 2008 before becoming president himself from 2008 to 2018, is also facing charges for alleged abuse of power or official authority as part of the case, the committee said.

Sargsyan was summoned to the Anti-Corruption Committee headquarters in Yerevan on Tuesday.

The elder Kocharyan leads the Moscow-friendly Armenia Alliance, parliament's second-largest opposition bloc.

Bagrat Mikoyan, who heads his office, described the detentions as "yet another attack on President Kocharyan and his family" by authorities. He added that Kocharyan felt ill after his detention and was taken to a hospital.

During his mandate as Armenia's president, Kocharyan deepened Yerevan's links to Moscow, signing a declaration of "allied partnership" with the Kremlin and overseeing a significant expansion of Russian investment in Armenia's economy.

He has maintained close personal ties with Vladimir Putin. In 2021, Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said the two had "good relations for a very long time" and were frequently in contact.

'A signal to the Kremlin'

The raids came less than 24 hours after Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan clashed with Kocharyan's younger son, Levon — who is part of Kocharyan senior's bloc — in a fiery exchange in parliament.

During a parliamentary question-and-answer session, Levon Kocharyan accused Pashinyan of pressuring the courts and law enforcement agencies to open investigations against individuals.

Pashinyan responded by asking Levon Kocharyan where his family's wealth came from, saying any assets gained at public expense should be returned to the state.

Robert Kocharyan went on trial in 2019, accused of ordering the illegal use of force by security officers against demonstrators protesting alleged fraud in the 2008 presidential election. At least 10 people were killed in the clashes. The charges were later dropped, and the legal proceedings ended in 2021.

Analyst Alexander Iskandaryan, director of the Caucasus Institute in Yerevan, said that critics have long accused Kocharyan of corruption while in power.

Iskandaryan said the case will intensify the conflict between the pro-Russian opposition and Pashinyan's government, which is pursuing a pro-Western course and prioritising closer ties with the European Union.

"Of course, this is a signal to the Kremlin," Iskandaryan said. "Kocharyan effectively positions himself as a Russian proxy, and we see a trend where the authorities have begun to fight — intensively and by all possible means — against political forces aligned with Russia."

Pashinyan, who was elected to office on the back of a 2018 street revolution, has often portrayed himself as a man of the people and supports closer ties with the West. The 51-year-old's party was re-elected in June.

The leader of the largest opposition party — Armenian-Russian billionaire Samvel Karapetyan — was arrested last year on suspicion of calling for the overthrow of Pashinyan.

Karapetyan is the founder of Russia's Tashir Group of Companies and has an estimated fortune of $4.1 billion (€3.5bn) — close to half of Armenia's annual public budget. He built his wealth primarily in Russia and also holds Russian and Cypriot citizenship.

In his criminal trial in April, Karapetyan told the court that he had begun the process of renouncing his Russian and Cypriot citizenships to be eligible to run in the June 2026 parliamentary elections. He and his lawyers have denied all charges.
