World.title: Wallabies workhorse Hooper embraces club-country juggling act
World.content:
SportRugby UnionWallabies Wallabies workhorse Hooper embraces club-country juggling act Jonathan Drennan August 26, 2026 — 7:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Wallabies back-rower Tom Hooper has a strong claim for overtime. The former Brumbies player has barely stopped playing rugby for 18 months, switching from Super Rugby to Tests and then moving straight into a long, gruelling season in England with Exeter. Hooper remains happy to hang around a little longer with the Wallabies and is set to join prop Taniela Tupou and return from two Tests in Argentina to face South Africa in Perth in September, but remains unlikely to be available for the Bledisloe Cup series in October. Tom Hooper facing Argentina last September. Getty Images Like Tupou, Hooper’s selection for the Wallabies falls under World Rugby’s regulation 9, which covers the mandatory release of players by clubs for Test rugby. “I’ll probably miss the start of the Exeter season (in September). I am available to play any kind of games in (World Rugby’s) Regulation 9 window, within that international window, so as long as they keep picking me, I’ll keep showing up,” Hooper said.



Related Article Wallabies ‘Beat fire with fire’: Wallabies braced for Argentina’s mountain cauldron “Whenever I’m not allowed to (play), because of rules and all that jazz, I’ll head back to Exeter and keep showing up for them, and then hopefully pop back in the Wallaby camp. So it’s a bit of a back and forth for me for the next couple of years.” Hooper, who fractured his shoulder blade during a 12-minute cameo against Ireland in July, will return to play in Australia with the Reds in 2028. The back-rower described the injury as a blessing in disguise given his need to rest body and mind. “You really notch up the games over there in (England). I’ve already played 20 or 25 odd games for the Exeter Chiefs, which is a massive workload,” Hooper said. “Obviously, I was absolutely gutted to be missing out on some quality Test matches (against Japan and Italy) ... but you definitely have just got to listen to your body and that’s what we learn as athletes.”



The Wallabies are currently training in Buenos Aires and will travel to Jujuy on Thursday before facing the Pumas at Estadio 23 de Agosto this Saturday. The stadium commemorates August 23, 1812, when Manuel Belgrano, a military leader in the Argentine War of Independence, ordered the locals in Jujuy to burn everything to the ground rather than give anything to the advancing Spanish loyalist army. Tom Hooper has had a long, tough season with Exeter in England. Getty Images Wallabies playmaker Ben Donaldson is far more aware of the city’s more recent history that includes a passionate rugby community, something that he is ready to embrace. “You hear stories of lasers, people throwing stuff on the field and whatnot, but you’ve just got to embrace whatever comes; it’s going to be a pretty cool experience,” Donaldson said.



“I’ve played in Argentina before and every stadium you play in, it’s quite compact and very hostile. It’s an awesome experience and the supporters are so passionate for their team, which is great to see. “When it comes to the game you just kind of dial into your process and everything should take care of itself; you’ve just got to embrace the experience and embrace the challenge.” Related Article Australian rugby Everyone has a take on Suaalii’s best role, but only Les Kiss’ view matters. And he has shared it The Pumas squad are missing French-based Test veterans such as hooker Julian Montoya, back-rower Marcos Kremer, centre Santiago Chocobares, winger Mateo Carreras and playmaker Tomas Albornoz. But after facing Argentine players throughout last season with Exeter in European and domestic competitions, Hooper is fully prepared for the threat they bring, regardless of who is in the Pumas squad.



“We know what (threat) Argentina pose; they’re threats in terms of a physical forward pack and really electric backs,” Hooper said. “Half of those boys have been to the Olympics and have played sevens in the past. We know that it’s a really good mix of a physical game and also really exciting prospects out wide, so we’re just going to match that in both areas.” News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Monday.

State and territory leaders are gearing up for a fight over federal Labor’s plan to impose national standards on data centres ahead of a national cabinet meeting today.

Northern Territory chief minister Lia Finocchiaro, who alongside Queensland’s premier has objected to renewable energy requirements for data centres, said the territory would argue against a mandate at the Sydney meeting.

“The territory should be able to decide its energy policy and its energy mix,” she told Radio National.

“We understand that the federal government are pursuing a renewable agenda, and there’s no problem with that per se. But what they should not be doing is trying to impose rules on states and territories when they, under their own steam, are able to make these decisions for themselves for their people.”

Energy Minister Chris Bowen has previously threatened to steamroll the states and territories with federal legislation.

I’ve already played 20 or 25 odd games for the Exeter Chiefs, which is a massive workload,” Hooper said. “Obviously, I was absolutely gutted to be missing out on some quality Test matches (against Japan and Italy) ... but you definitely have just got to listen to your body and that’s what we learn as athletes.”



The Wallabies are currently training in Buenos Aires and will travel to Jujuy on Thursday before facing the Pumas at Estadio 23 de Agosto this Saturday. The stadium commemorates August 23, 1812, when Manuel Belgrano, a military leader in the Argentine War of Independence, ordered the locals in Jujuy to burn everything to the ground rather than give anything to the advancing Spanish loyalist army. Tom Hooper has had a long, tough season with Exeter in England. Getty Images Wallabies playmaker Ben Donaldson is far more aware of the city’s more recent history that includes a passionate rugby community, something that he is ready to embrace. “You hear stories of lasers, people throwing stuff on the field and whatnot, but you’ve just got to embrace whatever comes; it’s going to be a pretty cool experience,” Donaldson said.



“I’ve played in Argentina before and every stadium you play in, it’s quite compact and very hostile. It’s an awesome experience and the supporters are so passionate for their team, which is great to see. “When it comes to the game you just kind of dial into your process and everything should take care of itself; you’ve just got to embrace the experience and embrace the challenge.” Related Article Australian rugby Everyone has a take on Suaalii’s best role, but only Les Kiss’ view matters. And he has shared it The Pumas squad are missing French-based Test veterans such as hooker Julian Montoya, back-rower Marcos Kremer, centre Santiago Chocobares, winger Mateo Carreras and playmaker Tomas Albornoz. But after facing Argentine players throughout last season with Exeter in European and domestic competitions, Hooper is fully prepared for the threat they bring, regardless of who is in the Pumas squad.



“We know what (threat) Argentina pose; they’re threats in terms of a physical forward pack and really electric backs,” Hooper said. “Half of those boys have been to the Olympics and have played sevens in the past. We know that it’s a really good mix of a physical game and also really exciting prospects out wide, so we’re just going to match that in both areas.” News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Monday.

World.title: Australia news LIVE: Australia, UK, Canada urged to consider probe into Zomi Frankcom killing; Tributes pour in for country music legend Dolly Parton
World.content:
State and territory leaders are gearing up for a fight over federal Labor’s plan to impose national standards on data centres ahead of a national cabinet meeting today.

Northern Territory chief minister Lia Finocchiaro, who alongside Queensland’s premier has objected to renewable energy requirements for data centres, said the territory would argue against a mandate at the Sydney meeting.

“The territory should be able to decide its energy policy and its energy mix,” she told Radio National.

“We understand that the federal government are pursuing a renewable agenda, and there’s no problem with that per se. But what they should not be doing is trying to impose rules on states and territories when they, under their own steam, are able to make these decisions for themselves for their people.”

Energy Minister Chris Bowen has previously threatened to steamroll the states and territories with federal legislation.

World.title: Calls for free flu vaccine for under-fives as hospitalisations soar
World.content:
Hospitalisation rates surge for Pasifika and Maori under-5s Morning Report Download MP3 6m

Hospitalisation rates are soaring for under-fives with flu-like illnesses, many of them in intensive care.

That has prompted a call from the National Immunisation Technical Advisory Group to make the flu vaccine free for young children.

Chair and GP Mamaeroa David said Māori and Pasifika children were bearing the brunt.

Some under-fives were ending up in intensive care - and some may never come home, she said.

Dr Mamaeroa David. Supplied / Immunisation Advisory Center

"It's a nightmare, honestly, John. I haven't felt this uncomfortable since 2019 and the measles outbreak, and that's including Covid," she told Morning Report's John Campbell.

"During Covid we threw the book at (it) and as we can see it was a highly successful campaign against Covid.

"But for measles back in 2019 and unfortunately more than 85 children that we know of died in Samoa during that time."

It was time to make the vaccine free, she said.

It was heartbreaking that so many children were so seriously ill when there was a highly effective vaccine, David said.

To have that feeling now with another vaccine-preventable disease was extremely distressing, she said.

Associate health minister David Seymour. RNZ / Nathan McKinnon

David said she knew parents who wanted to immunise their children against flu but could not afford it.

"Opening up the funding for at least our under-five babies, especially our Māori and Pacific babies, for dropping their age for the older population to down to 55 years of age," she said.

"I can't sit idly by. I'm in all of these positions that you've just named because of that 2019 measles outbreak."

She said she couldn't watch as Influenza A burned through her community, with Influenza B most likely next.

PHF Science data for the week to 16 August showed there had been a big spike (75 per 100,000) in under-fives in hospital with severe respiratory illnesses.

Pharmac chief advisor for pharmaceuticals, Adrienne Martin. Supplied / Pharmac

They were far more likely than any other age group to end up in hospital.

Currently, the flu vaccine was only free for under-fives who had a history of severe respiratory illness or who had another serious disease like diabetes, heart disease or asthma.

David said Māori and Pasifika were affected most.

"Ethnicity is likely a proxy for related factors such as housing conditions, crowding, access to health services and high prevalence of comorbidities," she said.

Pharmac said it had finished its public consultation on a proposal to widen access to funded flu vaccines to all children from six months up to five years.

Associate Health Minister David Seymour said Pharmac would make an announcement on Wednesday afternoon about a decision that would make flu season more manageable for all families.

The PHF data showed Pasifika people of all ages were more likely than any others to be in hospital with severe respiratory illness.

Flu hospitalisation rates across the board had increased significantly at the start of August and were at a 10-year high in Auckland.

Pharmac said around half of total doses of flu vaccine - or about 700,000 - used in New Zealand each year were publicly funded.

Its chief advisor for pharmaceuticals, Adrienne Martin, said funded flu vaccines were available for everyone 65 years old and over, and for people under 65 who were at higher risk of severe illness from influenza.

This included people who were pregnant and children aged four years and under who had been hospitalised for a respiratory illness or had a history of significant respiratory illness, she said.

"Earlier this year, Pharmac consulted on a proposal to widen access to the flu vaccine to all children from six months up to five years," Martin said.

The agency also consulted on changing to two new flu vaccine brands that would provide increased protection for eligible people, she said.

"The proposed changes are a result of the 2025 competitive procurement process Pharmac ran for the supply of funded vaccines, excluding the Covid-19 vaccine. If approved, these changes would take effect from the start of the 2027 influenza season on 1 April 2027."

Martin said ordering and manufacturing flu vaccine happened many months before the start of the flu season.

World.title: 'Don't want this to happen again': Cook Islands fisherman recounts finding cocaine washed ashore
World.content:
A fisherman from a remote island in the Cook Islands says he feared for his life after a routine reef fishing trip led to the discovery of a mysterious package containing cocaine worth millions of dollars in street value.

The fisherman, who RNZ Pacific has agreed not to name, discovered the package washed up on the reef in Mitiaro on 28 July, thinking it could be a body or a bomb.

Cook Islands fisherman recalls finding cocaine package on beach Pacific Waves Download MP3 4m

"I had two thoughts then: first, I thought this could be a human body chopped up ... [and] second, I was suddenly worried that I was wrong and this thing was a bomb and if it exploded right now I would die and no one would ever find me," he told RNZ Pacific.

The contents of the package, weighing more than 26kg, have since been tested by Cook Islands Police, with preliminary testing indicating the presence of cocaine.

Nineteen packages alleged to be containing cocaine was found washed ashore in Mitiaro, Cook Islands Cook Islands News

The fisherman recalled he initially thought he was looking at a turtle that had been killed by a shark and washed onto the reef. But as he got closer, he realised it was not a turtle.

While stricken with fear, he cautiously poked the package with his fishing rod to see if he could feel what it contained.

"So I rolled it to the other side and something fell out; this packet fell out, and that's when it hit me, this was probably drugs."

He then became concerned the package could be more dangerous than it looked, and still fearing it might be rigged with explosives, he left the package and continued fishing.

But while cleaning his catch back on shore, he could not stop thinking about it.

Worried the high tide might take it away, he reported his find to a local police officer who enlisted the help of a couple of young men to carry the package off the reef.

They also discovered two loose packets believed to have been knocked from the main package and washed further ashore by rough seas.

"We took the whole thing to the police officers house and then we cut into the package to have a proper look at what was inside. So there were 17 packets inside the sack and two found washed ashore, so there were 19 packets altogether."

The material was taken to Rarotonga, where Cook Islands police said preliminary testing indicated the presence of cocaine.

In a press statement, police confirmed there were 19 bricks found, weighing approximately 26.49kg, including packaging.

Police are investigating where the package came from and whether it could be connected to other investigations.

Cook Islands Customs has also strengthened vessel monitoring and searches.

The fisherman said he was concerned about what the discovery could mean for Mitiaro and the wider Cook Islands.

He said the finds indicated there could be vessels travelling through Cook Islands waters as part of a bigger drug operation.

"We don't know what their plan was," he said.

"Maybe they were throwing it in the sea for another ship or yacht to pick up, something like that, or maybe they planned it all along to throw it in the sea to wash up on Mitiaro."

Mitiaro is roughly 50 minutes by air from Rarotonga. RNZ Pacific/Tiana Haxton

He worries such operations are not a new occurrence and this was only the first time they have been discovered in Mitiaro, which is roughly 50 minutes by air from Rarotonga.

He wants the world to know that drugs should not be carried through the Pacific Ocean, and his island home and community needs to be protected.

"So what do we want? We want to be protected," he said.

"We don't want any more of this stuff landing in our paradise, otherwise maybe next time it'll be a young one that comes across a package while fishing, and maybe they'll hide it and keep it secret.

"But the main message is we don't want this to happen again."

Police thanked the fisherman and the Mitiaro community for their assistance and cooperation.

World.title: Storing carbon in sea could have huge potential for fighting climate change - report
World.content:
Storing carbon in the sea could have huge potential for fighting climate change but will need careful oversight because of its risks, a new report says.

A Royal Society of New Zealand report, released on Wednesday, said even a drastic reduction in emissions was no longer enough to keep global temperatures within the 1.5°C warming limit set out in the Paris Agreement.

Directly removing carbon dioxide already in the atmosphere would also be necessary.

New Zealand already removes millions of tonnes of CO2 each year through forestry, but technology to also store the gas in the sea was emerging, the report said.

"Marine carbon dioxide removal may be a future tool to help reduce atmospheric carbon levels."

Marine carbon dioxide removal, or mCDR, ranged from restoring and maintaining 'blue carbon' environments like mangroves, wetlands and salt marshes, to deliberately altering the chemistry of the ocean to allow it to absorb more CO2.

Read more about marine carbon dioxide removal in this RNZ explainer, published earlier in 2026.

Almost all of the techniques were at an early stage, the report said.

"Currently, mCDR is a collection of developing technologies that are not yet ready for large-scale deployment."

There was "significant uncertainty" about how well each technique worked, whether they could be scaled, how long carbon would be locked away for, the costs, and the environmental risks and side effects.

"Any potential mCDR technique would require more research, effective monitoring and verification, and in-depth societal discussions before considering large-scale use," it said.

Despite growing interest, there was "minimal regulation" for marine carbon dioxide removal in New Zealand.

At the moment, New Zealand's exclusive economic zone regulations, together with international laws governing the ocean, control what can be done in the country's waters.

They prohibit marine dumping and 'placement of matter', although there is an exclusion for legitimate scientific research.

New Zealand's regulations were developed before marine geengineering and mDCR technologies emerged.

At least one mCDR company, Gigablue, has been pushing for changes to allow it to carry out larger-scale research and future commercial activitites.

Restoring or maintaining mangroves is a 'blue carbon' technology that is already in use - but the report warns that habitats that degrade or are damaged in storms could release their stored carbon again. Veronika Meduna / RNZ

The Royal Society report said mCDR presented potential economic opportunities for coastal communities, but also risks, "if projects fail or damage the marine environment".

Ahead of any adoption, "New Zealand, together with our Pacific neighbours, will need to establish appropriate regulations and governance," it said.

Victoria University earth sciences professor Tim Naish, a veteran climate researcher, said some carbon removals on land or sea would be necessary to reverse climate warming.

However, they risked creating a "moral hazard" by allowing societies to keep emitting.

"We create this idea that we don't really need to reduce emissions - we can do other things," he said.

"If you create a narrative that, oh, she'll be right, we can get out of this with technology and clever use of natural sinks - I do worry about that."

Carbon removals would have to continue as long as humans kept creating emissions, rather than cutting them at their source.

"It's not just one dump of alkaline basalt in the ocean... It's got to be continuously done."

That could be both financially and environmentally costly, Naish said.

It was worth considering whether New Zealand could put its large amount of ocean to use, but there was plenty the country should be doing first.

"We're not even doing our bit on emissions reduction," he said.

World.title: 'Game changing': DNA clues track hornets in Auckland waterways
World.content:
Scientists are trialing using environmental DNA to track signs of yellow-legged hornets in Auckland waterways, with hornet queens potentially coming out of winter hibernation soon.

The last yellow-legged hornets - which have potentially deadly stings - were found in Auckland in April. Biosecurity NZ have been working to eradicate the invasive pest.

While yellow-legged hornets don't live in waterways, cells from their bodies can end up there. The environmental DNA trial may help scientists find nests or decide where to put traps.

Leader of the trial, Bioeconomy Science Institute entomologist Andrew Pugh said researchers were essentially leveraging waterways as natural collectors of genetic material.

Water samples will be collected from a range of streams and small waterways around Auckland's North Shore.

He said the same technology had been successfully used to detect pest wasps.

"What makes this research exciting is this will be the first time eDNA testing has been used in a New Zealand biosecurity insect incursion response.

"If successful, this work could help identify areas of hornet activity to quickly track down hard-to-find nests, and to optimise field deployment of surveillance traps."

To find the best trapping method, the institute is testing traps in the Northern Hemisphere, where there are established populations of Asian hornets.

Project lead, entomologist Natalie Page said the trial will run over several weeks starting across Jersey, the largest of the Channel Islands located between England and France.

"Hornets in the Northern Hemisphere are currently in their active season rather than hibernation, providing a valuable opportunity to work with international partners to test different lure and trap combinations," Page said.

More than 200 traps will be set up, in collaborating with beekeepers in Jersey and hornet management specialists, who will report their findings to New Zealand researchers.

Victoria University professor of ecology and entomology Phil Lester said the DNA trial was a promising approach.

"New Zealand's goal for the yellow-legged hornet incursion is eradication."

"That is an ambitious objective, and one that has proven difficult to achieve elsewhere in the world."

He said any advances in surveillance capability could increase the likely to eradicate the pest.

Lester said yellow-legged hornets are likely to arrive again, as they spread across Asia, Europe, and the United States.

"These projects will strengthen New Zealand's preparedness for future hornet incursions and other invasive insect threats."

An expert in environmental biosecurity, Benjamín Durán-Vinet said taking testing out of the lab and into the field could mean getting answers on the spot.

He said this was a "game changer".

World.title: Councils not spending ratepayer money 'willy nilly', mayor says over rates cap
World.content:
Mayors upset by latest sleight against local government Morning Report Download MP3 6m

Central Otago's mayor says a rates cap being introduced by the government is "pretty frustrating" and councils aren't just spending ratepayer money "willy nilly".

Local Government Minister Simon Watts made the announcement on Tuesday - saying the government was moving ahead with its plans to cap the amount councils can increase rates by to a maximum of 4 percent.

However, it won't be able to pass the legislation until next term.

Watts said the legislation would put "a brake on excessive increases and [give] ratepayers greater certainty".

He confirmed the average amount households would save is $34 a year.

Mayors across the country have been expressing their dismay, with Central Otago's Tamah Alley telling Morning Report "it's just pretty frustrating".

"We know that capping of rates has been incredibly popular with the public and we understand why," she said.

But every mayor, chair and councillor up and down the country has been working so hard over the last few years to catch up on huge infrastructure deficits and provide the services that our communities need and deserve."

Alley said Central Otago's rates remained "pretty low" on a national average but they had seen significant rises. This included a rise of 18 percent, followed by a rise of 12 percent - but this year, Alley said, the rise was 6.34 percent.

The council had experienced large price increases for items they purchased for community facilities, she said.

Local Government Minister Simon Watts. RNZ/Baz Macdonald

While they were looking to save money where they could, Alley said they were also trying to keep ahead of the "infrastructure curve" so people could move there.

When asked if her council wasted ratepayer money, Alley said she had yet to have someone in her district point out something and say "that's a waste of money".

She called out the idea that councils are "out there, spending willy nilly", when they too are accountable to the community.

Local Government Minister defends rates cap Morning Report Download MP3 6m

Earlier, Watts told Morning Report some rates rises people in New Zealand were experiencing were unaffordable.

"Under our model, that'll be capped at 4 percent and that means people have certainty.

"At the moment, they've got a rollercoaster of rates increases and it's one of the biggest household expenditure items that households have no control over and we're putting in place a cap that means they'll have certainty on what they pay."

Questioned on how councils would pay their bills, Watts reiterated the importance of ratepayers having certainty.

World.title: 'Totally wrong': Community up in arms about stormwater runoff into native forest park
World.content:
Warkworth's 800-year-old Kauri under threat by council plan Morning Report Download MP3 3m

A community is up in arms over plans to send stormwater runoff into a native forest where an 800-year-old kauri tree lives.

Resource consent has been granted for a housing development near Parry Kauri Park in Warkworth, which allows stormwater from four of the 12 lots to be diverted into the park's stream.

A freshwater ecologist said sending more water into the stream would increase erosion and sediment, harming trees and endangered native creatures.

But Auckland Council said any adverse effects on the park would be minimised.

Volunteer at the park, Nick Sharp, said any more stormwater running into the stream would be bad news for the native forest.

"It's erosion in the creek beds, which then kills all the life in the creek beds. And then eventually trees start falling down as we see in lots of parts of the country. This is totally wrong and what the heck is going wrong?"

Inside the kauri park. RNZ / Luka Forman

The park was bought with money raised by the community in 1965.

It's made up of 8.5 hectares of pristine native bush, which is now administered by Auckland Council, and maintained with the help of volunteers from the Kauri Bushmen's Association.

Freshwater ecologist Sophie Tweddle has been monitoring the stream in the park for the past five years.

Sending more stormwater into the stream would increase sediment and harm at-risk species like longfin eels, giant kokopu, and freshwater crayfish, she said.

A community is up in arms over plans to send stormwater runoff into a native forest in Parry Kauri Park in Warkworth, where an 800-year-old kauri tree lives. Supplied / Nick Sharp

"It clogs the gills and the eyes of the animals, it also stops them from feeding because they can't see their prey, it covers the habitat in the stream, so it reduces the amount of places where they can shelter."

Auckland Council had not properly considered how the extra runoff could harm the stream when granting resource consent, Tweddle said.

"It's kind of almost been just shrugged off. They just said 'oh it's going to have no effect'. But actually in a stream like this it could have a massive effect and that should have been considered."

However, Auckland Council's head of resource consents James Hassall said plans for the subdivision would ensure stormwater flow was appropriately managed, and effects on rivers and streams were minimised.

An 800-year-old McKinney kauri. RNZ / Luka Forman

Ray Jensen, who has volunteered at the park for more than 50 years, was concerned about kauri dieback being transported through the runoff from the new subdivision.

Hassall said there was a low risk of that because there were no kauri trees on the development site.

But Jensen worried residents could unwittingly spread it into the stormwater from other forests via their cars or shoes.

"And the trees drinking out of the creek could pick it up. Now these trees - this particular one [the McKinney kauri] has been here for over 800 years and I think it's not our right to kill it."

Sharp believed there was a simple solution to all of this - to divert the stormwater to the north instead.

"Why they never ran it that way I have absolutely no idea because that's naturally where it should flow. About 100 metres of pipe dug up down the side through the development ... would send the water where it should go, away from the park."

He and Jensen recently held a protest on the issue that about 50 people attended.

They contacted the council and local politicians calling for the water be diverted away from the park.

World.title: Jeffrey Epstein accomplice Ghislaine Maxwell loses bid to overturn US conviction
World.content:
A US federal judge on Tuesday rejected a bid by Ghislaine Maxwell, a key accomplice of notorious sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, to throw out her conviction on sex trafficking charges.

In his ruling, Judge Paul Engelmayer said that Maxwell's claims that her constitutional rights at trial and sentencing were violated "are all meritless and all or almost all are frivolous."

Maxwell was convicted in 2021 of supplying underage girls to Epstein, whose ties to powerful business executives, politicians, celebrities and academics have fueled years of scrutiny and conspiracy theories.

Under a new law passed last year, President Donald Trump's administration has released vast troves of investigative files relating to Epstein -- drawing huge public attention to the case.

High-profile figures including Britain's former prince Andrew have been publicly disgraced for their associations with Epstein.

In February, Maxwell was subpoenaed by the House Oversight Committee to discuss her relations with Epstein but refused to answer any questions. Her lawyer stated she would only speak if Trump granted her clemency.

The US Supreme Court last October declined to hear an appeal by Maxwell of her sex trafficking conviction.

Trump, who also had a years-long relationship with Epstein, initially opposed releasing the so-called Epstein files, prompting accusations of a cover-up that dogged his first year back in office.

The Republican has denied any link to Epstein's crimes.

World.title: ICE detainee dies in CNMI prison
World.content:
An immigration detainee being held at the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands (CNMI) Department of Corrections died early Sunday, authorities say.

Corrections Commissioner Anthony Torres identified the detainee as Lian Yong Wei and said staff found him during routine checks at the prison on Saipan.

Staff immediately initiated an emergency medical response, and Wei was transported to the Commonwealth Health Center, where he was pronounced dead.

The department said it would not release protected health information, including information about Lian's medical condition.

The Department of Public Safety and other appropriate investigative authorities have been notified, along with US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).

The circumstances surrounding Lian's death remain under investigation.

According to the Department of Corrections, Lian was initially brought into custody on charges of disturbing the peace, assault, assault and battery, aggravated assault and battery, assault with a dangerous weapon, and an immigration violation.

The department said it was reviewing its procedures following the death and will make any necessary changes to strengthen prevention and emergency response measures.

"The Department extends its condolences to the family of Mr Wei," Torres said.

World.title: Root left fuming as teammates 'continually keep making stupid mistakes'
World.content:
England captain Joe Root says he was "hacked off" and disappointed after another incident involving a teammate at a nightclub, adding that the national team players are trying to build a culture they can be proud of.

After videos on social media appeared to show England fast bowler Brydon Carse in handcuffs being spoken to by police officers, England's Cricket Board (ECB) dropped the 31-year-old from the second test against Pakistan, which starts on Thursday.

Carse is the latest England cricketer to be involved in a nightclub incident after Harry Brook, Ben Duckett, former captain Ben Stokes and Gus Atkinson, leading to accusations of a drinking culture amongst the players.

"If I'm being brutally honest, I'm really hacked off. I'm really disappointed," Root told reporters.

"It's not the isolated incident itself, it's the fact that we continually keep making stupid mistakes away from the game and it's detracting from what we're doing on the field."

Root, who returned as England captain after Stokes retired from international cricket, said the players had taken the incidents seriously.

"Clearly, we're not portraying ourselves how we want to. I think we've got an opportunity to build a culture that's very strong, something we can be proud of. Of course that's not going to happen overnight," he added.

Brydon Carse is the latest England cricketer to be involved in an off-field incident. (Getty Images: Jason McCawley/Cricket Australia)

"We've already had conversations as a team about what is expected from this group of players, what it means to play for England, what it takes to play for England. They are very clear about what is expected of them, and how we need to go about things moving forward."

Root said he had spoken to Carse, who was replaced by Sonny Baker for the second Test.

"When I first found out, my first concern was him as a person … I don't think I'm speaking out of turn by saying he's very upset, very apologetic and understands his actions. I'm sure when he gets his chance, he'll say that himself," the captain added.

Carse was briefly arrested and no charges were brought. The independent Cricket Regulator will investigate whether he breached the ECB's code of conduct, the sport's national governing body said on Monday.

England, who won the first test by an innings and 103 runs, will next face Pakistan at Lord's, followed by a third test in Birmingham next month.

Reuters

World.title: This shark attack hero believes Olympic inclusion could save lives
World.content:
What would the Australian summer — or indeed winter — be without the ubiquitous yellow and red flags on beaches around the country?

Surf life savers are as essential as sunscreen and deliver an unquestionable sense of comfort and ease among holiday-makers and residents alike.

And the competitive arm of the movement, the Iron Series, is almost as synonymous with the Australian sporting summer as the echo of leather on willow at the nation's cricket grounds or the thwack of tennis balls at Melbourne Park.

But as hard-fought and intense as the racing is throughout the series, the sporting aspect pales into insignificance when compared to the bigger picture of what Surf Life Saving is truly about.

"This sport is born out of such an important part of Australian culture," number one-seeded athlete Charlie Verco tells ABC Sport on the beach at Surfers Paradise.

"That is ocean safety and being able to help other people in danger."

Charlie Verco is the number one seed for this year's Iron Series championship. (Supplied)

Just like fellow Iron Series number one seed Tiarnee Massie, Verco has first-hand experience of just how important his skills are away from the sporting arena.

"I've had countless examples of having to just apply those skills in living my everyday life … the skills that you learn to how to rescue people," the 24-year-old says.

Almost drowning as a child, now saving others as Surf Life Saving's number one A childhood accident could so easily have cost Surf Life Saver Tiarnee Massie her life. But now the 28-year-old heads into this year's Iron Series as the number one seed.

"And for me recently, I had a pretty full-on one example of that with the shark attack with Leah."

Saturday, June 13, 2026, is a date that will not be quickly forgotten by Verco or anyone else who was on Coogee Beach.

Sydney teacher Leah Stewart was attacked by a three- to four-metre-long shark, believed to be a Great White, while swimming between the flags at the popular spot in Sydney's east.

Stewart's extensive injuries resulted in her having to undergo multiple surgeries and her arm being amputated during an extended hospital stay.

Fatefully and thankfully, Verco was also in the water that day and his training instantly kicked into gear as he rushed to Stewart's aid, his quick response earning widespread praise as being among the reasons Stewart was not killed.

Charlie Verco grew up at North Bondi surf club and now competes for Newport. (Supplied: Charlie Verco)

"There was definitely a lot of thoughts going through my head," Verco says.

"And it wasn't clear thinking, but that's what is going to happen no matter what, and it's having spent that time ingraining it so that you don't have to think about what the right thing to do is what made the difference.

"I actually had to tell some swimmers that were near me that wanted to get taken to the shore … I really wanted to paddle in, so picking up one of the swimmers near me would have been a really good excuse to go in.

"But then I assessed the shark and I thought because I was on such a big board I could scare away that shark if I went in there, maybe.

"Then I saw the shark come out of the water and I was like, 'that thing's not scared of me.'"

Swim for Sydney shark attack victim A Sydney shark attack victim has been hailed "a survivor" by her family in a letter read out at a community swim event.

Battling his fears, Verco plunged into the mix, getting Stewart onto his board and quickly backing them towards the shore and further assistance.

"I've never been more grateful to being part of this life-saving community and having experienced that training," Verco, who competes for Newport Surf Life Saving Club on Sydney's north shore, says.

"So many of the lessons I've learned through that have played in as factors to what allowed me to help her that day.

"When someone started screaming shark and I saw this thing in the water, all I wanted to do was paddle to shore.

"But growing up in the community embedded a sense of responsibility to help others, especially in the water when I have the ability to [do it]."

Charlie Verco will look to win the title outright for the first time when the series concludes at Surfers Paradise in February. (Supplied)

That was not the only time Verco has had to race to the aid of a member of the public in the ocean.

"The shark attack's definitely the most dramatic one that's happened and probably the scariest one because it was the one where I felt like I was in real danger," Verco says.

"But there's been countless examples where I've been out surfing in Bondi and people will swim out and I'll drag someone in.

"Up in Queensland, the beaches are so much longer so I've had to do some pretty serious rescues … we had to run 500 metres down the beach with a board before we actually padded out to get someone … they had some pretty serious water inhalation and got taken away to hospital but they would have died if we didn't have the combination of fitness skills and knowledge to help them.

"All of my mates have heaps of different anecdotal experiences, whether it's just driving to work and someone in the car in front of you had a heart attack, I have a mate who did CPR on the way to work, my mum and my sister were down at their camp for school and they had to do CPR on one of the parents, just out of nowhere.

"It happens. You never think it's going to happen. But I never thought I was going to be in a shark attack."

Charlie Verco finished the Moloka'i 2 Oahu Paddleboard World Championships in July in a new record time. (Supplied: Moloka'i 2 Oahu Paddleboard World Championships)

Verco, who is also a four-time Paddleboard World Champion, noted that the skills he has learned from a competitive aspects of Surf Life Saving helped him when it mattered most.

"Just in how to manage your mindset under a really high-stress environment," he says.

"There's a lot of pressure in being able to perform for that one race in massive surf to get that Iron Series title, but also when you're managing a huge amount of fear and you see a woman getting attacked by a shark and being able to take that pause and think what is the actual best action to do as opposed to just reacting off of a whim and potentially make mistakes and put yourself or other people in danger.

"I think that transfers across in so many different areas."

Olympic showcase with an important message

Australia's leading Surf Life Savers have their eyes set on joining the Olympic family. (Supplied)

In six years' time, Brisbane will showcase its sporting environment to the world when the 2032 Olympics roll into town.

Surf Life Saving is already making its case to organisers that their sport deserves to be included, and as two of the sport's biggest names, Massie and Verco, are fully behind it.

"Surf Life Saving is such an embedded part in Australian culture," Verco says.

"There's no better way to represent Australia at such an incredible event. The Olympics is the top tier, the pinnacle event of sporting competition.

Surf lifesaving is preparing its Olympic push Ali Day wants to figure in surf lifesaving's push for Olympic inclusion, determined to ensure his sport doesn't "cop it" like breaking did in Paris.

"It's what any athlete who grows up watching sport says 'that's where I want to go one day.'

"Not only is the sport incredible, but it's embedded in such an important idea around surf safety and helping others through surf safety as well.

"That is something that's so well ingrained in Australia, but I also think it's something that's really important to spread around the world.

"There's countless number of drownings on beaches all around the world every year, so I think being able to get this sport on a stage where people around the world can see it and see how incredible it is and maybe embed cultures that exist similar to the Nippers culture where you learn those skills about how to be safe in the water from an early age and then bring that experience and skill into helping others around the world I think will be able to save incredible numbers of lives every year.

"It's a no-brainer to put surf life saving in it. I think it's the best option there is."

There are plenty of things in favour of Surf Life Saving joining the Olympic movement.

Under current arrangements, the Brisbane 2032 organisers can propose a maximum of four additional disciplines from the core events.

One of the key aims of the Fit for the Future program is for the Olympics to help promote: "A future where sport is part of everyday life for more people, creating resilient communities, enabling health and well-being, education and inclusion."

No extra infrastructure is needed, and despite the sport being considered uniquely Australian, there is a world championships, which will take place this year in Gqeberha, South Africa.

Tiarnee Massie says giving Surf Life Saving a platform at the Olympics would be very important. (Getty Images: Matt Roberts)

Massie, who has previously made Australian national age group squads in the Olympic sport of kayaking, says having Surf Lifesaving at the 2032 Games would be "iconic".

"Having the Olympics in Brisbane for 2032 is so special for every sport that is in the Olympics," Massie says.

"But to get surf life saving into the Olympics is… it would be iconic.

"It is iconic to Australians, it's iconic to everyone who lives here, who lives near the water and the beach and I think it it's only right to have that in the Olympic Games, to showcase to the other countries what we can do and how important the sport is to Australians.

"No other sport does that; no other sport is trying to prepare to be the best at saving someone's life. But our sport is.

"To showcase that to the rest of the country and to the world would be so important, and to get that to the Olympic Games and get everyone's eyes on the importance of what we are doing, it would be so special."

World.title: Crows captain makes tearful speech as All Australian team is named
World.content:
Max Gawn has claimed a record ninth All Australian blazer, while Nick Daicos was named player of the year by both the coaches and his fellow players, but a speech from Adelaide captain Jordan Dawson stole the show at the AFL Awards.

Dawson won Best Captain and Most Courageous Player, before being selected in and named vice captain of the All Australian team, and spoke openly about his mental health on stage.

Dawson's brother died at the age of 35 earlier this year, something he says he has struggled to deal with throughout the season.

"It's been a struggle. It's not easy. It's a range of emotions and they come at different times," Dawson said.

"For me it's about creating safe spaces in the footy club and at home, and understanding there will be times when it's hard to go to work and that it is OK to feel a certain type of way.

"It's still raw, it's always going to be hard to talk about. I'm so lucky I have such supportive people around me.

"The mental health space is something new to me, but something I want to learn more about.

"I want everyone to know who is struggling with their mental health that you are definitely loved and that the world is a better place with you in it. You are enough. We all love you, you have friends and family around you."

Nick Daicos was a multiple winner at the AFL Awards. (Getty Images: Michael Willson)

Gawn, who was named captain of the All Australian side, became the first man to earn nine blazers. Marcus Bontempelli earned selection for an eighth time.

Daicos, selected in the All Australian time for the fourth time in the first five years of his career, also swept the Coaches Association Champion Player of the Year and Leigh Matthews MVP awards.

Carlton's Jagga Smith was named the Rising Star for 2026.

World.title: Richmond denies players 'making light' of Swans scandal on Mad Monday
World.content:
The Richmond Football Club has denied its players were "referencing or making light of recent matters" in footage recorded during their post-season celebrations.

Tiger players were recorded during a drinking session at a Victorian country pub, with one player seen feigning shock after being spanked on his rear by a teammate.

Another teammate whips a fellow player on the back with a belt in footage captured by news outlets yesterday, leading to speculation they were referencing the ongoing Sydney Swans scandal.

The club denied that was the case.

"Richmond is aware of a video circulating from a player end-of-season gathering," a statement read.

"The club has spoken to the players who have expressed their embarrassment over their behaviour.

"The players are adamant they were in no way referencing or making light of recent matters."

Swans will not be invited to Brownlow ceremony AFL boss Andrew Dillon speaks to the media about the Sydney Swans scandal, saying "the actions of a few don't define the actions of the entire industry".

The Tigers finished second last this season with a 3-20 win-loss record.

The pub that hosted Richmond's drinks said the controversy had been blown out of proportion.

"In our view, this has been blown out of proportion," the Garfield Hotel, 80 kilometres east of Melbourne, said in a statement posted on social media.

The hotel said it "could not speak more highly" of how players behaved.

"For such a young group, they were extremely respectful and a fun group of boys to deal with," the statement read.

Nick Blakey (left) is one of the Swans suspended for breaching club standards. (AAP Image: Dean Lewins)

"They enjoyed a few quiet beers to unwind after a long season and we see nothing wrong with that.

"They had booked out the venue for the afternoon, so they were the only patrons on site.

"They enjoyed their afternoon and moved on."

The hotel noted media were waiting for the Tigers players "in the hope of capturing a misstep, which we consider disappointing".

The Richmond footage emerged hours after AFL chief executive Andrew Dillon fronted the media for the first time since the Swans scandal began.

"I have been asked a lot in recent days, what message football should be sending young people and what we should be saying to our kids," Dillon said.

"For me, the answer is straightforward: it doesn't matter who you are, it doesn't matter what you do, whether you're an AFL footballer — the way we treat women says a lot about who we are as people, as a community and as a game.

"Quite simply, respect for women is not negotiable."

Dillon said the actions of the five suspended Swans players had "fallen well short of the standards our game expects and community deserves".

"While there are players involved, we cannot lose sight of the bigger picture. More importantly, there are women who have made a report to police and they should be shown care and respect," he said.

World.title: NRL changes rules to allow Jai Arrow to 'play' 100 games for Souths
World.content:
Jai Arrow will make cameo appearances in the final two rounds of the regular season in order to reach 100 games for South Sydney.

In one of the feel-good stories of the NRL season, the forward who retired with motor neurone disease in May has been approved to start on the field in rounds 26 and 27.

Arrow will then be substituted out in the opening seconds before any active involvement in play.

Arrow, in jersey number 23, has been named co-captain with Cameron Murray, who is listed to come off the bench.

It came after the Rabbitohs made an appeal to the NRL to grant the former Queensland representative an on-field swansong while still able to walk and run.

The initiative gives Arrow two final chances to farewell an NRL career that featured a grand-final appearance in 2021 and 12 State of Origin caps.

The NRL has granted Souths special dispensation to name Arrow as an extra player on today's team list and an extra substitution in their rotation.

Arrow vows to help others fight MND Former NRL player Jai Arrow says he is determined to raise money and awareness for Motor Neurone Disease until a cure is found.

The matches, against Gold Coast and the Sydney Roosters, will bring Arrow's tally to 180 career games and 100 for the Rabbitohs.

Arrow will lead the team out on both occasions and sit on the interchange bench in Souths kit after being substituted out.

The Titans and Roosters have both approved the plan, as have the Rugby League Players Association.

"We are very grateful to Peter [V'landys] and the NRL, and Clint [Newton] at the RLPA, for supporting our proposal," Souths chief executive Blake Solly said.

"We believe this will provide great inspiration for everyone watching the game from the stadium or at home, showing that MND will not hold Jai, or anyone else, back from achieving what they want to achieve in life."

The NRL world has rallied around Arrow since his shock diagnosis and immediate retirement in May.

The league threw Arrow "the world's biggest birthday party" on the day Souths beat Newcastle in July, rolling out a birthday cake in the shape of the 31-year-old's jersey and presenting him with a commemorative jersey.

Fundraising efforts have already passed $1 million in support of Arrow, who is the father of a young daughter.

Players from all clubs have shown their support by marking tries with arrow celebrations throughout the month of July.

World.title: McVeigh to canvass Hird return as icon urges Bombers fans to unite
World.content:
New Essendon coach Mark McVeigh says he will speak to James Hird about returning to the club in a different capacity after a second failed bid to be coach.

McVeigh was unveiled on Tuesday in a press conference that was also attended by a number of Essendon's current players.

Both he and club president Andrew Welsh indicated their desire to have Hird involved.

"I'd love to see James as a part of the club going forward. He's such a fantastic football person," Welsh said.

"I feel there's significant value James can bring, not just tokenistic, but real value to our club and our playing group.

"Certainly, part of my messaging was that Mark and I would want to catch up with him when the time is appropriate."

While Welsh said a pair of calls to Hird had gone unanswered on Monday night, McVeigh said he had shared a conversation with his former captain.

"I love James Hird, he's one of my best mates. It was difficult to go through the process against a good friend," he said.

McVeigh (right) called Hird (left) one of his "best mates" after beating him to the Essendon job. (Getty Images: Ryan Pierse)

"I don't fear those people [Hird's supporters], I actually embrace how they feel, and I understand it, to be fair.

"He's been a constant in my life since I was 17 years of age. We spoke this morning, and the way he spoke of how proud he was of this moment for me, it hasn't broken us, we're still together, but I understand and embrace the feelings of the people that love James Hird, because I do too."

McVeigh, Welsh and club CEO Tim Roberts called for unity at the club amid rumours of a potential board challenge from unimpressed Hird fans.

"I don't ask for your patience, I ask for your re-alignment to our club," McVeigh said.

"I sit here year after year, and we get people coming out of the shadows that want to challenge the board," added Welsh.

"I can tell you since I've been here that this club has never been more united.

"These people want to keep living in the shadows and keep on trying to destabilise our club, we don't jump at shadows.

"We're a strong club and we'll continue to make sure that we make the right decisions on behalf of our members and our teams and our staff to get this club moving forward again."

Tim Watson (pictured) has called for unity at Essendon after Mark McVeigh's signing. (Getty Images: Michael Willson)

The plea for unity came as Essendon legend Tim Watson has the club's passionate supporters to "put [their] weapons down".

"There's got to be a unification of the club now," he told SEN on Tuesday morning.

"People have to put down their weapons and get behind this appointment of a former player — somebody who has been passionate about the football club.

"This is part of the healing process that needs to take place. Ultimately, it's a much bigger thing than the emotion that might be associated with it now. There is an enormous amount of work to do.

Live Moment Look back at Mark McVeigh's first press conference as Essendon's new senior coach. McVeigh says Bombers 'won't live in the past' Pretty good way to end the press conference from the new Essendon coach. He receives another round of applause from those in attendance before walking off the podium. Welsh with another clue on Hird returning I reckon it's going to be a full-court press on the Dons trying to get Hird to say yes to some kind of role within the club. "We have great people that we want to get back involved with the club in meaningful ways," Welsh says. "I look at this as a point that we can re-align that passion." McVeigh with an insight into his game plan McVeigh explains what areas he's going to try and fix on-field. "In the phases of the game, we can't focus on one. If you look at the numbers, we're the bottom of the table in a lot of areas. "I do want them to be brave, I do want them to play with flare, but we do need to fix up our defence. "They [the players] need to come back prepared physically and ready to learn. "The system we'll put in place, you need to understand, otherwise you'll get found out. "When we get all three phases going in the right direction, Essendon will fly." Show more

"Congratulations to him. He's been an Essendon man all his life. He's loved this football club, that was clear in the days that he played.

"He's had a great development profile if you look at where he's been and what he's been doing. He's been part of elite coaching departments [at GWS and Sydney]."

McVeigh has signed a three-year contract with Essendon and was the unanimous choice of the Essendon board.

World.title: Piastri searching for answers as teammate re-enters F1 title picture
World.content:
Oscar Piastri's "disappointing" end to the Dutch Grand Prix has left the Australian and his McLaren team searching for answers, while his teammate has roared back into the Formula 1 title picture.

Last weekend in Zandvoort was shaping to be a good weekend for Piastri.

The Australian was matching the pace at the front through qualifying, and after a terrific second start in the grand prix following Max Verstappen's heavy crash, Piastri was on course for a first podium finish since Miami in May.

Piastri struggles after slow pit stop, Norris wins as Verstappen crashes Reigning world champion Lando Norris has doubled his grand prix win tally in 2026, producing a pair of brilliant overtakes to win the Dutch Grand Prix.

Piastri had performed a breathtaking overtake on Mercedes driver George Russell to move into third and was not far off the pace set by leaders Kimi Antonelli and teammate Lando Norris, despite being on a harder compound tyre.

But a slow first pit stop knocked Piastri back behind Russell and out of third place, and it only got worse from there.

Piastri, who won the Dutch Grand Prix in 2025, fell right off the pace and finished a distant sixth as Norris surged to victory.

Piastri was running third until a slow pit stop knocked him out of the podium position at Zandvoort. (Reuters: Benoit Tessier)

The sudden pace drop-off has left Piastri with plenty of questions that he and the team will want answers to.

"The first stint felt reasonable, but from the second stint onwards, the pace was simply not there, and it became a real struggle," he said.

"We will review the entire weekend and analyse to understand why we experienced such a significant performance drop-off.

"A slow pit stop didn't help, but the fundamental issue was the lack of pace, which is something we'll work on ahead of Monza.

"That's the priority now, to dig into the data with the team to find the root cause and ensure we can move forward in a more positive direction for the upcoming races."

Piastri's situation is a far cry from where he was at the conclusion of last year's Dutch Grand Prix, when he claimed his seventh grand prix win of the season and was the championship leader.

But while Piastri is seeking answers to get back to the front of the grid, Norris is threatening to stay there.

'The fight's still on': Norris re-enters the F1 title picture

McLaren entered the 2026 season having won the previous two constructors' championships, and with Lando Norris as reigning drivers' champion.

Reigning Formula 1 drivers' champion Lando Norris has won the past two grands prix. (Reuters: Benoit Tessier)

But with a new era of regulations, McLaren's 2026 season started poorly.

Piastri crashed on his way to the grid in Melbourne and he and Norris did not start in Shanghai due to car issues.

Norris then had back-to-back retirements in Montreal and Monaco, meaning he failed to finish three of the opening six grands prix.

But the reigning world champion has returned to winning ways, triumphing in Hungary before the mid-year break and then again last weekend in the Netherlands.

With back-to-back wins and growing confidence in his season, Norris has re-emerged as a drivers' championship contender.

F1 drivers' championship standings after Dutch Grand Prix 242 — Kimi Antonelli, Mercedes

183 — George Russell, Mercedes

183 — Lewis Hamilton, Ferrari

159 — Lando Norris, McLaren

155 — Charles Leclerc, Ferrari

With 10 or 11 rounds remaining this season, depending on conflict in the Middle East, Norris is sitting fourth in the standings, 83 points behind leader Kimi Antonelli.

It is a huge gap, but recent history shows it is not an impossible feat.

At the conclusion of last year's Dutch Grand Prix, Max Verstappen was 104 points behind then-leader Piastri with nine rounds remaining.

Verstappen surged towards the end of the season while Piastri slumped. Verstappen fell two points shy of Norris in the standings, but finished a stunning 11 points ahead of Piastri.

Having seen what is possible, Norris has made this year's title fight a four-way race with Antonelli, George Russell and Lewis Hamilton.

Norris's message to his team over the radio after taking the chequered flag on Sunday certainly sounded like the Briton believed his championship hopes are far from over.

"Let's keep pushing. Thank you for the hard work. Let's keep bringing upgrades, let's keep bringing performance, please," he said.

"The fight's still on."

Out of the car, Norris was quick to point out that there is a long season still ahead of the drivers and that he was not getting ahead of himself with an 83-point deficit.

"One race at a time. A lot of people say it now, but it is the truth of it. There's no point in thinking that far ahead," he said after winning on Sunday.

"There are plenty of things we can do better, and we need to do better if we want to fight for a championship.

"We have to keep working hard. There's still plenty of races, plenty of opportunity for everyone."

Norris's deficit to Antonelli was 101 points prior to the weekend in Hungary, but the McLaren champion has reduced that by 18 with two tremendous weekends.

However, the 83-point gap is significant and Antonelli has extended his overall championship lead.

Entering the Dutch Grand Prix weekend, the young Italian's lead over Hamilton was 50 points, and 59 over Russell.

After the weekend, his lead is 59 points over both Hamilton and Russell.

F1 heads to Monza for the Italian Grand Prix in two weeks, one of the fastest tracks on the calendar and vastly different to the tight and twisting circuits in Hungary and the Netherlands where Norris has won this year.

World.title: 'A dangerous individual': Ex-snooker champ convicted of child sex abuse
World.content:
Former world snooker champion Graeme Dott has been convicted of sexually abusing two primary school children in Scotland in the 1990s and early 2000s.

Dott, 49, was found guilty of abusing a girl from 1993-96 and a boy from 2006-10 after a five-day trial at the High Court in Glasgow. The judge ordered Dott to be held in custody ahead of his sentencing on September 29.

The woman, now in her 40s, testified that Dott sexually abused her on multiple occasions, "caressing" her bottom over her clothing, exposing himself and touching her with parts of his body, including his penis.

The man, now in his late 20s, said he was abused on multiple occasions, with Dott touching him inappropriately, kissing him and performing sexual acts.

Dott with his wife Elaine after winning the snooker world championship in 2006. (Getty Images: Rui Vieira)

"Dott is a dangerous individual, and I hope this conviction provides some measure of comfort to those impacted by his crimes," Detective Inspector Gary Smillie from Police Scotland said.

Snooker's governing body suspended Dott in April 2025 after he was charged in the case. The Scot was ranked number 56 in the world at the time and dropped from the rankings after the season.

On Monday, the World Professional Billiards and Snooker Association revoked Dott's membership following an emergency board meeting. The WPBSA also said it wrote to the World Snooker Tour to request his immediate removal from the WST Hall of Fame.

Dott won the World Snooker Championship in 2006 and was a runner-up twice.

AP/Reuters

Tech.title: Trump is upping the price of Big Tech’s favorite visa
Tech.content:
In the span of a few hours on Monday, the Department of Homeland Security announced that it would be implementing a fee of over $103,000 on H-1B visas, and news broke that the State Department plans on revoking the visas of up to 200,000 asylum seekers — which, according to The Associated Press, would be the largest mass visa revocation in US history.

More than a year into President Donald Trump’s second term, it’s become clear that the only way Trump can get the deportation numbers he wants is by stripping legal immigrants of status. Beyond having ICE arrest, detain, and deport immigrants, the administration is pressuring noncitizens to “self-deport,” in some cases imposing civil fines on them and threatening to seize their assets. It’s creating legal hurdles not only for new legal immigrants but for those already in the country, and in the process, likely hurting businesses and social services nationwide.

H-1B visas are often seen as synonymous with Big Tech, in no small part because Amazon, Meta, and Microsoft are the three biggest employers of H-1B workers. A federal judge struck down Trump’s previous attempt to raise the cost of these high-skilled employment visas in June, but not until over 70 employers paid the $100,000 fee. Now Trump wants to raise the cost to $103,265. Advocates and business leaders are worried Trump will soon come after the Optional Practical Training (OPT) program, which DHS hinted may soon carry a $100,000 fee of its own. OPT lets international students work in their field of study for 12 months, with extensions of up to 24 months for some STEM students and additional extensions for holders of certain graduate degrees.

“Every single other pathway is harder, outlawed, eliminated, more bureaucratic, more difficult across the board.”

“This is clearly unlawful,” said Todd Schulte, the president of FWD.us, an immigration reform organization founded by Mark Zuckerberg and other tech executives in 2013. “We don’t have to guess what this is for. This is to get rid of the OPT and H-1B program, which will have upstream and downstream devastating consequences: companies will be started elsewhere, people will be hired elsewhere.”

This won’t just hurt the tech industry. The previous fee hike exacerbated labor shortages at rural hospitals across the country and Alaska public schools, both of which have increasingly turned to high-skilled immigrant workers in the wake of local population decline. If the $100,000 fee was an inconvenience for Amazon and Meta, it was utterly catastrophic for rural communities already having trouble attracting qualified candidates.

Foreign workers aren’t the only legal immigrants Trump is targeting. According to the AP, which broke the news, the State Department will rescind up to 200,000 business and travel visas issued between 2016 and 2026 to people who applied for asylum after arriving in the US. Beyond limiting their ability to travel outside the country, this move won’t change much for asylum seekers who came to the US on nonimmigrant visas — at least not for now. But Schulte said the visa revocations are part of Trump’s efforts to gut the humanitarian immigration system. “Every single other pathway is harder, outlawed, eliminated, more bureaucratic, more difficult across the board,” he said. “It’s an all-of-government approach.”

The administration is framing this change as a way of closing a loophole in the asylum system: people coming to the country on nonimmigrant visas, ostensibly for work or pleasure, only to ask for asylum upon setting foot in the country.

“We are coordinating with DHS to identify and revoke the nonimmigrant visas of foreigners who have come to the United States claiming to be short-term visitors, but then file for asylum to stay here permanently,” State Department spokesperson Tommy Pigott told the AP.

But the people who applied for asylum this way didn’t break any laws. In fact, a person needs to be present on US soil to apply for asylum; there’s no way to apply from outside the country. And Trump has closed most other avenues for humanitarian migration. There’s an effective “asylum ban” in place at the US-Mexico border. Refugee admissions have dropped to record lows, and the administration is now prioritizing the resettlement of white South Africans and denying almost everyone else.

In his second term, Trump has shown that the only immigrants he wants are those who look a certain way — or who can pay a small fortune for the privilege of working in America.

Tech.title: At just $8, you owe it to yourself to grab Inscryption
Tech.content:
is a tech journalist and commerce writer based out of Portland, Oregon. He’s contributed to sites like Digital Trends, Business Insider, and WIRED.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

If you watched the Gamescom 2026 announcements, you might have caught a trailer for the bizarre, frenetic Pony Island 2: Panda Circus, a game from Daniel Mullins. In case you haven’t heard of him, get a crash course with a fantastic discount on Inscryption. Humble is currently selling Steam versions of the secret-packed deckbuilder for $7.99, a sizable discount from its usual price of $20. It’s compatible with Windows, macOS, and Linux machines.

The game starts out as a fairly straightforward deckbuilding roguelike game with a dark atmosphere. Stick with it, and it’ll evolve, defying genres, breaking the fourth wall, and leading you through a twisted story with plenty of surprises. Part of the fun is discovering those twists yourself, so I won’t say anything else. It’s one of my personal favorite games, and it’s best to go in knowing as little as possible. Thankfully, taking the leap isn’t expensive at all.

Tech.title: The Witcher 3 is getting a remaster
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more. He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

CD Projekt Red is remastering The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt, the hit RPG that first launched in 2015, and the updated game will be available starting September 29th. The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt — Remastered will bring improvements to visuals and combat, a “reimagined” skill tree, and more, and it also includes the first two expansions, Hearts of Stone and Blood and Wine.

Remastered will be a free upgrade for players who own the base game on GOG, Steam, Epic Games Store, PlayStation 5, and Xbox Series X / S. With the launch of Remastered, The Witches 3 will also be coming to the Nintendo Switch 2.

This remastered version of The Witcher 3 (which follows a next-gen upgrade released in 2022) is the start of a big push for the franchise over the next few years. CDPR is set to launch a brand new Witcher 3 expansion, titled Songs of the Past, in 2027, and it’s aiming to release its next mainline Witcher game, The Witcher 4, in 2028.

Tech.title: Dreame’s dream of a rocket-powered car is dead
Tech.content:
is transportation editor with 10+ years of experience who covers EVs, public transportation, and aviation. His work has appeared in The New York Daily News and City & State.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Dreame, the Chinese vacuum company that aspires to be a global technology giant, is reportedly shutting down its automotive project after funding from the government dried up.

According to CarNewsChina, the company’s automotive division called “Project Starry Sky” once employed over 1,000 people, but now only a handful legal and HR staffers remain, charged with winding down the operation. In a statement, Dreame said it “recently adjusted certain operations that were in the exploratory phase,” and that going forward, it would focus on four key business areas: “smart home, outdoor/garden, smart mobility, and embodied AI.” (A spokesperson for the company didn’t respond to a request for comment.)

The news comes after China’s government issued new rules aimed at tightening oversight of the $3.4 trillion private fund industry, singling out Dreame in the process. After becoming one of the world’s largest manufacturer of vacuums, the company quickly moved into a variety of new businesses, spawning nearly a thousand affiliated ventures related to smartphones, robotics, and cars. But much of that expansion was funded by China’s government — and the government is now starting to take a closer look at how Dreame spends that money, according to CNBC.

The NEXT 01 JET Edition Car at the Dreame NEXT event during the Silicon Valley Summit at the Palace of Fine Arts on April 29, 2026 in San Francisco, CA. Photo by Kelsey McClellan / The Verge

Dreame wowed audiences at a San Francisco expo earlier this year with “Nebula Next 01 Jet Edition,” a sleek looking concept car equipped with a pair of rocket engines that theoretically can accelerate from 0 to 60 mph in 0.9 seconds. The vehicle was allegedly equipped with a sulfide-based solid-state battery with a record-breaking energy density exceeding 450 Wh/kg and a purported range of over 550 km (341.7 miles). The company claimed its boosters would deliver 100 kilo-Newtons of force.

But the concept raised a lot of questions, including some basic ones about how Dreame could make a car accelerate so quickly without breaking the laws of physics. Apparently Dreame didn’t have any answers to these questions, as the car itself was fully vaporware. Former employees told China Economy that the concept that was shown off in San Francisco lacked an actual chassis and was driven via remote control. (Concept cars are rarely “real” cars, in the technical sense — but even this is a little shocking in its level of deception.)

The news that Dreame’s vaporware car was totally vaporware will come as little shock to those familiar with the showy, boastful promises of companies that have never actually built a car suddenly deciding to build a car. Faraday Future, another Chinese companies with ambitions to build all manner of electric, autonomous vehicles, ran into this exact problem nearly a decade ago. And it also faced accusations of operating self-driving cars for public demos via offstage remote control.
